========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M3-OV/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M3-OV — narration

**video_id:** V-M3-OV  
**Title:** Module 3 overview: probability, models and simulation  
**Word count:** 1193  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 7:57 (target 6–8 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:32)

Welcome to Module 3 of FlippedStat: Probability, Distributions and Simulation. This is a short tour of the interactive site, with a few callouts on top of the pages. There is no filmed presenter. We will not cover every topic in the module, and we will not restage the later motion graphics on two conditionals, on Bayes, or on the law of large numbers. Where a page uses a course illustration, the site already labels it, and so will we.

## Beat 2 (0:32–1:35)

Here is the Module 3 page. The official title is Probability, Distributions and Simulation. When you finish this module, you should be able to use the addition and multiplication laws, and conditional probability, correctly; apply Bayes’ theorem to screening problems, and explain the role of base rates; model counts with the binomial and Poisson distributions, and measurements with the normal distribution; and use simulation to estimate a probability and judge when the estimate is stable. The module has eighteen topics. Marking a topic done is how the site records progress, and the module is complete when at least eighty percent of its topics are marked done. That completion rule is the same on every official module. Today we visit five pages: the multiplication law and two conditionals, Bayes’ theorem, the binomial, the normal, and simulation. When we reach named models we will also give a short, labelled pointer to Topic 6.3’s official Poisson illustration, without restaging that whole lesson.

## Beat 3 (1:35–2:40)

Topic 5.6 is the multiplication law and conditional probability. The student-facing official illustration is a two-way table of official 2025 mid-year land population, classed by region and by a FlippedStat gained-or-lost flag. The probability of a gained-population district given Kowloon is 1,535.3 over 2,242.7, or 68.5 percent. The other way around, the probability of Kowloon given a gained-population district, is 1,535.3 over 4,831.0, or 31.8 percent — not 68.5. Same joint count, different denominators. Those percentages are FlippedStat calculations on official figures, not official C and SD probabilities. A labelled course illustration on the same page uses 1,000 students and the same swap: 60 over 200 is 0.30, and 60 over 110 is 0.55. A later video, V-M3-COND, swaps those two slices on screen. The audit lab in Topic 5.10 is the same idea in a screening claim: “90% accurate” is not the same as “90% certain you have the condition.” The habit is to write the denominator before you trust the percentage.

## Beat 4 (2:40–3:35)

Topic 5.8 is total probability and Bayes’ theorem. A rare event, a sensitive test, and a positive result still do not give you the same number as the sensitivity. The positive predictive value also depends on the base rate — how common the condition was before the test. An independent check already on the page uses a 1,000-person table: sensitivity 0.90, specificity 0.90, prevalence 1%. Ten people have the condition, nine are true positives; 990 do not, and 99 are false positives. The positive predictive value is 9 over 108, which is 0.083. The next concept video, V-M3-BAYES, fills that table so the 9 over 108 is something you see, not only a fraction you are told. Topic 5.9 then changes the prevalence and watches the predictive value move, even though the test itself has not changed.

## Beat 5 (3:35–6:21)

Named models come next. Topic 6.2 is the binomial. A course illustration is a ten-question multiple-choice quiz with four options, so a guesser has p equal to 0.25. The probability of at least five correct is 0.078. The mean is 2.5 and the standard deviation is about 1.37. The binomial needs fixed n, two outcomes, constant p, and independent trials. Topic 6.3 is the Poisson. The official illustration is the number of June, July and August days, 2016 to 2025, with at least one official cloud-to-ground lightning record over Hong Kong: 30 month-counts, mean 17.17 days, sample variance 18.35, variance-to-mean ratio 1.07. Those are FlippedStat calculations on a derived table, not official Hong Kong Observatory statistics. Official daily stroke totals are not used as a constant-rate Poisson example, because storms cluster. Official annual live births from table 115-01012A were 60,856 in 2016 and 31,053 in 2025 — a changing-rate caution, not a Poisson fit. OpenIntro’s New York AMI figure stays a labelled book illustration. Topic 6.5 is the normal. The official illustration is the 920 official June–August daily mean temperatures at the Hong Kong Observatory, 2016 to 2025: mean 29.23 degrees Celsius, sample standard deviation 1.35 degrees. Of those 920 days, 633, or 68.8 percent, fall within one sample standard deviation of the mean; 875, or 95.1 percent, within two; and 918, or 99.8 percent, within three. That is a course illustration of a reasonably mound-shaped official measurement, not a claim that the official series is exactly normal. The full-year series is only a contrast, because the seasonal cycle makes it a poor normal-curve demonstration. SAT scores and US adult heights remain labelled book illustrations. The page still carries a simple course illustration — not an official Census and Statistics Department figure — that heights of Hong Kong adult men are roughly normal with mean 171 centimetres and standard deviation 6. A height of 183 centimetres is two standard deviations above 171, and about 2.3 percent of a normal curve sits beyond z = 2. Use that integer picture to write the rule; use the official summer temperatures to see a close, but not exact, empirical match. A normal approximation to a binomial is a later convenience, and only when both n p and n times one minus p are at least 10. A QQ-plot that is roughly straight is a visual check that data are close to normal. Name the variable, the units, and whether the illustration is official data or a course example.

## Beat 6 (6:21–7:31)

Topic 6.6 is simulation and the law of large numbers. Beside the classic birthday illustration — in a tutorial of 23 people, the exact probability that at least two share a birthday is 0.507 — the page now also uses a known official population proportion: 4,092.7 over 7,497.8, or 54.6 percent, the official 2025 New Territories share of mid-year land population. If simple random teaching samples of residents were drawn, the sample proportion living in the New Territories would settle toward that 54.6 percent as the sample grew. Those draws are FlippedStat teaching samples, not a C and SD survey. A Monte Carlo estimate should come with a seed, and with a sense of Monte Carlo error, which shrinks like one over the square root of the number of repetitions. The motion of a running proportion as it settles is already the subject of V-M3-SIM. Watch that video for the simulation itself. The habit to take from this page is: estimate, then judge whether the estimate is stable enough for the decision you need.

## Beat 7 (7:31–7:57)

That is the spine of Module 3: a law for combining probabilities, a table for base rates, named models you can defend, and a simulation you can repeat. Pause here, and open the pages yourself. The next videos stay with two conditionals, with the 1,000-person Bayes table, and — if you have not watched it yet — with the law of large numbers in motion.

- Binomial model, Topic 6.7: X ~ Binomial(1000, 0.001); P(X ≥ 3) = 0.0802. Seeded Python default_rng(1), R = 10,000: 0.0844, MC SE 0.0028, +1.5 SE. Seed 0: 0.0778. Seed 2: 0.0818. Unrecorded earlier seed: 0.0797 ± 0.0027. All 20 of 20 seeds on the page land within ±2 MC SE of 0.0802.
- Do not expect R’s set.seed(1) to match 0.0844; that caution is on the #codeprompt extension.
- Do not invent other probabilities or “typical” software output.

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M3-SIM/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M3-SIM — narration

**video_id:** V-M3-SIM  
**Title:** Simulation and the law of large numbers  
**Word count:** 875  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:50 (target 5–7 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:33)

This video is about simulation, and the law of large numbers, from Topics 6.6 and 6.7. When a probability is hard to see in a formula, you can write down the random process, play it many times, and count. That estimate is useful only if you know how precise it is, and only if the model is the one you meant. This is a motion graphic. There is no filmed presenter. The figures we use are the ones already keyed on those pages.

## Beat 2 (0:33–1:58)

Topic 6.6 calls this Monte Carlo simulation. You define the model and its assumptions; you simulate the process once; you repeat it R times; you summarise how often the event happened; and you report the Monte Carlo error. The proportion of repeats in which the event occurs estimates the probability. “The computer said so” is never a justification. The assumptions are. The page’s birthday illustration makes the settling visible: in a tutorial of 23 people, with 365 equally likely independent birthdays, the exact probability of a shared birthday is 0.507. After 10,000 simulated tutorials, the running proportion on the page is 0.499, sitting inside a band of plus or minus two Monte Carlo standard errors. The line wanders at first, and then it settles. That is the law of large numbers, on a screen. The same page now also uses a known official population proportion: 4,092.7 over 7,497.8, or 54.6 percent, the official 2025 New Territories share of mid-year land population. If simple random teaching samples of residents were drawn, the sample proportion living in the New Territories would settle toward that 54.6 percent as the sample grew. Those draws are FlippedStat teaching samples, not a C and SD survey, and official weather or birth series are not treated as independent draws.

## Beat 3 (1:58–2:48)

A simulation has to be reproducible, and it has to carry an error bar of its own. Computers produce pseudo-random numbers from a seed. The same seed, the same code, and the same software give the same results. Set the seed once, write it in the log, and never shop for a seed that looks nicer. The number of repeats, R, controls precision, not whether the model is right. Precision improves with the square root of R: a hundred times as many runs gives you about ten times smaller Monte Carlo error. For a proportion, that error is approximately the square root of p-hat times one minus p-hat, over R. Report the estimate plus or minus two of those standard errors, and round to match.

## Beat 4 (2:48–4:02)

Topic 6.7 puts a named model underneath the same habit. Each of 1,000 independent runs fails with probability 0.001, and the event of interest is three or more failures. If X follows a binomial distribution with those values of n and p, the exact probability that X is at least 3 is one minus the binomial cumulative probability at 2, which the page gives as 0.0802. That exact value is the referee. The simulation is a check of your code, and of Monte Carlo error. It is not a substitute for the exact tail. If an AI switches to a Poisson model, or to the event X greater than 3, that is a different question, and it must be labelled as one. Beside the lab, a parallel official-share illustration — not a replacement for 0.0802 — uses the official 2025 Islands mid-year land population, 198.4 thousand out of 7,497.8 thousand, or about 2.65 percent. If 50 residents were drawn independently from that official population, the probability of at least one Islands resident is about 74 percent. Do not swap that contrast for the 0.0802 lab key.

## Beat 5 (4:02–5:14)

Now watch a seeded run. With Python’s default_rng of 1, and R equals 10,000 repeats, the page’s estimate is 0.0844, with a Monte Carlo standard error of 0.0028 — about one and a half standard errors above 0.0802, which is consistent, and reproducible. The same page compares other seeds, still with 10,000 repeats: seed 0 gives 0.0778; seed 2 gives 0.0818. Neither is “wrong.” An earlier, unrecorded seed on a previous version of the topic printed 0.0797, plus or minus 0.0027 — consistent with the truth, but not reproducible, because no seed was logged. That is why the prompt must name the seed, and name R. Across twenty seeds on the page, all twenty estimates land within plus or minus two Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.0802. No seed was chosen for looks. One caution, also on the extension page: R’s set.seed of 1 is a different generator from numpy’s default_rng of 1. Do not treat a mismatch with 0.0844 as an error in the R run. Judge the R run against 0.0802, and against its own Monte Carlo error.

## Beat 6 (5:14–5:50)

So, when you prompt Copilot, Qwen or Grok for a simulation, name the model, the event, the seed, and R, and ask for the exact probability as well. Then check: is the event still X at least 3? Is the seed printed? Does the estimate sit within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.0802? A second AI that “agrees” on a rounded 0.08, with no seed, is not a check. Open Topic 6.6, Topic 6.7, and Task 2 on the extension page, and run the prompt yourself.

# V-M4-CLT — beats sheet

**video_id:** V-M4-CLT  
**Title:** Sampling distributions and the central limit theorem  
**Module / outcome:** Module 4 — explain sampling distributions and the CLT through simulation.  
**Format:** motion-graphics (digital blackboard allowed). No live-action people.  
**Target length:** 5–7 minutes  
**Draft length (at 150 wpm):** 6:12 (target 5–7 minutes)  
**Source pages:** Topics 7.2, 7.3.  
**Why this is a video:** The sampling distribution has to be built from repeated samples.  

## Beats

| # | Time | What is on screen | Narration job (one sentence) | On-screen words / colour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0:00–0:28 | Title on a blackboard. “Motion graphics. Topics 7.2 and 7.3.” | Say that a sampling distribution is a thought experiment we can watch being built. | Title in navy; source line in muted grey |
| 2 | 0:28–1:09 | Many small samples are drawn from a population and each mean is dropped onto a growing histogram. Labels: centre, spread (SE), shape. Caption: “each bar counts sample means, not people.” | Define sampling variability and the sampling distribution, and name its centre, spread and shape. | Population in navy; sample means as teal dots; histogram in teal; “not people” in amber |

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M4-CLT/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M4-CLT — narration

**video_id:** V-M4-CLT  
**Title:** Sampling distributions and the central limit theorem  
**Word count:** 930  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 6:12 (target 5–7 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:28)

This video is about sampling distributions, and the central limit theorem, from Topics 7.2 and 7.3. In real life you get one sample, and one statistic. A sampling distribution is the thought experiment that tells you how far that one statistic is likely to be from the thing it estimates. We will build it on screen. There is no filmed presenter. The figures come from those two topic pages.

## Beat 2 (0:28–1:09)

A statistic varies from sample to sample. That is sampling variability. The distribution of a statistic, over all possible samples of the same size, is its sampling distribution. Three things about it matter: its centre — does it aim at the parameter, or is it biased? — its spread, which we call the standard error, and its shape, which is often approximately normal, for a reason we will come to. Simulation lets you see the distribution: draw thousands of samples from a known population, and plot the statistic. Each bar in that plot counts sample means, or sample proportions — not individual people.

## Beat 3 (1:09–2:22)

The standard error is the standard deviation of a statistic’s sampling distribution. Roughly, it is the typical distance between the statistic and the parameter. For a mean, it is sigma over square root of n, or s over square root of n if sigma is unknown. For a proportion, it is the square root of p-hat times one minus p-hat, over n. Standard deviation and standard error are easy to confuse. A standard deviation describes how individuals vary. A standard error describes how a statistic varies. If you write “mean 6.6 hours, SD 1.2,” you are telling readers about people. If you write “mean 6.6 hours, SE 0.24,” you are telling them about precision. Error bars must say which they show. The standard error shrinks with the square root of n. Double n, and the standard error is only about twenty-nine percent smaller. Quadruple n, and it halves. The first few hundred observations buy a lot; later thousands buy much less. And when the population is much larger than the sample, precision depends on n, not on how large the population is.

## Beat 4 (2:22–3:40)

Topic 7.2 has two pictures worth watching. In one, two thousand samples of twenty-five measurements are drawn, and the standard deviation of those two thousand means is 0.243 hours, against a theoretical sigma-over-square-root-n of 0.240 hours. Bigger samples would narrow the same picture, without moving its centre. In another, ten thousand simulated sample proportions are drawn, with a population proportion of 0.88 and n of 1,000. That histogram is a sampling distribution. Its centre is 0.880 — the parameter itself — its spread is 0.010, the standard error of the sample proportion, and its shape is symmetric and bell-shaped. These are the course’s illustrations, including a poll example used to show the idea. They are not a claim about a current public-opinion result. The same page now also uses a known official population proportion: 4,092.7 over 7,497.8, or 54.6 percent, the official 2025 New Territories share. For simple random teaching samples of n = 400, the sampling distribution of that share is centred at 54.6 percent, with a standard error of about 0.0249, or about 2.5 percentage points. Those are FlippedStat calculations, not official C and SD standard errors, and not a C and SD survey.

## Beat 5 (3:40–5:20)

Why the bell? That is the central limit theorem, in Topic 7.3. For a random sample of n independent observations from a population with mean mu and a finite standard deviation sigma, the sample mean is approximately normal, with mean mu and standard deviation sigma over square root of n, when n is large enough. The intuition is that averaging cancels extremes. The same idea holds for sums, and for proportions, which are averages of zeros and ones. How large is “large enough” depends on the population’s shape. If the population is already normal, any n will do. Mild skew might need something like 15 to 30. Strong skew or heavy tails can need hundreds. “n at least 30” is a teaching rule of thumb, not a law. Look at the data, or simulate. The page uses a Hong Kong dollar example: daily spending that is strongly right-skewed, with a population mean of 80 dollars and a standard deviation of 80 dollars. Watch, on the page, as the sampling distribution of the mean becomes more bell-shaped as n grows. At moderate n, a little skew can remain, and normal-based intervals can cover a little less often than they claim. The official 54.6 percent share in a teaching sample of n = 400 also satisfies the success-failure counts — about 218 and 182 — so the normal approximation for that sample proportion is reasonable. Official daily weather and monthly birth series are not treated as independent draws for this argument.

## Beat 6 (5:20–6:12)

The theorem has a sharp limit, and Topic 7.3 is frank about it. The central limit theorem covers random sampling error only. It does not fix bias, dependence, or a non-random sample. With a large biased sample, standard errors become tiny while the bias stays put — very precise intervals around the wrong value. The page calls this a “big data paradox.” Students in the same class, repeated measures, and time series also break the simple sigma-over-square-root-n formula. So when an AI reports a confidence interval, check the design first. A formula applied to a biased sample gives confident nonsense, which this course would code as H4: over-reach. Open Topic 7.2 and Topic 7.3, and watch the sampling distribution being built, rather than only reading the statement of the theorem.

# V-M4-COVER — beats sheet

**video_id:** V-M4-COVER  
**Title:** What “95% confidence” actually covers  
**Module / outcome:** Module 4 — interpret a confidence interval.  
**Format:** motion-graphics (digital blackboard allowed). No live-action people.  
**Target length:** 4–6 minutes  
**Draft length (at 150 wpm):** 5:06 (target 4–6 minutes)  
**Source pages:** Topics 7.6, 7.7. Coverage illustration: 24 of 25 simulated solar-poll intervals capture p = 0.88 (Topic 7.6 / FSA, course illustration, not a current poll). One-sample mean interval: Topic 7.7 sleep illustration.  
**Why this is a video:** Coverage is a long-run property; only animation shows intervals catching, or missing, a fixed value.

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M4-COVER/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M4-COVER — narration

**video_id:** V-M4-COVER  
**Title:** What “95% confidence” actually covers  
**Word count:** 766  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:06 (target 4–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:26)

This video is about what “95% confidence” actually covers. It is a motion graphic. There is no filmed presenter. The numbers come from Topics 7.6 and 7.7. They are course illustrations, not a current poll and not a real sleep study. The parameter we are estimating — a population mean, or a population proportion — will stay still on the screen. The intervals will move.

## Beat 2 (0:26–1:14)

A sentence you will meet on the page sounds like this: “We are 95% confident the mean is between 6.2 and 7.0 hours.” What is the 95% about? It is not that the true mean is a moving target with a 95% chance of landing in this interval. The true value is fixed, whether or not we know it. The randomness is in the sample, and therefore in the interval the sample produces. In repeated samples, 95% of intervals built this way contain the true value. Any one interval either contains it, or it does not. We do not get to say, of a single finished interval, that there is still a 95% chance the mean will wander into it.

## Beat 3 (1:14–2:43)

Topic 7.6 has a picture you can count. In 25 simulated solar polls, 24 of the 95% intervals capture the population proportion 0.88, and one misses. The 0.88 is the same course illustration used with the sampling-distribution topic — it is not a current poll, and we will not treat it as one. One miss in 25 does not prove that the population proportion could not be 0.88. A 95% method is expected to miss about five times in 100, or about once in a display of this size. The page’s hook also speaks of 100 simulated intervals, of which about 95 cover and about 5 miss. That “about” is the idea. This video will not invent a tally from a 100-run widget that is not keyed in the teaching text. Count the 24 and the 1 that the page already gives you. The same coverage claim can be told with a known official parameter. If we repeatedly drew simple random teaching samples of n = 400 and built a 95 percent Wald interval for the New Territories share, about 95 percent of those intervals would contain the official 54.6 percent. Any one interval either does or does not contain that official share. The official table is not itself an interval, and these intervals would not be official C and SD estimates.

## Beat 4 (2:43–3:23)

Two things change the width, and they pull in different directions. Larger n shrinks the standard error, like the square root of the sample size, so the intervals get narrower. A higher confidence level uses a larger critical value, so the intervals get wider. You cannot have a very short interval and 99% coverage from the same small sample without changing the method. And coverage, as the page reminds you, is about sampling error under the stated conditions. It does not protect you from bias. Careful data collection is still the only protection against a sample that systematically misses people.

## Beat 5 (3:23–4:48)

Topic 7.7 builds one such interval for a mean. The course illustration is the sleep of 16 students: the sample mean is 6.6 hours, the sample standard deviation is 1.2, and we want a 95% interval. The formula is the mean plus or minus a t critical value, with n minus 1 degrees of freedom, times s over square root of n. Here t star is 2.131, the standard error is 0.3, and 2.131 times 0.3 is a margin of 0.64, or 0.639 in Excel’s CONFIDENCE.T of 0.05, 1.2 and 16. The interval is 5.96 to 7.24 hours. That interval either covers the population mean or it does not. We report it, we state the confidence level and the n, and we do not say that 95% of students sleep between 5.96 and 7.24 hours. An interval for a mean is not a range for individual observations, and it is not a prediction of the next sample mean. Beside that sleep illustration, Topic 7.7 also has a labelled synthetic teaching sample: six quiet-floor quiz scores with mean 75.67 and a 95 percent t interval of about 71.4 to 80.0 points. That sample is not official CUHK data, and official district medians were not used as if they were a random sample of people.

## Beat 6 (4:48–5:06)

So, 95% confidence is a claim about a method in the long run, not a claim that a fixed parameter will now jump into this interval. Open Topic 7.6 and generate intervals you can count; open Topic 7.7 and recompute the 16-student sleep interval yourself.

# V-M4-OV — narration

**video_id:** V-M4-OV  
**Title:** Module 4 overview: estimation and testing  
**Word count:** 1111  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 7:24 (target 6–8 minutes)

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:33)

Welcome to Module 4 of FlippedStat: Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. This is a short tour of the interactive site, with a few callouts on top of the pages. There is no filmed presenter. We will not cover every topic in the module, and we will not restage the later motion graphics on the central limit theorem, on what a p-value is not, or on what 95% confidence actually covers. Where a page uses a course illustration, it is labelled, and so will we.

## Beat 2 (0:33–1:36)

Here is the Module 4 page. The official title is Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. When you finish this module, you should be able to explain sampling distributions and the central limit theorem through simulation; construct and interpret confidence intervals for means, proportions and differences; carry out and interpret t, chi-square and one-way ANOVA tests, and choose a test for a design; state what a p-value does not mean, and discuss power, effect size and multiple comparisons; and audit an AI-produced test report for the wrong test, the wrong data, or an overclaim. The module has twenty-two topics. Marking a topic done is how the site records progress, and the module is complete when at least eighty percent of its topics are marked done. That completion rule is the same on every official module. Today we visit five pages: sampling distributions, confidence intervals, the anatomy of a test, what p-values do not mean, and choosing a test.

## Beat 3 (1:36–2:56)

Topic 7.2 is sampling distributions. A statistic varies from sample to sample; the distribution of that statistic is the sampling distribution, and its standard deviation is the standard error. For a sample mean, the standard error is sigma over square root of n, so four times the sample size halves the standard error. A hook on the page asks you to imagine 1,000 samples of 25 students each, and to look at the pile of means. The page also uses a known official population proportion: 4,092.7 over 7,497.8, or 54.6 percent, the official 2025 New Territories share. For simple random teaching samples of n = 400, the sampling distribution of that share is centred at 54.6 percent, with a standard error of about 0.0249. Those are FlippedStat calculations, not official C and SD standard errors, and not a C and SD survey. The motion of building the pile, and the central limit theorem that describes it, is already the subject of V-M4-CLT, including the page’s sleep and proportion illustrations. Take from this tour only the habit: before you interpret one mean, or one interval, remember that it came from a process that would have moved if you had drawn another sample.

## Beat 4 (2:56–4:36)

Topic 7.6 is confidence intervals and coverage. When we say we are 95% confident that a mean lies between two numbers, the 95% is about the method: in repeated samples, 95% of intervals built this way contain the true value. Any one interval either contains it or not. The value we are estimating does not jump into the interval. Width shrinks with the square root of n, and grows if you ask for more confidence. In the teaching experiment that uses the official 54.6 percent New Territories share as a known parameter, repeated 95 percent Wald intervals from n = 400 teaching samples would cover that official share about 95 percent of the time. The official table is not itself an interval. A later video, V-M4-COVER, animates that long-run picture, including a keyed illustration of 25 simulated intervals at the course proportion 0.88. Topic 7.7 then builds a 95% interval for a mean. The course illustration is the sleep of 16 students: mean 6.6 hours, standard deviation 1.2. The critical t, with 15 degrees of freedom, is 2.131; the standard error is 0.3; the margin is 0.64; the interval is 5.96 to 7.24 hours. Excel’s CONFIDENCE.T of 0.05, 1.2 and 16 gives 0.639, which is that same margin. Those 16 students are a course illustration, not a real sleep study. Beside them, a labelled synthetic hostel quiz sample on the same page gives a 95 percent t interval of about 71.4 to 80.0 points; that sample is not official CUHK data.

## Beat 5 (4:36–5:57)

Topic 8.1 is the anatomy of a hypothesis test. The page’s hook is a coin that lands heads 16 times in 20. The null is the “nothing special” claim — here, a fair coin, p = 0.5. The alternative is what you suspected, preferably before you saw the data. A test statistic summarises the evidence. The p-value is the probability of a statistic at least this extreme, computed in the world where the null is true. For this coin, the two-sided probability is given on the page as about 0.012, and V-M4-PVAL uses the keyed figure 0.0118 for the two tails together. Topic 8.2 is what p-values do not mean. A p-value is not the probability that the null is true. It is not the probability that the results were “due to chance.” It is not an effect size. A p-value larger than 0.05 is not proof of no effect. Statistical significance is not the same as practical importance: the page’s illustration uses two huge groups and a difference of 0.1 marks that is detectable only because n is enormous. The motion that stops the “probability the null is true” reading is V-M4-PVAL. Watch that video before you memorise a flowchart.

## Beat 6 (5:57–7:01)

Topic 8.7 is choosing a test. Ask three questions: is the outcome numerical or categorical; how many groups are there; and are the observations independent or paired? For a numerical outcome, one group leads to a t interval or a t test; two independent groups to a two-sample t; a before-and-after on the same people to a paired t; three or more groups to one-way ANOVA. For a categorical outcome, a chi-square test of independence — or Fisher’s exact test when counts are small — and, for paired binary data, McNemar’s test. The worked case on the page is pass or fail in three independent groups: a chi-square test of independence on a two-by-three table. In this course, Welch’s t-test is the default two-sample t, as elsewhere on the site and in R. An AI that “just runs a t-test” has not answered those three questions for you. Audit the choice, and audit the claim the output is asked to support.

## Beat 7 (7:01–7:24)

That is the spine of Module 4: a sampling distribution, an interval whose coverage is a long-run property, a test whose p-value lives in the null world, and a chooser you can defend. Pause here, and open the pages yourself. The next videos stay with coverage, if you have not watched the CLT and p-value films already.

# V-M4-PVAL — beats sheet

**video_id:** V-M4-PVAL  
**Title:** What a p-value is not  
**Module / outcome:** Module 4 — state what a p-value does not mean, and report an effect size with a CI.  
**Format:** motion-graphics (digital blackboard allowed). No live-action people.  
**Target length:** 5–7 minutes  
**Draft length (at 150 wpm):** 5:03 (target 5–7 minutes)  
**Source pages:** Topics 8.1, 8.2, 8.3.  
**Why this is a video:** A repeating-sample picture stops the “probability the null is true” reading.  

## Beats

| # | Time | What is on screen | Narration job (one sentence) | On-screen words / colour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0:00–0:22 | Title on a blackboard. “What a p-value is not. Topics 8.1, 8.2, 8.3.” | Announce the job: define p, then dismantle the usual misreadings. | Title in navy; source line in muted grey |
| 2 | 0:22–1:49 | Anatomy diagram: H0 and H1 about a population, a test statistic, a null distribution, a tail probability labelled p. “Two-sided is the default.” “0.05 is a convention, not a law.” | Give the Topic 8.1 definition and the reporting rules, including the two-sided default. | H0 / H1 in navy; tail in teal; p in teal; “not a proof” in amber; “p-hacking” in red |
| 3 | 1:49–2:20 | A binomial picture for 20 fair tosses. Tails at 16 or more, and 4 or fewer, shaded in teal. On screen: P = 0.0118, “about 1.2% of the time, if the coin were fair.” A red cross through “so the coin is unfair with probability 98.8%.” | Use the fair-coin illustration as a correctly worded p-value, and block the inverse reading. | 0.0118 in green; inverse reading in red; “if the coin were fair” in navy |
| 4 | 2:20–3:09 | Three crossed-out sentences in red: “P(H0 | data)”; “due to chance”; “1 − p = the effect is real.” The definition stays in green: P(data at least this extreme | H0). | State, clearly, what a p-value is not. | Definition in green; three misreadings in red; “confusion of the inverse” in amber |
| 5 | 3:09–4:22 | A flat histogram of p-values under H0, from the page’s 3,000-study simulation: 5.5% below 0.05. Then the “real effect, d = 0.5, n = 30” histogram, with 47.7% below 0.05. Labels for Type I, Type II and power. | Show that p is uniform under the null, and that a real effect can still be missed in a small study, using the page’s simulation figures. | 5.5% and the flat histogram in teal; 47.7% in navy; “page simulation” in muted grey; Type I in amber; Type II in red |
| 6 | 4:22–5:03 | “Significant ≠ important” in navy. A tiny effect with huge n gets a star, in amber; a large effect with small n does not. End card: #t/8.1, #t/8.2, #t/8.3. Version line. | Separate statistical from practical significance, and point back to the pages. | “Significant ≠ important” in amber; “effect size + CI in units” in teal; hashes in teal; “FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.0-dev” in muted grey |

## Production notes

- Fair coin, 20 tosses: P(≥ 16 or ≤ 4) = 0.0118, on Topic 8.1. Keep the wording “if the coin were fair.”
- Topic 8.2 simulation: 3,000 studies with no effect, p flat, 5.5% below 0.05 (a finite-simulation stand-in for the designed 5%). With d = 0.5, n = 30: 47.7% below 0.05. Always call these “the page’s simulation.”
- Do not invent a specific medical or CUHK study as the running example.
- Welch’s t-test is not needed in this video; if a two-sample t appears in a later cut, Welch is the default.
- Palette: navy text, teal highlights, amber warnings, red for errors, green for a verified number. High contrast. Captions live in `captions.vtt`, not burned in until access-checked.
- Voice: one warm narrator, English, conversational, no jokes at students’ expense. Cantonese / Traditional Chinese versions come later.
- Do not show real student data, CUHK logos in a way that implies approval, or invented policy text. Label synthetic data as synthetic.

# V-M4-PVAL — narration

**video_id:** V-M4-PVAL  
**Title:** What a p-value is not  
**Word count:** 758  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:03 (target 5–7 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:22)

This video is about what a p-value is, and, just as important, what a p-value is not. The source pages are Topics 8.1, 8.2 and 8.3. We will watch repeated samples under a null hypothesis, because that is the only way the definition stays honest. There is no filmed presenter.

## Beat 2 (0:22–1:49)

Topic 8.1 sets the anatomy. A hypothesis test compares two statements about a population or a process: the null, H-nought, which is “nothing special,” and which carries an equals sign; and the alternative, H-one, which is what you suspect. Hypotheses are never about the sample. You can already see the sample. A test statistic measures how far the data sit from the null, usually in standard errors. The null distribution is the sampling distribution of that statistic if the null is true, from theory or from a simulation — for example, by shuffling group labels. The p-value is the probability, computed assuming the null is true, of a statistic at least as extreme as the one you observed. A small p-value means the data would be surprising if the null were true, and that is evidence against the null. It is not a proof. A pre-chosen significance level alpha, often 0.05, can turn p into a decision, but 0.05 is a convention, not a law. Report the exact p, with the estimate and a confidence interval. Two-sided tests are the default in this course. A one-sided test is justified only if the direction was fixed before the data were seen, and switching after you see the direction is p-hacking.

## Beat 3 (1:49–2:20)

Here is a small picture from the page. For a fair coin, in twenty tosses, the probability of sixteen or more heads, or four or fewer, is 0.0118. If the coin were fair, results this lopsided would happen about 1.2 percent of the time. That sentence is already a p-value: it is a probability of data at least this extreme, computed from the null. It is not the probability that the coin is fair.

## Beat 4 (2:20–3:09)

That last confusion is the one Topic 8.2 exists to stop. The p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme, given the null. It is not the probability that the null is true, given the data. It is not “the chance the result is due to chance.” And one minus p is not the probability that the effect is real. Moving from the probability of the data given the null, to the probability of the null given the data, needs Bayes’ theorem and a prior. That is the confusion of the inverse again, from earlier in the course. A p-value also says nothing about how large or how important an effect is. That is the next point.

## Beat 5 (3:09–4:22)

Watch what happens when the null is actually true. Under the null, p-values are uniform: five percent fall below 0.05, by design. In the page’s simulation of three thousand studies with no effect, the histogram of p is flat, and 5.5 percent fall below 0.05 — close to the designed five percent, in a finite simulation. That is not a scandal. That is the definition at work. Switch the same picture to a real effect, of size d equals 0.5, with n equals 30, and the page finds that 47.7 percent of studies have p below 0.05. A little under half still miss it. So a non-significant result, especially in a small study, is not a demonstration that nothing is going on. Topic 8.3 names the two errors: a Type I error is a false alarm, rejecting a true null, with probability alpha; a Type II error is a missed effect, with probability beta; and power is one minus beta. Power rises with the effect size, with n, with alpha, and with lower variability.

## Beat 6 (4:22–5:03)

Statistical significance is evidence of a non-zero effect. Practical significance is an effect large enough to matter. A large n can make a tiny effect statistically significant. A small n can hide an important one. Always report an effect size, with a confidence interval, in meaningful units, and compare that interval with a threshold of practical importance agreed in advance. “Significant” in a headline usually means statistical, not important. Open Topics 8.1, 8.2 and 8.3, and, when an AI hands you a p-value, ask first: the probability of what, given what, and how large was the effect?

# V-M5-CONF — narration

**video_id:** V-M5-CONF  
**Title:** Correlation, confounding and the missing third variable  
**Word count:** 820  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:28 (target 5–7 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:28)

This video is about correlation, confounding, and the missing third variable, from Topics 9.7 and 11.3. A tight scatter can be real, and still not mean what a headline wants it to mean. We will watch a third variable rearrange a picture. There is no filmed presenter. When we use a number from the pages, we will treat it as a course example, not as a study of real students.

## Beat 2 (0:28–1:23)

Topic 9.7 starts with Pearson’s r, which describes linear association in the sample. Inference is about the population correlation, rho. In the course’s worked example, r is 0.30 between exercise and sleep quality, in a sample of 50. The t statistic is 0.30 times the square root of 48, over the square root of 0.91, which equals 2.18, on 48 degrees of freedom, with p equal to 0.034. A ninety-five percent confidence interval for rho runs from 0.02 to 0.53, and it is not symmetric. Those figures answer a narrow question: is a linear association of this size distinguishable from zero, in this sample, under the usual conditions? They do not say that exercise improves sleep, and they do not describe a relationship that is curved.

## Beat 3 (1:23–2:33)

r measures linear association only. An r near zero means “no straight-line association.” It does not mean “no relationship.” A U-shape can have an r near zero, and Spearman’s rank correlation, which is Pearson’s r computed on the ranks, can miss a U-shape too. Always plot first, and describe a curve in words. In AI output, watch for the leap “no correlation, therefore no relationship,” which this course would code as H2 or H4. Two other limits sit on the same page. If a sample covers only part of the range of x — only admitted students, or only the top of a score — r is usually smaller than in the full range, even when the underlying relationship is unchanged. And one outlier, especially one that is extreme in both x and y, can create, destroy, or reverse a correlation. Points with extreme x have high leverage. Plot, identify, check for a data error, and, if the conclusion changes, report the correlation with and without the point. Never delete it silently.

## Beat 4 (2:33–3:23)

Even a straight, well-behaved scatter can still mislead, if a third variable is at work. Topic 11.3 is about confounding in regression, but the same idea applies to a correlation. A confounder is related to both x and y. Left out, its association leaks into the relationship you think you are looking at. If it is positively related to both, the simple association is too large, and adjusting for the confounder shrinks it. If it is positively related to one and negatively to the other, the simple association can be too small, or even the wrong sign. The direction of that bias is the product of those two signs. You can only adjust for a confounder you have measured. Adjustment is not randomisation.

## Beat 5 (3:23–4:29)

Watch a slope move. In a worked example from Lab 11.6, on the Topic 11.3 page, a simple slope of quiz score on minutes is 0.316; once a prior measure is added, the slope is 0.116. The association shrank, because a variable related to both had been sitting in the background. The page also recalls a classic pattern: an association between coffee and heart disease that largely disappears once smoking is adjusted for, because smokers drank more coffee. That is the third variable, in words. A more dramatic version is Simpson’s paradox: an association in the combined data reverses when you split by a third variable, because the groups differ greatly in their mix of that variable. The page’s hospital-style sketch is of one unit that treats mostly severe cases, and another that treats mostly mild ones. The unit with the harder case mix can look worse overall, even if, within each level of severity, it does not.

## Beat 6 (4:29–5:28)

What adjustment cannot fix is just as important. It cannot fix unmeasured confounders, measurement error, or reverse causation. It should not be used, if you want a total effect, by adjusting for a mediator that sits on the path from x to y; and it can be harmed by adjusting for a collider, a consequence of both x and y. Only randomisation balances the confounders you did not measure. So, when an AI describes a correlation, or a regression slope, with a causal verb, stop. Ask what else could be related to both, and whether the design can support the verb. Open Topic 9.7 and Topic 11.3, and, if you want to prompt a model to fit a line, remember the rule from the extension page: ask for the coefficients and the residuals, and do not ask the model to invent a causal story.

---

Plot, identify, check for a data error, and, if the conclusion changes, report the correlation with and without the point. Never delete it silently.

Even a straight, well-behaved scatter can still mislead, if a third variable is at work. Topic 11.3 is about confounding in regression, but the same idea applies to a correlation. A confounder is related to both x and y. Left out, its association leaks into the relationship you think you are looking at. If it is positively related to both, the simple association is too large, and adjusting for the confounder shrinks it. If it is positively related to one and negatively to the other, the simple association can be too small, or even the wrong sign. The direction of that bias is the product of those two signs. You can only adjust for a confounder you have measured. Adjustment is not randomisation.

Watch a slope move. In a worked example from Lab 11.6, on the Topic 11.3 page, a simple slope of quiz score on minutes is 0.316; once a prior measure is added, the slope is 0.116. The association shrank, because a variable related to both had been sitting in the background. The page also recalls a classic pattern: an association between coffee and heart disease that largely disappears once smoking is adjusted for, because smokers drank more coffee. That is the third variable, in words. A more dramatic version is Simpson’s paradox: an association in the combined data reverses when you split by a third variable, because the groups differ greatly in their mix of that variable. The page’s hospital-style sketch is of one unit that treats mostly severe cases, and another that treats mostly mild ones. The unit with the harder case mix can look worse overall, even if, within each level of severity, it does not.

What adjustment cannot fix is just as important. It cannot fix unmeasured confounders, measurement error, or reverse causation. It should not be used, if you want a total effect, by adjusting for a mediator that sits on the path from x to y; and it can be harmed by adjusting for a collider, a consequence of both x and y. Only randomisation balances the confounders you did not measure. So, when an AI describes a correlation, or a regression slope, with a causal verb, stop. Ask what else could be related to both, and whether the design can support the verb. Open Topic 9.7 and Topic 11.3, and, if you want to prompt a model to fit a line, remember the rule from the extension page: ask for the coefficients and the residuals, and do not ask the model to invent a causal story.

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M5-LEAK/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M5-LEAK — narration

**video_id:** V-M5-LEAK  
**Title:** Prediction is not explanation, and training is not the test  
**Word count:** 751  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:00 (target 5–7 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:46)

This video is about two separations that are easy to blur: prediction is not explanation, and a training set is not a test set. It is a site screencast of FlippedStat v10.4-dev, with a few callouts. There is no filmed presenter. The library, student-day and default examples are the course illustrations already on Topics 12.1 to 12.4. They are not real student records and not a real bank file. We will use figures the student pages already show. We will not invent a collapse of “89%”; the keyed split on the page is 89.8% against 48.8%. Record the site version in your log: this pass should be recorded on v10.4-dev, not on an older standalone.

## Beat 2 (0:46–1:45)

Topic 12.1 asks whether a university should mandate library visits, because a model predicts exam failure well from the number of visits. Loss functions tell you how wrong predictions are penalised — squared error, absolute error, or a misclassification. Training error, computed on the same rows the model already saw, is optimistic. Test error on new data is what you should care about. But even an honest test error does not turn a predictor into a cause. Visits may mark students who were already going to sit down and work. If you mandate visits, you change what the predictor means. Good prediction is not, by itself, a reason to intervene as if you had run an experiment. The same warning applies to any “risk score” built from a behaviour people already chose. If you change the behaviour, you may change the relationship you were using to predict.

## Beat 3 (1:45–3:04)

Topic 12.2 is validation and leakage. The hook is a random train–test split of 5,000 rows of daily data: 50 students, each with 100 days, and an accuracy of 89.8%. Why might that number be fake? Because the same student’s days can land in both the training set and the test set. The model can memorise the student. When the page holds out whole students, the accuracy is 48.8% — no better than chance. Deploying to new students would give you the second number, not the first. A holdout keeps a test set untouched until the end. k-fold cross-validation rotates the test fold and averages the error. Grouped splits keep every row of a student together. Time-ordered splits train on the past and test on the future. Leakage is a predictor that already contains the answer, or that comes from after the outcome was known. Switch the folds on the page, and watch the estimate move. k-fold is not a licence to ignore groups or time. If days are nested in students, or months are nested in years, a random shuffle of rows is the kind of convenient split that produces the 89.8% and hides the 48.8%.

## Beat 4 (3:04–4:20)

Topic 12.3 is baselines and metrics. Only 2% of applicants default, in the page’s illustration. A model that is 98% accurate may simply be predicting “no default” for everyone. That majority baseline already has 98% accuracy, and recall of 0: it never catches a default. Precision and recall, from a confusion matrix, tell you what the accuracy hid. Topic 12.4 is an audit lab on a dropout model that is “98% accurate, so it works.” The student page already states the worked figures we need: the base rate is 2%; the majority baseline accuracy is 98%; a leakage column, withdrawal_form_date, is there to be found; and recall for the positive class, once leakage is removed, is 0.25. Compare with the baseline before you congratulate the model, and ask whether any column could only have been known after the outcome. A date of withdrawal, a field filled in at exit, or a label that already contains the answer will travel with the row into any random split. Grouping and time-ordering are not polish. They are how you stop the test set from quietly seeing the future, or seeing the same person twice.

## Beat 5 (4:20–5:00)

So, a model can predict without explaining, and a random split can flatter you. For this course illustration, the number to remember is not 89.8%. It is 48.8%, once whole students are held out. Open Topic 12.1, Topic 12.2, Topic 12.3 and the audit lab in Topic 12.4, switch the split yourself on the v10.4-dev site, and write down both accuracies — 89.8% and 48.8% — in the same log, with the split rule that produced each one, and with a short note that agreement between two tools on the first number is still not itself the independent check you need.

- log(rent) = 8.1 + 0.012 × area (≈ +1.2% per m²) is the Topic 10.5 course illustration, not an official rent series.
- Leakage hook (5,000 rows; 50 students × 100 days; 89.8% random-row accuracy vs 48.8% when whole students are held out) is on Topic 12.2; the full screencast is V-M5-LEAK. Use 89.8%, not a rounded 89%.

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M5-OV/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M5-OV — narration

**video_id:** V-M5-OV  
**Title:** Module 5 overview: correlation, regression and prediction  
**Word count:** 992  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 6:37 (target 6–8 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:26)

Welcome to Module 5 of FlippedStat: Correlation, Regression and Prediction. This is a short tour of the interactive site, with a few callouts on top of the pages. There is no filmed presenter. We will not cover every topic, and we will not restage the later videos on confounding, on residuals and influence, or on leakage. Course illustrations stay labelled. Synthetic files stay labelled synthetic.

## Beat 2 (0:26–1:12)

Here is the Module 5 page. The official title is Correlation, Regression and Prediction. When you finish this module, you should be able to interpret correlation and explain its limits, including confounding; fit, interpret and diagnose simple and multiple linear regression models; identify outliers, leverage and influence, and report their effect on conclusions; and distinguish prediction from explanation, and validate predictions on held-out data. The module has twenty-three topics. The module is complete when at least eighty percent of its topics are marked done, as on every official module. Today we visit six pages: correlation and its limits, the simple linear model, residuals and R-squared, residual diagnostics, prediction versus explanation, and validation and leakage.

## Beat 3 (1:12–2:19)

Topic 9.7 is correlation and its limits. Pearson’s r measures linear association. Spearman’s rho is the correlation of ranks: it tracks a monotone pattern and is more resistant to outliers. A curve can hide from r. A single extreme point can make or break it. And correlation, by itself, is not a cause. The motion of a lurking variable rearranging a scatter is already V-M5-CONF, including the page’s worked correlation example and the confounding lab. This tour will not use the restriction-of-range numbers that sit under an audit-gap flag on Topic 9.7.4, because that subsection still has no textbook source. The idea that a narrower range can shrink r can wait until that gap is closed, or until you read the flag on the page yourself. What you can already take from Topic 9.7 is the habit: look at the scatter, not only at r; compare Pearson with Spearman when a point or a curve is in play; and do not let a correlation sentence grow a causal verb.

## Beat 4 (2:19–4:18)

Topic 10.1 is the simple linear model: y equals beta 0 plus beta 1 x plus error. The conditions have a mnemonic, LINE: linearity of the mean, independence of errors, normal errors — which matters most for inference in small samples — and equal variance. Every later calculation on these pages uses the fitted line from revision_quiz.csv: y-hat equals 60.15 plus 0.610 times hours, with a residual standard deviation of 7.39. That file is a course illustration, not a real quiz log. Topic 10.3 is residuals and R-squared. A residual is y minus y-hat. R-squared is the share of the variance in y that the line explains. On this fit, the slope is 0.61 points per hour, and R-squared is 0.09, which is 9% of the variance. “Hours explain 61% of score” confuses a rate in points per hour with a share of variance. A later video, V-M5-RESID, watches a residual plot and a line that moves when one row is dragged. The LINE conditions are not a decoration. If residuals fan out as hours increase, equal variance has failed, and the usual standard errors are no longer a safe story. If the mean of the score is curved in hours, no p-value for a straight slope will make the line honest. Beside that keyed course fit, Topic 10.1 now also shows a descriptive least-squares line through 18 official 2025 pairs: median income in Hong Kong dollars is about 34,283 minus 0.121 times density, or about 121 Hong Kong dollars lower district median income for each additional 1,000 persons per square kilometre. R-squared is about 0.14. That line is a census summary of official district aggregates, not a household slope, not a causal claim, and not a sampling estimate. Slope inference on a sample is a later topic.

## Beat 5 (4:18–4:57)

Topic 10.5 is residual diagnostics. Plot residuals against fitted values and look for curves and funnels. A funnel — unequal variance — makes standard errors untrustworthy; a curve means the straight line is the wrong mean. One course illustration on the page is a log of rent, equal to 8.1 plus 0.012 times area: each extra square metre is about a 1.2% increase in rent, for a small slope on the log scale. That illustration is not an official rent series. The residual plot, and the single row that moves the line, are the job of V-M5-RESID.

## Beat 6 (4:57–6:05)

Topic 12.1 separates prediction from explanation. A model can predict exam failure from the number of library visits and still give you no licence to mandate more visits. A good predictor can be a symptom. Training error is optimistic; test error on new data is what matters. Topic 12.2 is validation and leakage. A hook on the page randomly splits 5,000 rows of daily data — 50 students times 100 days — and gets 89.8% accuracy. Hold out whole students, and the accuracy is 48.8%, no better than chance. The model had been recognising the student, not learning something that travels. The screencast of that bad split is V-M5-LEAK. Topic 12.3 will also ask you to compare a model with a majority-class baseline before you celebrate a 98% accuracy, and Topic 12.4 puts a leakage column on the table for you to find. Take from this tour only the rule: a random row split is not always an honest test, and a high accuracy is not always a cause.

## Beat 7 (6:05–6:37)

That is the spine of Module 5: a correlation with limits, a line you can write, a residual plot you actually look at, and a validation scheme that does not leak. Pause here, and open the pages yourself. The next videos stay with residuals, and with a train–test split that looks better than it is. When you are ready to prompt an AI to write a fit or a split, use the prompt contract, then recompute one number yourself.

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M5-RESID/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M5-RESID — narration

**video_id:** V-M5-RESID  
**Title:** Residuals, leverage and a line that moves  
**Word count:** 802  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:21 (target 5–7 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:34)

This video is about residuals, leverage, and a line that moves when one row is taken out. It is a motion graphic. There is no filmed presenter. The fitted line comes from revision_quiz.csv, the course illustration on Topics 10.3, 10.6 and 10.8. It is not a real quiz log, and it does not describe real students. We will first separate a slope from R-squared, then watch a residual plot change shape, then drag one unusual row and report the fit with and without it.

## Beat 2 (0:34–1:53)

The fitted line on the page is y-hat equals 60.15 plus 0.610 times hours. A fitted value sits on that line. A residual is y minus y-hat: the vertical gap from a point to the line. The residual standard deviation is 7.39 points — a typical size of prediction error, in the units of the quiz score. R-squared is 0.09, which is 9% of the variance in the score. The slope is 0.61 points per hour. That 0.61 is a rate. It is not “61% of performance.” Topic 10.8 starts from an AI sentence that makes exactly that swap: “Revision hours explain 61% of quiz performance.” Count n, recompute the slope and R-squared, and keep the two numbers in their own units. A formal reminder, in words, is that R-squared is one minus the residual sum of squares over the total sum of squares, and that the residual standard deviation uses n minus 2 in the divisor — two points having already been spent on the intercept and the slope. You do not need to recite the formula. You do need to know that a tidy slope and a tiny R-squared can live together in the same fit.

## Beat 3 (1:53–3:20)

Topic 10.5 asks you to plot residuals against fitted values. Look for a curve, which means the straight line is the wrong shape for the mean, and look for a funnel, which means the variance is not constant. Unequal variance makes the usual standard errors untrustworthy. One remedy on the page is a transformation. In a course illustration — not an official rent series — the log of rent equals 8.1 plus 0.012 times area. For a small slope on the log scale, each extra square metre is about a 1.2% increase in rent. After the log, the funnel flattens. The residual plot is doing work that the slope, by itself, cannot do. If an assistant prints only a p-value for the slope, ask to see this plot. Curvature has a different remedy from a funnel: add a term, or transform, rather than pretending the straight line was only a little bit off. And residuals that look dependent — a run of positive gaps followed by a run of negative ones — are a warning that the independence part of LINE is in trouble, especially if the rows have a time order. We will not invent a residual-correlation figure that the page does not give; we will only name the pattern you are supposed to look for.

## Beat 4 (3:20–4:54)

Topic 10.6 asks what one student who studied 30 hours — when the others studied 12 hours or fewer — does to the line. An outlier has a large residual. A high-leverage point is unusual in x: it sits far left or far right of the other hours. A point is influential when removing it changes the fit a lot, usually because it has high leverage and does not sit on the trend the other points suggest. Cook’s distance is a number that combines residual and leverage; this page does not key a Cook’s-distance value for the 30-hour row, and we will not invent one. What the page does give you is the slope itself: 0.61 with the 30-hour row in the fit, and 0.57 without it. Always compare with and without the point, and report both. The audit lab in Topic 10.8 asks for exactly that comparison, and also reminds you that if you regress hours on score, the slope is not the reciprocal of 0.61. Leverage is about unusual hours; a residual is about an unusual score given those hours; influence is about whether the line, the slope, or the conclusions move when the row is removed. Reporting only the more convenient of the two slopes is itself a kind of overclaim. Record both, with n, and say that one row is a 30-hour point when the others are at 12 hours or fewer.

## Beat 5 (4:54–5:21)

So, a residual is a gap, R-squared is a share of variance, a slope is a rate, and one unusual row can move the rate. For this course illustration, report 0.61 with the 30-hour row and 0.57 without it, and do not let anyone read 0.61 as 61%. Open Topic 10.3, Topic 10.5, Topic 10.6 and the audit lab in Topic 10.8, and drag the point yourself.

---

# V-M6-CLUSTER — narration

**video_id:** V-M6-CLUSTER  
**Title:** Four classrooms are not forty students  
**Word count:** 600  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:00 (target 4–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:38)

This video is about a unit-of-analysis error that is easy to miss in a spreadsheet and hard to miss once you see it: four classrooms are not forty students. It is a motion graphic, built from Topics E1.15 and E1.13, with the design idea already named on Topic E1.3. There is no filmed presenter. The 40 students and four classes are a course illustration, not a real school study. We will first show the tempting student-level claim, then collapse the dots, then write the unit into a protocol so the error is harder to repeat.

## Beat 2 (0:38–1:24)

The audit lab in Topic E1.15 starts from an AI sentence: “The new method works,” with p less than 0.001 and n equal to 40. If you only look at the spreadsheet, you do see 40 rows. Each row is a student, and a student-level test can produce a very small p-value. The hidden structure is how the method was assigned. On Topic E1.3, the same story is told as a hook: four classes, 40 students, the method assigned by class. The unit that was randomised is the class, not the student. Treating 40 students as 40 independent coin-flips is pseudo-replication: it pretends you have more independent pieces of information than the design gave you.

## Beat 3 (1:24–2:09)

Now watch the picture correct itself. The 40 dots pull together into four classrooms, and each classroom collapses to one class mean. You now have four independent units, not 40. Re-test at the class level, as the audit lab asks you to do, and the page’s worked result is a p-value of about 0.2 — weak evidence, not a triumph. The approximately is important: the page writes p approximately 0.2, and we will not pretend we have a more precise class-level p-value than that. The method may still be worth studying. This design, analysed honestly, simply does not support the original sentence. The unit of analysis is the unit that was randomised.

## Beat 4 (2:09–3:24)

Topic E1.13 is how you stop this error before it starts. Write the unit of analysis down in the protocol, with the primary outcome, the analysis, the sample size, and the stopping rule, before the data arrive. If the method will be assigned by class, the n you power and the n you report are numbers of classes, not numbers of students who happen to sit in them. Pre-registration, as a named practice, still has no textbook source on this page — audit gap E1.13 — and the page also notes that the unit-of-analysis discussion has an instructor source only, NUS Chapter 10, and is otherwise FlippedStat material. We will not invent a journal or a CUHK policy to close those flags. The official outcome still stands: fix the analysis before the data are seen, and keep the unit honest. If an assistant reports n equals 40 because there are 40 rows, ask it to count classrooms, or sites, or days — whatever was actually assigned — and to show the class-level analysis beside the student-level one. Record both. The smaller n is usually the honest one.

## Beat 5 (3:24–4:00)

So, before you trust a tiny p-value, ask what was randomised, and count those units. In this course illustration, the honest n is 4, and the class-level p-value is about 0.2, not the p less than 0.001 that treated 40 students as independent. Open Topic E1.15, Topic E1.13 and Topic E1.3, aggregate to the four class means yourself, and write the unit into the protocol before you look at the outcome or at the student-level p-value that treated the forty rows as if they were forty truly independent random treatment assignments.

# V-M6-DESIGN — narration

**video_id:** V-M6-DESIGN  
**Title:** Randomisation, replication and blocking  
**Word count:** 750  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:00 (target 5–7 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:31)

This video is about three design elements that have to be watched as a process: randomisation, replication, and blocking. It is a motion graphic. There is no filmed presenter. The examples come from Topics E1.2, E1.3 and E1.5. Some are course illustrations; one blocking picture is a labelled OpenIntro illustration. None of them is a real trial we ran. The four-classrooms story, and its p-values, belong to a later video, V-M6-CLUSTER. We will not steal those numbers here.

## Beat 2 (0:31–1:47)

Start with randomisation. In an experiment, units receive treatments and responses are measured. Random assignment gives every unit the same chance of each treatment, so the groups differ on age, motivation, diet — everything measured and unmeasured — only by chance. A systematic difference in the outcome can then be attributed to the treatment, which is what internal validity is about. A labelled illustration from Navarro, in the in-depth lesson, asks first-years and third-years each to write an essay and counts the errors. Third-years make fewer errors, but they are also older and have written more already. Education, age and experience are bundled. You cannot randomly assign people to three years of university, so this comparison cannot tell you which of those things improved the writing. Record the allocation, preferably with a seeded computer generator, before the outcomes are known. Do not let people choose their own treatment and then call the study an experiment. Random assignment licenses a causal claim for the units you actually randomised. It does not, by itself, license a generalisation to a population you never sampled, as Module 1 already taught with the two-by-two grid.

## Beat 3 (1:47–2:28)

Topic E1.2 fills in the rest of a simple experiment. A new revision app tested only on volunteers who are told they are using it can inflate the effect: people who volunteer are already keen, and people who know they are treated may try harder, or may report that they feel better. A control group gives the comparison. A placebo — an inactive version — can match expectations. Blinding means participants, and often assessors, do not know the group. None of that replaces randomisation, and randomisation does not replace a control. The design is a set of choices, not a single magic word.

## Beat 4 (2:28–3:14)

Replication is the second element: independent units receiving each treatment. Measuring the same person ten times is not ten replications. Assigning a method to a whole class and then treating the 40 students as 40 independent coin-flips is the same kind of problem. The unit of analysis should be the unit that was randomised. The page calls the cheaper version pseudo-replication. We will watch those 40 dots collapse into four classes in V-M6-CLUSTER. Here, take only the principle: count the independent units, not the rows that happen to sit in the spreadsheet. If you are unsure, write one sentence in the protocol: “What was randomised, and how many of those units are there?”

## Beat 5 (3:14–4:13)

Blocking is the third element. If a variable other than the treatment is known, or strongly suspected, to affect the response, first group the units into blocks by that variable, then randomise within each block. A labelled OpenIntro illustration on the page is a heart-attack drug trial: split patients into low-risk and high-risk blocks, and randomly assign half of each block to each group, so both groups get equal numbers of each kind of patient. We will not invent enrolment counts, event rates, or a p-value for that picture. The page also says that blocking is a more advanced technique, and that analysing a blocked design properly needs extensions of the methods in this course — the randomised-block ANOVA of Topic E1.4.1. Control, randomisation and replication belong in every experiment; blocking is how you use a factor you already understand, without pretending it was discovered after the data arrived.

## Beat 6 (4:13–5:00)

Topic E1.5 adds a factorial question: does a study app help more for night-owls than for early birds? A course illustration on the page has the app helping night-owls by 8 and early birds by 1 — an interaction, visible as non-parallel lines. Those plus-8 and plus-1 figures are not a real experiment. They are there so you can see what an interaction looks like, and so you remember to plan for it if you care about it. Open Topic E1.2, Topic E1.3 and Topic E1.5, and then, when you are ready to count classrooms instead of students, watch V-M6-CLUSTER and write the unit of analysis into the protocol first, before any outcome is on the screen.

## Continuous script (for the recording booth)

This video is about three design elements that have to be watched as a process: randomisation, replication, and blocking. It is a motion graphic. There is no filmed presenter. The examples come from Topics E1.2, E1.3 and E1.5. Some are course illustrations; one blocking picture is a labelled OpenIntro illustration. None of them is a real trial we ran. The four-classrooms story, and its p-values, belong to a later video, V-M6-CLUSTER. We will not steal those numbers here.
