========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M6-OV/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M6-OV — narration

**video_id:** V-M6-OV  
**Title:** Module 6 overview: design and rank-based tests  
**Word count:** 900  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 6:00 (target 6–8 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

Welcome to Module 6 of FlippedStat: Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. This is a short tour of the interactive site, with a few callouts on top of the pages. There is no filmed presenter. We will not cover every topic in the module, and we will not restage the later videos on randomisation, replication and blocking, on rank-based tests, or on clustered classrooms. Course illustrations stay labelled. Where a page still carries an audit-gap flag, we will not invent a textbook source to close it. Reliability and validity of a questionnaire, and the handling of non-response, sit on other topics in this module; we will only meet them as part of the official outcomes, not as a second film.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:44)

Here is the Module 6 page. The official title is Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. When you finish this module, you should be able to design an experiment or a survey using randomisation, replication, blocking and suitable sampling; apply rank-based tests when distributional assumptions fail, and justify the choice; assess questionnaire reliability and validity, and handle non-response; and write a protocol that fixes the analysis before the data are seen. The module has twenty-five topics. The module is complete when at least eighty percent of its topics are marked done, as on every official module. Today we visit four pages: randomisation, replication and blocking; questionnaire design and Likert data; rank-based tests; and protocols. ANOVA for designed experiments, and the rest of the survey and sampling topics, are in the same official module; this tour will not try to film them all.

## Beat 3 (1:44–2:41)

Topic E1.3 is randomisation, replication and blocking. Random assignment gives every unit the same chance of each treatment, so groups are alike on average in respects you measured and in respects you did not. Replication means independent units receiving each treatment — not repeated measurements of the same unit counted as if they were new people. Blocking groups units by a variable you already know will affect the response, then randomises inside each block, so the treatments stay balanced on that variable. The motion of units being assigned, repeated and blocked is V-M6-DESIGN, including a labelled OpenIntro picture of blocking by patient risk. A hook on this same page — four classes, 40 students, method assigned by class — is the clustering problem. We will not steal that animation here. V-M6-CLUSTER is the place where those 40 dots collapse into four classrooms.

## Beat 4 (2:41–3:37)

Topic E1.8 is questionnaire design and Likert data. A hook on the page asks what is wrong with “How satisfied and engaged are you with the course?” It is double-barrelled: satisfaction and engagement are two ideas, and a person can be high on one and low on the other. Split them. Use neutral wording, one idea per item, and labels on the response scale. Think about whether a neutral option belongs. Then display the answers. A mean of a Likert item can hide a pile at each end. The page’s habit is to report the distribution — for example with stacked bars — not only the mean. That reporting advice still has no textbook source on the page, under audit gap E1.8.4. We will treat it as a FlippedStat practice, and we will not invent a citation to dress it up.

## Beat 5 (3:37–4:24)

Topic E1.12 is rank-based tests. The hook is reaction times that are very skewed, with n equal to 8 in each group, and the question whether a t-test is still honest. When a distribution is badly skewed, or an outlier would dominate a mean, a rank test can be the more honest tool: Mann–Whitney for two groups, Wilcoxon signed-rank for paired data, Kruskal–Wallis for three or more. The price, when a t-test’s assumptions do hold, is often lower power. The motion of an outlier breaking a t, then ranks restoring order, is V-M6-RANK. That video will use the worked figures already on the page. This tour will not invent a t-test p-value the hook does not give.

## Beat 6 (4:24–5:13)

Topic E1.13 is protocols and pre-registration. The question is what must be written down before the data are collected: the primary outcome, the analysis, the sample size, and the stopping rule. Deviations can happen; if they do, report them and justify them. Pre-registration, as a named practice, still has no textbook source on this page — audit gap E1.13. The habit itself is already an official module outcome: write a protocol that fixes the analysis before the data are seen. We will not invent a journal policy, a CUHK policy, or a registration number to stand in for that missing source. If you later use a public registry, say so in the log; do not pretend this course has already named one.

## Beat 7 (5:13–6:00)

That is the spine of Module 6: a design you can name, a questionnaire you can defend, a rank test you can justify, and a protocol you wrote before you looked. Pause here, and open the pages yourself. The next videos stay with the three design elements, with ranks, and with four classrooms that are not forty students. If you later ask an AI to choose a test or to write a protocol, keep the prompt contract at the top, and check the unit of analysis yourself before you trust a tiny p-value on a long student-level spreadsheet that has quietly treated clustered rows as if those clustered rows were fully independent observations of that assigned treatment condition.

---

Replication means independent units receiving each treatment — not repeated measurements of the same unit counted as if they were new people. Blocking groups units by a variable you already know will affect the response, then randomises inside each block, so the treatments stay balanced on that variable. The motion of units being assigned, repeated and blocked is V-M6-DESIGN, including a labelled OpenIntro picture of blocking by patient risk. A hook on this same page — four classes, 40 students, method assigned by class — is the clustering problem. We will not steal that animation here. V-M6-CLUSTER is the place where those 40 dots collapse into four classrooms.

Topic E1.8 is questionnaire design and Likert data. A hook on the page asks what is wrong with “How satisfied and engaged are you with the course?” It is double-barrelled: satisfaction and engagement are two ideas, and a person can be high on one and low on the other. Split them. Use neutral wording, one idea per item, and labels on the response scale. Think about whether a neutral option belongs. Then display the answers. A mean of a Likert item can hide a pile at each end. The page’s habit is to report the distribution — for example with stacked bars — not only the mean. That reporting advice still has no textbook source on the page, under audit gap E1.8.4. We will treat it as a FlippedStat practice, and we will not invent a citation to dress it up.

Topic E1.12 is rank-based tests. The hook is reaction times that are very skewed, with n equal to 8 in each group, and the question whether a t-test is still honest. When a distribution is badly skewed, or an outlier would dominate a mean, a rank test can be the more honest tool: Mann–Whitney for two groups, Wilcoxon signed-rank for paired data, Kruskal–Wallis for three or more. The price, when a t-test’s assumptions do hold, is often lower power. The motion of an outlier breaking a t, then ranks restoring order, is V-M6-RANK. That video will use the worked figures already on the page. This tour will not invent a t-test p-value the hook does not give.

Topic E1.13 is protocols and pre-registration. The question is what must be written down before the data are collected: the primary outcome, the analysis, the sample size, and the stopping rule. Deviations can happen; if they do, report them and justify them. Pre-registration, as a named practice, still has no textbook source on this page — audit gap E1.13. The habit itself is already an official module outcome: write a protocol that fixes the analysis before the data are seen. We will not invent a journal policy, a CUHK policy, or a registration number to stand in for that missing source. If you later use a public registry, say so in the log; do not pretend this course has already named one.

That is the spine of Module 6: a design you can name, a questionnaire you can defend, a rank test you can justify, and a protocol you wrote before you looked. Pause here, and open the pages yourself. The next videos stay with the three design elements, with ranks, and with four classrooms that are not forty students. If you later ask an AI to choose a test or to write a protocol, keep the prompt contract at the top, and check the unit of analysis yourself before you trust a tiny p-value on a long student-level spreadsheet that has quietly treated clustered rows as if those clustered rows were fully independent observations of that assigned treatment condition.

# V-M6-RANK — narration

**video_id:** V-M6-RANK  
**Title:** When ranks are the honest test  
**Word count:** 697  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:39 (target 4–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:41)

This video is about when ranks are the honest test, and about what you give up when you use them. It is a motion graphic, built from Topic E1.12. There is no filmed presenter. The leading example is the page’s own hook: reaction times that are very skewed, with eight observations in each group. That is a course illustration, not a lab we ran. The page does not give a t-test p-value for this hook, and we will not invent one. We will watch the idea of a t-test being pulled by an outlier, then use the rank-test figures the page does give.

## Beat 2 (0:41–1:30)

A t-test compares means, and a mean is pulled by the long tail. With n equal to 8, one slow reaction time can change the mean, the standard deviation, and the test decision. The page’s task is exactly that: drag an outlier, and watch a t-test change a lot while a rank test barely moves. Ranking replaces each time by its place in the ordered list. The extreme time is still the largest, but it is no longer “many seconds slower than everyone else”; it is simply last. That is the robustness. It is also the price: you have stopped asking a question about mean reaction time, and started asking a question about whether one group tends to outrank the other.

## Beat 3 (1:30–2:55)

For two independent groups, the usual rank test is the Mann–Whitney U test — also called Wilcoxon rank-sum. The worked figures on the topic page are U equal to 12, p equal to 0.04, and a rank-biserial correlation of 0.63 as an effect size. Those numbers belong to the page’s illustration; they are not a result you should quote about real operators or real patients. For paired data, or a single sample of change scores, the sibling test is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. For three or more groups, Kruskal–Wallis is ANOVA done on the ranks: you rank everyone together, then ask whether the groups’ mean ranks differ. Robust summaries sit beside these tests: the median and the IQR, not only the mean and the standard deviation. The same page now also has a labelled synthetic teaching sample of hostel quiz scores, not official CUHK data. The quiet- and social-floor scores have no overlap, so a two-sided Mann-Whitney test gives U = 36, the largest possible with n = 6 and 6, and p about 0.002. A Kruskal-Wallis test on all three floors gives H about 13.56, on 2 degrees of freedom, p about 0.0011. Do not mix those teaching-sample figures with the hook’s U = 12, or with the book illustration’s U = 3.

## Beat 4 (2:55–3:49)

The in-depth lesson also walks two labelled book illustrations from Learning Statistics with jamovi. Ten people take a “test of awesomeness,” five in each group, and every A score is compared with every B score; the number of winning comparisons is U, here equal to 3, with p equal to 0.05556. R reports the same statistic as W. A second illustration uses happiness scores before and after a class: the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic is 7, and p is 0.03711. Those figures belong to the book examples, not to the reaction-time hook. Do not mix U = 3 with U = 12. We will also not make a designated-textbook file such as clinicaltrial.csv the main example in this video; if you meet it in the Kruskal–Wallis lesson, keep it labelled as a book file.

## Beat 5 (3:49–4:39)

What is lost? When a t-test’s assumptions do hold, a rank test usually has lower power: a higher chance of missing a real difference. You also answer a slightly different question, about ranks rather than about means. That can be the honest trade. It is not a reason to run both tests and keep the more convenient p-value. Choose the test to match the design and the shape, write it down, and report an effect size with it. Open Topic E1.12, drag the outlier yourself, and recompute the Mann–Whitney statistic from the page’s illustration before you trust an AI to “just run a non-parametric test.” Agreement between two tools on a p-value is not the check; the ranks, and the choice of test, are.

## Production notes

- Keyed Topic E5.7 course illustration: two independent random walks, r = 0.311; their changes, r = 0.042. Do not invent p-values. FST also keys ACF values (acf_raw_12 = 0.872, acf_diff_1 = 0.572, bands, spur_share05 = 43.3, and so on); this script stays with the hook’s 0.311 / 0.042 pair and a qualitative ACF, and does not recite extra lag numbers that the topic hook does not use, to avoid an unsourced-on-the-page recital.
- Keyed Topic E5.8 synthetic Harbourside path: AR(3) on year-over-year differences R² = 0.323; integrated retrodictions R² = 0.922. Retrodiction is not an honest future holdout (that is V-M7-EVAL).
- Do not mix official CPI practice into these keys. Do not pile the full SARIMA catalogue (orders, AIC, coverage) into this short video.
- Matching short Beamer decks (not compiled in this environment) and OpenShot scaffolds (stills only; not finished films): No dedicated `V-M7-ACF.osp` was generated in this pass. Use the official-topic scaffolds and short decks: `#t/E5.7` deck under `stage8/slides/topics/M7/`; OpenShot `stage8/openshot/projects/M7/V-T-E5.7.osp` `#t/E5.8` deck under `stage8/slides/topics/M7/`; OpenShot `stage8/openshot/projects/M7/V-T-E5.8.osp`

- Voice: one warm narrator, English, conversational, no jokes at students’ expense. Cantonese / Traditional Chinese versions come later.
- Do not show real student data, CUHK logos in a way that implies approval, or invented policy text. Label synthetic data as synthetic. Label official C&SD / DATA.GOV.HK extracts as official extracts, and FlippedStat calculations as FlippedStat calculations, not as official statistics.
- If a site recording is used: record the v10.4-dev standalone (`build/FlippedStat_v10.4-dev_standalone.html`, SHA-256 `2acbd8967cfc7849b309af8cc1e3f0a5ab0db9c05a2d4eae337cabb522d4f089`); hide any personal profile; pause before each click so captions can land. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M7-ACF/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M7-ACF — narration

**video_id:** V-M7-ACF  
**Title:** Autocorrelation and a correlation that is only time  
**Word count:** 601  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:00 (target 4–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:36)

This video is about autocorrelation, and about a correlation that is only time. It is a motion graphic, built from Topics E5.7 and E5.8. There is no filmed presenter. The worked figures are course illustrations and FlippedStat calculations on the synthetic Harbourside series, not official statistics. The opening question is the one on Topic E5.7: if two series both rise for 20 years, are they related? We will first watch two unrelated trends produce a tempting correlation, then build an autocorrelation function, then put a simple autoregression on year-over-year changes.

## Beat 2 (0:36–1:22)

Trending series can correlate by accident. The page’s worked illustration is two independent random walks: their correlation is 0.311. After you take changes — first differences — the correlation of those changes is 0.042. The shared rise was time, not a link you should act on. Difference first when a trend is the obvious feature, then ask the correlation question again. We will not invent a p-value or a longer catalogue of spurious examples than the page gives; 0.311 against 0.042 is the picture to remember. Shared time is a confounder. It can make two energy series, two prices, or two counts look like one story when each is mostly walking upward on its own.

## Beat 3 (1:22–2:30)

Autocorrelation at lag k is the correlation between the series and a copy of itself shifted by k steps. The autocorrelation function, the ACF, is that correlation plotted for lag 1, lag 2, and so on. A slowly decaying ACF often means a trend is still in the series. A spike at lag 12 in monthly data often means a seasonal pattern is still in the series. After you difference, or seasonally difference, the ACF of what is left tells you whether neighbouring changes still move together. Read the plot; do not treat every bar as a separate story. If you later use a formal significance band, use the one the page computes for that series, and do not invent a band here. A single large bar is a clue, not a licence to tell a causal story about that lag. Read neighbouring bars together, and say whether you are looking at the raw series or at a differenced one, because those two plots will not make the same claim.

## Beat 4 (2:30–3:30)

Topic E5.8 asks whether last year, and the last few months, can help you predict next month. One keyed path on the synthetic Harbourside series is to form a seasonal difference: this month minus the same month a year earlier. Then regress that change on the last three such changes — an autoregression of order 3. The R-squared of that AR(3) on the differences is 0.323. When you add the predicted differences back — integration — the retrodictions of the original series have R-squared 0.922. Retrodiction means a “prediction” of a value already observed, used to test the model; it is not, by itself, an honest forecast of the future. For honest forecasts, stay with the time-ordered holdout in V-M7-EVAL. Here, the lesson is narrower: model the changes, then put the series back together, and do not confuse a high retrodiction R-squared with a licence to skip the holdout.

## Beat 5 (3:30–4:00)

So, two series can move together only because both have a trend, and a useful correlation is often a correlation of changes. For the page’s random-walk illustration, that means 0.311 before differencing and 0.042 after. Open Topic E5.7 and Topic E5.8, switch the ACF from the raw series to the differenced series, and do not report a shared rise as if that shared rise were already evidence of a genuine shared causal link between those two series.

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M7-DECOMP/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M7-DECOMP — narration

**video_id:** V-M7-DECOMP  
**Title:** Trend, season and residual coming apart  
**Word count:** 750  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:00 (target 5–7 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:50)

This video is about watching a series come apart into a trend, a seasonal pattern, and a residual, and about choosing an additive or a multiplicative model. It is a motion graphic. There is no filmed presenter. The keyed figures come from Topics E5.2, E5.4 and E5.5, and they are FlippedStat calculations on synthetic series — Harbourside demand, and a solar series — not official statistics. The official Composite CPI extract on Topic E5.2 is optional practice. We will not use it for the decomposition keys, and we will not invent official CPI values. We will first look at the synthetic Harbourside series as a whole, then take it apart additively, then switch to a solar series whose seasonal swing grows with its level.

## Beat 2 (0:50–1:50)

Start with the synthetic file harbourside_demand.csv, as Topic E5.2 does. There are 228 consecutive months, from January 2006 to December 2024. Demand runs from 2733 to 4142 gigawatt-hours, and every year peaks in July and August. The mean of the series is 3511 gigawatt-hours, as keyed in the module data. If you shuffle the rows, the calendar disappears: the August peaks no longer sit eight months apart, and every later lag and seasonal position is silently wrong. Parse the month as a date, set a monthly frequency, and confirm there are no gaps and no negative values before you decompose or forecast. A missing month is not a cosmetic hole; it shifts everything after it. Count the 228 months in Excel as the page suggests, and plot demand against month before you ask a model to decompose anything. Looking is part of the method, not a courtesy before the “real” work.

## Beat 3 (1:50–3:11)

Topic E5.4 writes the additive model as y equals trend plus seasonal plus residual. The seasonal effect is the average detrended value for each calendar month. On this synthetic series, the additive decomposition has R-squared 0.973: almost all of the variation is trend plus a fixed seasonal pattern. The August effect is plus 395.7 gigawatt-hours, and the February effect is minus 415.2. Those are keyed FlippedStat calculations, not official energy statistics and not Census and Statistics Department figures. The residual is what is left: on this series the residual standard deviation is keyed at 56.8 gigawatt-hours, small beside a seasonal swing of several hundred. Read the four panels in order. Do not jump to a forecast until you can say what the seasonal wave is doing in a named month. An additive model says August is a fixed number of gigawatt-hours above the trend, every year. If later years have much larger August peaks than early years, that fixed-amount story will start to fail, and the residuals will show it. Residuals are not automatically “the interesting bit.” They are what the trend-plus-season story could not explain, and a patterned residual is a reason to change the story, not a reason to ignore it.

## Beat 4 (3:11–4:27)

Not every series wants a fixed plus-or-minus seasonal amount. Topic E5.5 uses a synthetic solar series whose output grew about elevenfold, and whose summer–winter swing grew with it, from 14.2 to 151.7 gigawatt-hours. If the swing grows with the level, write y as trend times seasonal times residual, or take logs and work additively on the log scale. A curved trend may also need a quadratic term. On this series, a multiplicative model with a quadratic trend has a forecast MAPE of 2.36%, against 12.21% for an additive model. Those MAPEs are keyed on the page, still on synthetic data. The choice is a picture first: does the seasonal wave stay about the same height, or does it scale as the series rises? Logs are a convenience for the second case, because a multiplicative seasonal piece becomes an additive piece on the log scale, which is easier to estimate and easier to explain as an approximate percentage. Switch the two models on the page, on both series, and say which picture you are using before you report a seasonal effect as if it were a fixed law of nature.

## Beat 5 (4:27–5:00)

If you practise on the official Composite CPI extract, confirm dates and gaps the same way, and keep those official figures in their own log. Do not paste them into the Harbourside answer keys, and do not treat a FlippedStat R-squared as an official statistic. Open Topic E5.2, Topic E5.4 and Topic E5.5, watch the four panels come apart, and then go to V-M7-EVAL for the forecast that has to be scored on later months, not on the months that built the trend.

**Word count:** 784  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:14 (target 5–7 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:38)

This video is about forecasts that peek, and forecasts that do not. It is a motion graphic, built from Topics E5.6, E5.11 and E5.12, using the synthetic Harbourside demand series. There is no filmed presenter. These keyed figures are FlippedStat calculations on that synthetic file, not official statistics. We will watch a training window that stays in the past, and one that quietly includes the future. The order of work is fixed: split in time first, score the baselines on the test months, then score the method you actually care about, then ask whether anyone peeked.

## Beat 2 (0:38–1:46)

Topic E5.6 is honest evaluation. Train on the past only; test on months the model has not been shown. On this series, the keyed split uses training through December 2021, and a test starting in January 2022: the last 36 months. Always report a naive baseline — often the last observed value — and a seasonal-naive baseline, which repeats last year’s pattern. Report MAE in gigawatt-hours, and MAPE in percent, on those test months. In-sample fit is not the same check. The page also keys an in-sample decomposition MAPE of 1.9%, which looks tidier than the holdout and is not the number you should lead with. MAPE is a percentage, so it is useful for a quick comparison; MAE stays in gigawatt-hours, so it tells you the typical size of an error in the units a planner would recognise. Report both. And do not change the holdout after you have seen which method wins. The test months are a commitment, not a slider you tune until the story improves.

## Beat 3 (1:46–2:44)

Here are the keyed holdout figures for those last 36 months. The decomposition has MAPE 3.33%, MAE 121.0, and RMSE 133.8. The seasonal naive has MAPE 2.76%, MAE 102.5, and RMSE 119.5. The naive has MAPE 7.83%, MAE 301.6, and RMSE 369.4. On this test set, repeating last year beats the decomposition. That is not an embarrassment; it is the point of a baseline. A method has to earn its keep against a simple alternative, on months it did not see. If an assistant reports only a beautiful in-sample R-squared, ask for the holdout MAPE and for the seasonal naive beside it. A method that cannot beat last year, on months it did not see, has not yet earned a more complicated name. That is true even if the in-sample panels look almost perfect, as a high decomposition R-squared on the full series can.

## Beat 4 (2:44–3:55)

Now the error the audit lab is built for. Topic E5.12 starts from an AI sentence: “Our model forecasts monthly demand with only 1.19% error.” Watch the training window stretch until it includes the months you were supposed to be forecasting. That 1.19% is the peeked in-sample-style figure keyed on the page, not the honest holdout. Re-fit on the training months only, score the held-back months, and you are back at a decomposition MAPE of 3.33%, with the seasonal naive still at 2.76%. Peeking is a motion error: the future was quietly in the room while the model was being dressed. A time-ordered test set is how you keep the door shut. The same error has other costumes: scoring on the same months you used to choose a model, or dropping a difficult year because it made the MAPE look worse. Topic E5.11 specifically asks you to look at the 2020 months, where a structural break can sit. If a break is in the test window, say so. Do not silently start the test after the awkward year.

## Beat 5 (3:55–5:14)

Topic E5.11 is a Copilot lab on a seasonal forecast. The page already describes the typical pattern: the assistant reports a good in-sample fit first; on the holdout, a SARIMA MAPE of 2.34% beats the seasonal naive of 2.76% by less than the in-sample numbers had suggested. Recompute the test MAPE yourself, check the forecast interval, and look at the 2020 months, where a structural break can sit. Those lab figures are on the student page; we will not invent a tighter secret key. The official monthly Composite CPI extract remains available for optional practice, as on Topic E5.2, but it is a different series: do not mix official CPI figures into those Harbourside test MAPE keys. Open Topic E5.6, Topic E5.11 and Topic E5.12, keep the test months out of the training window, and write both MAPEs in the log: the one that peeked, and the one that did not. If a tool reports only 1.19%, ask where the training window ended, and whether last year’s seasonal pattern was also scored on the same later held-out months, and not only in-sample on those same earlier training months already used to fit that same forecasting model. ---

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M7-OV/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M7-OV — narration

**video_id:** V-M7-OV  
**Title:** Module 7 overview: time series and honest forecasts  
**Word count:** 901  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 6:00 (target 6–8 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:40)

Welcome to Module 7 of FlippedStat: Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting. This is a short tour of the interactive site on FlippedStat v10.4-dev, with a few callouts on top of the pages. There is no filmed presenter. We will not cover every topic, and we will not restage the later videos on decomposition, on honest forecast evaluation, or on autocorrelation. Where the site offers an official Hong Kong extract, it is labelled as official practice. Where the keyed worked example is the synthetic Harbourside series, it stays labelled synthetic. We will not mix official Consumer Price Index numbers with Harbourside answer keys.

## Beat 2 (0:40–1:39)

Here is the Module 7 page. The official title is Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting. When you finish this module, you should be able to describe a time series by trend, seasonal component and residual, and choose an additive or a multiplicative decomposition; forecast from a time-ordered training set and compare with naive and seasonal-naive baselines using MAE, RMSE and MAPE; read an autocorrelation function, recognise spurious correlation, and build autoregression on differenced data; fit and check a seasonal ARIMA model and report a forecast with its interval; and audit a forecast claim for peeking, in-sample evaluation, missing baselines and structural breaks. The module has thirteen topics. The module is complete when at least eighty percent of its topics are marked done, as on every official module. Today we visit four pages: what makes a time series different, seasonal decomposition, honest evaluation, and the forecast that peeked.

## Beat 3 (1:39–3:16)

Topic E5.2 asks why you cannot shuffle the rows of a monthly file before you analyse it. A time series is indexed by time at a fixed frequency. Neighbouring months are related, so “n independent rows” is the wrong story. On v10.4-dev, a licence-clean official series for practice is the Census and Statistics Department Composite Consumer Price Index, table 510-60001, with base period October 2019 to September 2020 equal to 100. The teaching extract, hk_cpi_composite_monthly_510-60001.csv, runs monthly from January 2015 to September 2026, with a year-month column, the official index, and the official year-on-year percentage change. Parse the dates, set a monthly frequency, and confirm there are no gaps before you smooth or forecast. Source: Census and Statistics Department, Hong Kong SAR Government. This is not a government publication, and no endorsement is implied. The page does not key individual CPI values in the lesson text, and we will not invent any. This official series is optional practice. The keyed worked example on the topic remains the synthetic file harbourside_demand.csv: 228 consecutive months, from January 2006 to December 2024, demand from 2733 to 4142 gigawatt-hours, peaking every year in July and August. Do not mix official CPI numbers with those Harbourside keys. A designated-textbook Think Stats electricity series also remains on the page as a labelled book illustration; we will not make that optional Python route the spine of this video, and we will not treat its book figures as Harbourside answers.

## Beat 4 (3:16–4:00)

Topic E5.4 is seasonal decomposition. The additive model writes the series as trend plus a seasonal pattern plus a residual. On the synthetic Harbourside series, the additive decomposition has R-squared 0.973; the August effect is plus 395.7 gigawatt-hours, and the February effect is minus 415.2. Those are keyed FlippedStat calculations on the synthetic file, not official statistics. If the seasonal swing grows with the level, a multiplicative model is the better first choice — that comparison, including the solar series, is part of V-M7-DECOMP. This tour only needs the habit: look first, then take the series apart, and say whether the seasonal piece is a fixed amount or a changing share.

## Beat 5 (4:00–5:06)

Topic E5.6 is forecasting and honest evaluation. Train on the past only; test on later months. Always report a naive baseline — last value, or last year’s pattern — and report MAE in the units of the series, and MAPE in percent, on the test months, not only in-sample. For the last 36 months of the synthetic Harbourside series, the page’s keyed figures are a decomposition MAPE of 3.33%, a seasonal-naive MAPE of 2.76%, and a naive MAPE of 7.83%. The seasonal naive beats the decomposition on that holdout. Topic E5.12 is the audit lab: an AI says the model forecasts monthly demand with only 1.19% error. That 1.19% is a peeking figure, not the honest holdout. V-M7-EVAL watches the training window include, or not include, the future. Autocorrelation, and a correlation that is only shared trend, is V-M7-ACF. Take from this tour the rule: a forecast you cannot compare with last year, on months the model did not see, is not ready to report.

## Beat 6 (5:06–6:00)

That is the spine of Module 7: a series you do not shuffle, a decomposition you can read, a forecast you evaluate on later months, and an audit for peeking. Pause here, and open the pages yourself. Practise, if you wish, on the official CPI extract, and keep those official figures out of the Harbourside answer keys. The next videos stay with decomposition, with forecasts that peek, and with autocorrelation. If you prompt an assistant to decompose or to forecast, keep the prompt contract at the top, lock the training end date in the prompt, and recompute one holdout MAPE yourself before you trust a tidy in-sample figure, or a forecast interval that was never scored on later months than the months that were used to fit it in the first place, on this v10.4-dev site.

# V-M8-AGREE — narration

**video_id:** V-M8-AGREE  
**Title:** Agreement is not proof  
**Word count:** 818  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:27 (target 5–7 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:41)

This video is a screen recording of two related pages: Topic 13.2, “Agreement is not proof,” and the Module 8 three-tool comparison lab. The habit is one you have been building since Module 1. Three tools can agree, and still be wrong together, especially when they share a default. There is no filmed presenter. The data files on these pages are synthetic, and the site labels them that way. We will use the keyed ledger on Topic 13.2. We will not read out the hidden answer key of the Module 8 lab — that check is for you, after you recompute.

## Beat 2 (0:41–1:38)

Open Topic 13.2. The hook on the page is easy to feel: three AI tools agree on n equals 228, and you are tempted to stop checking. The file is satisfaction300.csv, a synthetic survey. The ledger on the page is: 300 rows in the file; a satisfaction rating is present for 289 of them; 228 rows are complete on all three columns; a listwise default therefore drops 72 rows. Give the same file, and the same neutral prompt, to three tools, and ask each for n used, missing counts, the median and the mean, with code. Fill a three-tool log, and keep an Excel column as the referee. Agreement between tools is weak evidence if they share a default. Your column must be computed independently, with settings you can see. Disagreement is a gift: it shows exactly where to look.

## Beat 3 (1:38–2:40)

Here is what the shared default did, on this page. All three tools ran a drop-na that removes a row if any column is missing, and they summarised satisfaction on the 228 complete rows. The mean of satisfaction on those 228 rows is 4.10. If instead you use every row that actually has a satisfaction answer — 289 rows — the mean is 3.97. The tools did not only shrink n. They dropped people who were, disproportionately, the less satisfied ones. Among all answers, 29.4 percent rated three or lower. The course codes this as H1, misread data, caused by a shared method default. The independent check is not a fourth chatbot. It is a count and a mean you can see: in Excel, COUNT on the satisfaction column should give 289, and an average of those 289 should give 3.97. A second AI, with the same prompt, is not an independent check.

## Beat 4 (2:40–3:44)

Now follow the banner on Topic 13.2 through to the Module 8 kit, and open the three-tool comparison lab. The same logic, a new synthetic file. The file is tutorial_scores.csv, 154 rows, synthetic. The task on the page is: how many usable rows are there, and what did you exclude? What is the mean exam score for tutorial A, and for tutorial B? Test whether the means differ, and give the p-value and a ninety-five percent confidence interval for B minus A. And state what the data allow you to conclude. Show all code, and the n used for every number. Paste the prompt contract from Topic 1.9 first. For any tool other than Copilot with a CUHK sign-in, upload only this synthetic file, and never personal or confidential data. Tool availability is a living thing; the page itself says the project team has not yet completed that live check.

## Beat 5 (3:44–4:52)

The lab table makes the traps visible, without telling you the answers. There is a column for whether the tool removed duplicates, and a column for whether it treated minus 99 as missing. There is a column for whether it showed runnable code, and a column for whether it made a causal claim. The file is observational: students chose their tutorial format, so a causal conclusion would be an over-claim, H4. The default two-sample t in this course, and in R, is Welch’s test: do not pool the variances unless you have a reason, and say so. Fill every tool’s row with the numbers it actually printed, copied exactly. Then fill “my own recomputation” yourself, in Excel or in code you have checked. Then write the judgement: which tools were wrong, on what, and how did you know? Did they agree on anything that was wrong? Only then use “Check against the answer.” The point of the page is the check, not a shortcut to the key.

## Beat 6 (4:52–5:27)

So, three tools in agreement are three copies of the same default, until you have an independent number. On Topic 13.2, that independent number is 289 rows and a mean of 3.97, not the shared 228 and 4.10. On the Module 8 lab, the independent number is the one you recompute, after you have dealt with duplicates, with minus 99, and with the limits of an observational file. Agreement is not proof. Open Topic 13.2, open the lab, and fill the table yourself.

Fill a three-tool log, and keep an Excel column as the referee. Agreement between tools is weak evidence if they share a default. Your column must be computed independently, with settings you can see. Disagreement is a gift: it shows exactly where to look.

Here is what the shared default did, on this page. All three tools ran a drop-na that removes a row if any column is missing, and they summarised satisfaction on the 228 complete rows. The mean of satisfaction on those 228 rows is 4.10. If instead you use every row that actually has a satisfaction answer — 289 rows — the mean is 3.97. The tools did not only shrink n. They dropped people who were, disproportionately, the less satisfied ones. Among all answers, 29.4 percent rated three or lower. The course codes this as H1, misread data, caused by a shared method default. The independent check is not a fourth chatbot. It is a count and a mean you can see: in Excel, COUNT on the satisfaction column should give 289, and an average of those 289 should give 3.97. A second AI, with the same prompt, is not an independent check.

Now follow the banner on Topic 13.2 through to the Module 8 kit, and open the three-tool comparison lab. The same logic, a new synthetic file. The file is tutorial_scores.csv, 154 rows, synthetic. The task on the page is: how many usable rows are there, and what did you exclude? What is the mean exam score for tutorial A, and for tutorial B? Test whether the means differ, and give the p-value and a ninety-five percent confidence interval for B minus A. And state what the data allow you to conclude. Show all code, and the n used for every number. Paste the prompt contract from Topic 1.9 first. For any tool other than Copilot with a CUHK sign-in, upload only this synthetic file, and never personal or confidential data. Tool availability is a living thing; the page itself says the project team has not yet completed that live check.

The lab table makes the traps visible, without telling you the answers. There is a column for whether the tool removed duplicates, and a column for whether it treated minus 99 as missing. There is a column for whether it showed runnable code, and a column for whether it made a causal claim. The file is observational: students chose their tutorial format, so a causal conclusion would be an over-claim, H4. The default two-sample t in this course, and in R, is Welch’s test: do not pool the variances unless you have a reason, and say so. Fill every tool’s row with the numbers it actually printed, copied exactly. Then fill “my own recomputation” yourself, in Excel or in code you have checked. Then write the judgement: which tools were wrong, on what, and how did you know? Did they agree on anything that was wrong? Only then use “Check against the answer.” The point of the page is the check, not a shortcut to the key.

So, three tools in agreement are three copies of the same default, until you have an independent number. On Topic 13.2, that independent number is 289 rows and a mean of 3.97, not the shared 228 and 4.10. On the Module 8 lab, the independent number is the one you recompute, after you have dealt with duplicates, with minus 99, and with the limits of an observational file. Agreement is not proof. Open Topic 13.2, open the lab, and fill the table yourself.

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M8-FAIL/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M8-FAIL — narration

**video_id:** V-M8-FAIL  
**Title:** How generative AI fails at statistics  
**Word count:** 750  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:00 (target 5–7 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:50)

This video is about how generative AI fails at statistics, and about recognising those failures before you pass them on. It is a motion graphic, built from Topics 13.1 and 9.3. There is no filmed presenter. We will first walk a short catalogue of the course’s six error codes, then work one miss in detail: three references that do not all exist, and do not all say what was claimed. We will not invent a real paper, a DOI, or a student dataset to dramatise the point. A failure type is useful only if you can name it, find it in an output, and write down what you checked. The catalogue is a memory aid, not a way to score models in the abstract.

## Beat 2 (0:50–1:52)

Topic 13.1 consolidates six codes you have been using since Module 1. H1 is misread data: the wrong column, a code treated as a measurement, blanks filled with zeros. H2 is the wrong method or the wrong type: a t-test on the wrong design, or a causal verb on an observational table. H3 is a calculation error: arithmetic that was guessed as text, a slipped divisor, or a total that does not add up. You have already seen versions of these in earlier videos: a minus-99 that pulled a mean, a test chosen before the questions were asked, a language-model number that was never computed. The habit is the same. Demand the file, demand the code or the formula, and recompute one number yourself. If the assistant cannot show how a total was built, treat the total as unverified text, even if it is formatted like a table. Confidence in the prose is not evidence.

## Beat 3 (1:52–3:00)

H4 is over-reach: a conclusion the design cannot support, or a “95% certain” that has swapped two conditionals. H5 is fabrication: a source, a statistic, or a quotation that is not there. H6 is biased framing: a wording, a baseline, or a comparison that tilts the story before the numbers arrive. Topic 13.1 also names two neighbouring habits. First, run-to-run variation: rerun a prompt before you trust a once-off figure, and log the seed and the tool version. Second, sycophancy: models often adopt the user’s framing, especially if the prompt begins with “confirm that” and already states the hoped-for conclusion. Rewrite the prompt so it asks for a method, a table, and a check, not for a verdict you have already written. “Confirm that the difference is significant and write the R” is the kind of prompt earlier modules already crossed out. It invites H2, H4 and sycophancy at once. Start from the file, the question, and the design, and let the conclusion wait until a number has been checked.

## Beat 4 (3:00–4:16)

Now the worked miss, from Topic 9.3. An assistant gives you three references for a capstone. The page’s illustration is simple, and it is enough: of those three, one is real and relevant, one is real but says the opposite of what was claimed, and one does not exist. Open every source. Check the author, the year, the venue, and the DOI. Find the sentence that supports the claim. If you cannot open it, you cannot cite it. Log fabricated items as H5. A DOI that resolves to a different paper is also a citation error to fix — H5, if the source was invented or swapped. The task on the page is to check three citations against a mock library. We will not invent titles, years, or DOIs of our own. The point is the habit, not a sensational fake paper. A real article that says the opposite is, in some ways, more dangerous than a missing one, because it looks citable in a reference list. You still have to read the sentence you are relying on. “I found a paper with a similar title” is not a source check.

## Beat 5 (4:16–5:00)

So, learn the six codes, watch for a prompt that already contains its own answer, and open every source. Of the three references in the Topic 9.3 illustration, only one is real and actually supports the claim. Open Topic 13.1 and Topic 9.3, try the classification task, and then use V-M8-AGREE to practise cross-checking one analysis on three tools — because three tools can share the same H1, and agreement is still not the check. Record the AI’s sources, and your own source check, as two different lines in the log, even when the reference list looks complete, numbered, and tidy at the first quick and confident glance over it.

---

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M8-FAIR/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M8-FAIR — narration

**video_id:** V-M8-FAIR  
**Title:** Bias, fairness definitions and a feedback loop  
**Word count:** 876  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:50 (target 5–7 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This video is about bias, fairness definitions, and a feedback loop. It is a motion graphic, built from Topics 12.5, 12.6 and 12.7. There is no filmed presenter. The tables are course illustrations, not a real lending file and not official statistics about any Hong Kong district. Nothing in this video is legal advice, and nothing is a claim that a model has been audited in the wild. We will apply definitions the pages already give, and we will watch equal accuracy hide a very different predictive value. If you have watched the Bayes video in Module 3, you already know the mechanism: when two groups have different base rates, the same test can produce very different positive predictive values. Fairness is that fact, named as a choice among definitions, not a different branch of mathematics.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:57)

Topic 12.5 starts from a fair-sounding sentence: a flagging tool has equal sensitivity in two groups — is it fair? Equal sensitivity, sometimes called equal opportunity, means the same true-positive rate in each group. Predictive parity means the same positive predictive value. Selection-rate parity means the same proportion flagged; the page mentions the four-fifths rule as a screening flag, not as a legal test we will apply, and we will not turn it into one. The hard fact on the page is this: when base rates differ, these definitions cannot all hold at once, unless the model is perfect. Choosing one definition is a decision. Announcing “fair” without naming the definition is a slogan. You may have a reason to care more about equal sensitivity, or more about equal predictive value, depending on what a false negative or a false positive costs. State that reason. Do not let a single convenient percentage choose it for you.

## Beat 3 (1:57–3:14)

Here is the worked illustration on Topics 12.5 and 12.7. Sensitivity is 0.85 and specificity is 0.90 in both groups. The base rates are not the same: 20% in one group, 5.3% in the other. The positive predictive values are 0.68 and 0.32. Accuracy is about 0.89 in one group and about 0.90 in the other — almost the same. An AI that says “the tool is equally accurate in both groups, therefore fair” has chosen the number that hides the gap. The audit lab asks you to build both 1,000-person tables, compute accuracy, sensitivity and PPV by group, and explain the PPV gap through the base rates. We will keep the page’s “about 0.89 and 0.90”; we will not invent more precise accuracies, or cell counts the hook does not state, just to make the tables look tidier. If you rebuild the tables by hand, use the sensitivity, the specificity and the two base rates the page gives, and stop when you have recovered the two predictive values and the two accuracies already stated. The audit is to see the gap, not to produce a more impressive spreadsheet than the lesson.

## Beat 4 (3:14–5:20)

Topic 12.6 asks what can go wrong when a model uses a postcode, or a district, to predict loan default. Sampling bias: the training data under-represent some groups. Label bias: the outcome you recorded already reflects past decisions. Proxy variables: a postcode can stand in for ethnicity or income. Feedback loops: the decision shapes the next year’s data. The page’s sketch is simple: fewer loans given in district X, so fewer repayments are observed, so the model learns that X is risky, and the next round is worse. That is a course illustration. It is not an official finding about any named Hong Kong district, and this video will not paste official population or income figures into the loop. The habit is to ask what past decisions are already inside the label, and what a “neutral” postcode might be standing in for. A loop like this can make a model look as if it is “learning from data” when it is mostly learning from yesterday’s refusals. Sensitivity checks — different predictors, different training windows, a grouped split — will not all be possible in every exercise, but the question is always available: if the decision we take today becomes tomorrow’s training label, what will grow? A different bias of interpretation sits in official area-level figures already on the site: Pearson r = minus 0.38 between the 18 official 2025 district median household incomes and official 2025 densities is an ecological association among aggregates, not a household law and not a causal effect of density. The Boston and Chicago résumé-callback experiment remains the named study on Topic 12.6; its figures are not replaced. The same proxy point applies in a Hong Kong hiring setting — a name, or a residential district, can stand in for a protected characteristic in a model trained on past decisions — but this video does not invent a local audit’s callback rates.

## Beat 5 (5:20–5:50)

So, equal accuracy is not, by itself, fairness, and a feedback loop can grow a gap that a single snapshot will miss. In this course illustration, both groups can have sensitivity 0.85 and almost the same accuracy, while the positive predictive values are 0.68 and 0.32. Open Topic 12.5, Topic 12.6 and the audit lab in Topic 12.7, build both 1,000-person tables, and name the definition you are using before you use the word “fair.”

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/V-M8-OV/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-M8-OV — narration

**video_id:** V-M8-OV  
**Title:** Module 8 overview: responsible AI-assisted analysis  
**Word count:** 902  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 6:01 (target 6–8 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

Welcome to Module 8 of FlippedStat: Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. This is a short tour of the interactive site on FlippedStat v10.4-dev, with a few callouts on top of the pages. There is no filmed presenter. We will not cover every topic, and we will not restage the later videos on how generative AI fails, on the comparison lab, or on fairness. We will not invent CUHK policy text, and we will not describe certificate, endorsement, or distinction wording. Synthetic files stay labelled synthetic. The later videos will carry the long animations; this tour is a map, a ledger, and a list of habits you will need in the capstone, without treating the capstone as a certificate of competence.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:40)

Here is the Module 8 page. The official title is Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. When you finish this module, you should be able to recognise how generative AI fails at statistics — fabricated sources, wrong arithmetic, the wrong test, overclaim; cross-check one task across several AI tools and explain why agreement is not proof; identify bias and apply fairness definitions to a model or a dataset; protect privacy and disclose AI assistance reproducibly; and complete a verified capstone analysis with sensitivity checks. The module has eighteen topics. The module is complete when at least eighty percent of its topics are marked done, as on every official module. Today we visit five pages: how generative AI fails, the agreement lab, reproducibility and disclosure, fairness definitions, and the hallucination quiz.

## Beat 3 (1:40–2:44)

Topic 13.1 is how generative AI fails at statistics. The course already uses six error codes: H1, misread data; H2, wrong method or type; H3, a calculation error; H4, over-reach; H5, fabrication; and H6, biased framing. The same topic adds two habits that are easy to skip: run the same prompt again before you trust a once-off number, because runs can vary; and watch for sycophancy, when a model adopts your framing, especially if you began with “confirm that.” The animated catalogue, and one worked miss, is V-M8-FAIL, which will also open Topic 9.3’s fabricated-sources illustration. This tour only needs the names, and the refusal to treat a confident paragraph as a check. C.R.O.S.S. is still the daily method: count rows and missing values, recompute a key number, treat other tools as a hint, check statistical principles, and check sources and scope. Module 8 is that habit under a brighter light, not a new personality for the course.

## Beat 4 (2:44–3:59)

Topic 13.2 is the Copilot lab whose rule is already a course motto: agreement is not proof. Three tools can share the same silent error. The keyed ledger on the page, for the synthetic file satisfaction300.csv, is 300 rows in the file; satisfaction present on 289; 228 complete on all three columns; 72 dropped listwise. The mean is 4.10 on the 228 complete rows, and 3.97 on the 289 rows that actually have a satisfaction score. The tempting agreement was n equals 228. The independent check is the 289. A later video, V-M8-AGREE, already walks the comparison lab and this ledger. If you record this overview, do not treat the page’s interactive widget under a default seed as the referee: that widget can show a different n and mean — including a 241-row, mean-4.23 seed — and that readout is not the keyed ledger. Stay with 300, 289, 228, 72, 3.97 and 4.10. The page also notes that 29.4% of all answers were rated 3 or lower; that figure is part of the same keyed ledger, and it is one reason a silent listwise drop can move a mean.

## Beat 5 (3:59–5:26)

Topic 13.3 is reproducibility, provenance and disclosure. Keep prompts, outputs, code, seeds and file versions. Name files with dates. Write an AI-use statement: the tool, the version, the purpose, and what you checked. The page reminds you to cite the CUHK AI-use policy before publication. This video will not invent or paraphrase that policy, because the wording is not ours to write, and the human decision on an AI-use policy remains open. Open the template on the page, and follow whatever official policy your course later names. Topic 12.5 is fairness definitions — equal sensitivity, predictive parity, selection-rate parity — and the motion of equal accuracy hiding a different error is V-M8-FAIR. Topic 13.6 is a ten-item hallucination quiz with a confidence rating. We will not read items or scores here; attempt it without notes or AI, then use the feedback to plan revision. Privacy, a verified capstone, and sensitivity checks sit later in the same official module. Protecting data means, at the very least, not uploading real student or patient files to a tool that the course has not cleared, and preferring synthetic files when you are on a public assistant. The site already states that kind of caution; we will not invent a longer policy paragraph to stand in for a decision that is still open.

## Beat 6 (5:26–6:01)

That is the spine of Module 8: name the failure, refuse to treat agreement as proof, disclose what you used, and check fairness as a set of definitions rather than a slogan. Pause here, and open the pages yourself. The next videos stay with the failure-type catalogue, if you have not already watched the agreement lab, and with a fairness definition applied to a two-group table you can actually count by hand from the page’s own stated base rates and named fairness definitions on the page.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import json
    from pathlib import Path
    from pack import fmt_draft, word_count, secs_for
    out = []
    for fn in VIDEOS:
        vid = fn()
        meta = __import__("pack").write_video(vid)
        lo, hi = [int(x) for x in vid["target"].replace("minutes", "").replace("–", " ").split() if x.isdigit()][:2]
        words = meta["words"]
        mins = words / 150
        flag = ""
        if mins < lo or mins > hi:
            flag = " OUT OF RANGE"
        print(f"{meta['id']}: {words} words, {meta['draft']} (target {vid['target']}){flag}")
        out.append(meta)
    Path("/tmp/group1_meta.json").write_text(json.dumps(out, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/_batch2_tools/pack.py ==========

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Write Stage 8 batch-2 script folders to match batch-1 format."""
from __future__ import annotations

import math
import re
import textwrap
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path("/workspace/flippedstat_v99/stage8/scripts")
WPM = 150
LINE_WIDTH = 42


def word_count(text: str) -> int:
    return len(text.split())


def secs_for(text: str) -> float:
    return word_count(text) / WPM * 60.0


def fmt_mmss(seconds: float) -> str:
    seconds = max(0, int(round(seconds)))
    m, s = divmod(seconds, 60)
    return f"{m}:{s:02d}"


def fmt_draft(seconds: float) -> str:
    m, rem = divmod(int(round(seconds)), 60)
    return f"{m}:{rem:02d}"


def fmt_vtt(seconds: float) -> str:
    if seconds < 0:
        seconds = 0
    ms_total = int(round(seconds * 1000))
    h, rem = divmod(ms_total, 3_600_000)
    m, rem = divmod(rem, 60_000)
    s, ms = divmod(rem, 1000)
    return f"{h:02d}:{m:02d}:{s:02d}.{ms:03d}"


def wrap_cue(text: str, width: int = LINE_WIDTH) -> str:
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    return "\n".join(textwrap.wrap(text, width=width, break_long_words=False, break_on_hyphens=False))


_SPLIT_RE = re.compile(
    r"(?<=[\.!?])\s+(?=[A-Z“\"'(\d])"
    r"|(?<=:)\s+"
    r"|(?<=;)\s+"
    r"|(?<=—)\s+"
    r"|(?<=–)\s+"
    r"|(?<=,)\s+"
)


def _split_clauses(text: str) -> list[str]:
    # Keep abbreviation-friendly sentence splits first, then clauses.
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    parts: list[str] = []
    # Sentence first
    sentences = re.split(r"(?<=[\.!?])\s+", text)
    for sent in sentences:
        sent = sent.strip()
        if not sent:
            continue
        if word_count(sent) <= 16:
            parts.append(sent)
            continue
        # split on ; : — – or commas when long
        bits = re.split(r"(?<=[;:—,–])\s+|(?<=,)\s+", sent)
        buf = ""
        for b in bits:
            b = b.strip()
            if not b:
                continue
            cand = (buf + " " + b).strip()
            if buf and word_count(cand) > 16:
                parts.append(buf)
                buf = b
            else:
                buf = cand
        if buf:
            parts.append(buf)
    return parts


def pack_cues(text: str, target_lo: int = 8, target_hi: int = 16) -> list[str]:
    clauses = _split_clauses(text)
    cues: list[str] = []
    buf = ""
    for cl in clauses:
        cl = cl.strip()
        if not cl:
            continue
        if not buf:
            buf = cl
            if word_count(buf) >= target_lo and word_count(buf) <= target_hi:
                # keep going if very short
                if word_count(buf) >= target_lo:
                    pass
            continue
        cand = (buf + " " + cl).strip()
        if word_count(cand) <= target_hi:
            buf = cand
        else:
            if word_count(buf) >= 1:
                cues.append(buf)
            buf = cl
            # if a single clause is very long, hard-split by words
            if word_count(buf) > 21:
                words = buf.split()
                chunk = []
                for w in words:
                    chunk.append(w)
                    if len(chunk) >= target_hi:
                        cues.append(" ".join(chunk))
                        chunk = []
                buf = " ".join(chunk)
    if buf:
        cues.append(buf)
    # merge leftover tiny cues into previous
    merged: list[str] = []
    for c in cues:
        if merged and word_count(c) <= 3 and word_count(merged[-1] + " " + c) <= 21:
            merged[-1] = merged[-1] + " " + c
        else:
            merged.append(c)
    return merged


def captions_vtt(continuous: str) -> str:
    cues = pack_cues(continuous)
    t = 0.0
    out = ["WEBVTT", ""]
    for i, cue in enumerate(cues, 1):
        dur = secs_for(cue)
        # match batch 1 style: duration exactly words/2.5
        start, end = t, t + dur
        out.append(str(i))
        out.append(f"{fmt_vtt(start)} --> {fmt_vtt(end)}")
        out.append(wrap_cue(cue))
        out.append("")
        t = end
    return "\n".join(out).rstrip() + "\n"


def write_video(vid: dict) -> dict:
    folder = ROOT / vid["id"]
    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    beats = vid["beats"]
    t = 0.0
    timed = []
    for b in beats:
        dur = secs_for(b["narration"])
        timed.append({**b, "t0": t, "t1": t + dur})
        t += dur
    total_s = t
    total_words = word_count("\n\n".join(b["narration"] for b in beats))
    # continuous script is the narrations joined with blank lines removed into paragraphs
    continuous = "\n\n".join(b["narration"].strip() for b in beats)
    # word count of continuous (same words)
    assert word_count(continuous) == total_words

    draft = fmt_draft(total_s)
    target = vid["target"]

    # BEATS.md
    rows = []
    for i, b in enumerate(timed, 1):
        rows.append(
            f"| {i} | {fmt_mmss(b['t0'])}–{fmt_mmss(b['t1'])} | {b['screen']} | {b['job']} | {b['colour']} |"
        )
    beats_md = "\n".join(
        [
            f"# {vid['id']} — beats sheet",
            "",
            f"**video_id:** {vid['id']}  ",
            f"**Title:** {vid['title']}  ",
            f"**Module / outcome:** {vid['module_outcome']}  ",
            f"**Format:** {vid['format']}  ",
            f"**Target length:** {target}  ",
            f"**Draft length (at 150 wpm):** {draft} (target {target})  ",
            f"**Source pages:** {vid['sources']}  ",
            f"**Why this is a video:** {vid['why']}  ",
            "",
            "## Beats",
            "",
            "| # | Time | What is on screen | Narration job (one sentence) | On-screen words / colour |",
            "|---|---|---|---|---|",
            *rows,
            "",
            "## Production notes",
            "",
            *vid["production"],
            "",
        ]
    )

    nar_parts = [
        f"# {vid['id']} — narration",
        "",
        f"**video_id:** {vid['id']}  ",
        f"**Title:** {vid['title']}  ",
        f"**Word count:** {total_words}  ",
        f"**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** {draft} (target {target})  ",
        "",
        "Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.",
        "",
    ]
    for i, b in enumerate(timed, 1):
        nar_parts.append(f"## Beat {i} ({fmt_mmss(b['t0'])}–{fmt_mmss(b['t1'])})")
        nar_parts.append("")
        nar_parts.append(b["narration"].strip())
        nar_parts.append("")
    nar_parts += [
        "---",
        "",
        "## Continuous script (for the recording booth)",
        "",
        continuous,
        "",
    ]
    narration_md = "\n".join(nar_parts)
    vtt = captions_vtt(continuous)

    (folder / "BEATS.md").write_text(beats_md, encoding="utf-8")
    (folder / "NARRATION.md").write_text(narration_md, encoding="utf-8")
    (folder / "captions.vtt").write_text(vtt, encoding="utf-8")

    return {
        "id": vid["id"],
        "title": vid["title"],
        "format": vid["format"].split(".")[0].strip(),
        "target": target,
        "draft": draft,
        "words": total_words,
        "seconds": total_s,
        "folder": f"stage8/scripts/{vid['id']}/",
        "placeholders": vid.get("placeholders", []),
    }


STD_NOTES = [
    "- Palette: navy text, teal highlights, amber warnings, red for errors, green for a verified number. High contrast. Captions live in `captions.vtt`, not burned in until access-checked.",
    "- Voice: one warm narrator, English, conversational, no jokes at students’ expense. Cantonese / Traditional Chinese versions come later.",
    "- Do not show real student data, CUHK logos in a way that implies approval, or invented policy text. Label synthetic data as synthetic. Label official C&SD / DATA.GOV.HK extracts as official extracts, and FlippedStat calculations as FlippedStat calculations, not as official statistics.",
    "- If a site recording is used: record the v10.4-dev standalone (`build/FlippedStat_v10.4-dev_standalone.html`, SHA-256 `2acbd8967cfc7849b309af8cc1e3f0a5ab0db9c05a2d4eae337cabb522d4f089`); hide any personal profile; pause before each click so captions can land. Do not record older site copy for `#codeprompt`, WebR, or official-extract pages.",
    "- End card version line: FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.4-dev. Do not claim WCAG compliance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. Films are not finished: these files are scripts and captions only.",
]


def notes(*extra: str, visual: str | None = None) -> list[str]:
    items = list(extra)
    if visual:
        items.append(visual)
    items.extend(STD_NOTES)
    return ["- " + x if not x.startswith("- ") else x for x in items]


def visual_paths(module: int, video_id: str, topics: list[str], overview: bool = False) -> str:
    lines = [
        "Matching short Beamer decks (not compiled in this environment) and OpenShot scaffolds (stills only; not finished films):",
    ]
    if overview:
        lines.append(
            f"`stage8/slides/topics/M{module}/M{module}_overview.tex`; OpenShot scaffold `stage8/openshot/projects/M{module}/{video_id}.osp` (currently an 80-second still sequence — do not treat it as timed to this script; this pass does not regenerate `.osp` files)."
        )
    else:
        lines.append(
            f"No dedicated `{video_id}.osp` was generated in this pass. Use the official-topic scaffolds and short decks:"
        )
        deck_bits = []
        for t in topics:
            # find typical tex from known pattern is in manifest; keep generic
            deck_bits.append(f"`#t/{t}` deck under `stage8/slides/topics/M{module}/`; OpenShot `stage8/openshot/projects/M{module}/V-T-{t}.osp`")
        lines.append(" ".join(deck_bits))
    return "- " + " ".join(lines)
