========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/_topic_tools/build_topic_scripts.py ==========

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Draft English topic-level video scripts for official FlippedStat Modules 1-8.

Writes stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-<id>/{BEATS.md,NARRATION.md,captions.vtt}
for every official topic (153). Does not rewrite the 32 programme-map
scripts under stage8/scripts/V-*/. Does not treat Module 9 as official.
Duration method: 150 words/minute on the continuous booth script, same
as the programme-map packs. No ffmpeg. No invented official statistics.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import csv
import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
ROOT = HERE.parents[2]
sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE))
from pack import write_video_to, word_count, secs_for, fmt_draft  # noqa: E402

CATALOG = ROOT / "stage8" / "catalog" / "topic_frames.json"
SPOKEN_JSON = HERE / "official_spoken.json"
INVENTORY = ROOT / "logs" / "HK_DATA_LOCALISATION_INVENTORY_2026-11-18-wave5.csv"
SLIDES_MANIFEST = ROOT / "stage8" / "slides" / "topics" / "manifest.csv"
OUT_ROOT = ROOT / "stage8" / "scripts" / "topics"
LOG = ROOT / "logs" / "stage8_topic_scripts_2026-11-18.md"

SITE_VERSION = "FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev"
SITE_HTML = "build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html"
SITE_SHA = "7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2"
WPM = 150
TARGET = "3–6 minutes"

# Topics whose pages still use a labelled keyed textbook file as the
# teaching object. Scripts must not invent replacement figures.
# Wave-5 topics now have official-extract or labelled-synthetic spoken cards
# in official_spoken.json. C4.8 / C4.9 are also spoken as related-page pointers;
# the companion cards themselves were not rewritten.
DEFERRED_KEYED = {
    # Intentionally empty after wave 5 for official Modules 1-8 topic scripts.
}

NAMED_CASES = {"C4.1", "C4.2", "C4.7", "C4.8", "C4.9"}

STALE = (
    ("every one of the 177 topics", "every official topic in Modules 1 to 8, and the other topics on this site"),
    ("the 177 topics", "the topics on this site"),
    ("177 topics", "the topics on this site"),
)


def tidy(s: str) -> str:
    if not s:
        return ""
    out = str(s)
    for a, b in STALE:
        out = out.replace(a, b)
    out = out.replace("…", "...")
    out = out.replace(" : ", ": ")
    out = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", out).strip()
    if out.endswith("..."):
        cut = out[:-3].rstrip()
        last = max(cut.rfind("."), cut.rfind("!"), cut.rfind("?"))
        if last > 40:
            out = cut[: last + 1]
        else:
            out = cut.rstrip(" ,;:") + "."
    return out


def first_sentences(s: str, n: int = 2) -> str:
    s = tidy(s)
    if not s:
        return ""
    parts = re.split(r"(?<=[\.!?])\s+", s)
    parts = [p.strip() for p in parts if p.strip()]
    return " ".join(parts[:n]).strip()


def load_catalog() -> dict:
    return json.loads(CATALOG.read_text(encoding="utf8"))


def load_spoken() -> dict:
    if SPOKEN_JSON.exists():
        return json.loads(SPOKEN_JSON.read_text(encoding="utf8"))
    return {}


def load_inventory() -> dict:
    out = {}
    if not INVENTORY.exists():
        return out
    with INVENTORY.open(encoding="utf8") as f:
        for row in csv.DictReader(f):
            tid = (row.get("topic_id") or "").strip()
            if tid:
                out[tid] = row
    return out


def load_slide_paths() -> dict:
    out = {}
    if not SLIDES_MANIFEST.exists():
        return out
    with SLIDES_MANIFEST.open(encoding="utf8") as f:
        for row in csv.DictReader(f):
            out[row["topic_id"]] = row.get("tex_path") or ""
    return out


def beamer_path(mod_n: int, tid: str, title: str, slide_map: dict) -> str:
    if tid in slide_map and slide_map[tid]:
        return slide_map[tid]
    folder = ROOT / "stage8" / "slides" / "topics" / f"M{mod_n}"
    hits = sorted(folder.glob(f"T-{tid}_*.tex"))
    if hits:
        return str(hits[0].relative_to(ROOT))
    return f"stage8/slides/topics/M{mod_n}/T-{tid}_*.tex"


def osp_path(mod_n: int, tid: str) -> str:
    return f"stage8/openshot/projects/M{mod_n}/V-T-{tid}.osp"


def context_label(tid: str, inv: dict, spoken: dict) -> str:
    if tid in spoken:
        kind = spoken[tid].get("kind") or "official extract"
        return f"This topic already uses a labelled {kind} on the site."
    row = inv.get(tid) or {}
    kind = (row.get("US_or_generic_or_already_HK") or "").strip()
    action = (row.get("action_taken_or_deferred") or "").strip()
    if kind == "already-HK" or action == "already-HK-kept":
        return "This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table."
    if kind == "mixed-US-and-HK":
        return "This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible."
    if kind in {"US-or-textbook"} or action in {"deferred", "textbook-illustration-kept", "case-study-deferred"}:
        return "The site still uses a labelled textbook or overseas illustration here. Copyright clearance is later. This video adapts the teaching point and does not copy book prose, and it does not invent official Hong Kong statistics."
    return "This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page."


def format_for(topic: dict) -> str:
    act = (topic.get("activity") or "").lower()
    if any(k in act for k in ("lab", "audit", "assessment", "exam", "probe", "placement", "capstone")):
        return "site-screencast (motion-graphics stills allowed until the recording). No live-action people."
    return "motion-graphics (digital blackboard allowed). No live-action people."


def script_frames(topic: dict) -> dict:
    fr = topic.get("frames") or {}
    long = fr.get("frames_script") or {}
    return {
        "bridge": tidy(long.get("bridge") or fr.get("bridge") or ""),
        "concept": tidy(long.get("concept") or fr.get("concept") or ""),
        "interp": [tidy(x) for x in (long.get("interp") or fr.get("interp") or []) if tidy(x)],
        "summary": tidy(long.get("summary") or fr.get("summary") or ""),
        "pitfalls": [tidy(x) for x in (long.get("pitfalls") or fr.get("pitfalls") or []) if tidy(x)],
    }


def cross_block(tid: str) -> str:
    variants = [
        "This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number.",
        "Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify.",
        "Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it.",
        "Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify.",
    ]
    # stable, not random
    idx = sum(ord(ch) for ch in tid) % len(variants)
    return variants[idx]


def why_video(topic: dict, fact: dict | None) -> str:
    if fact:
        return "A short one-concept video can hold the official or labelled figures still, and keep book illustrations visibly separate."
    title = (topic.get("title") or "").lower()
    if any(k in title for k in ("lab", "audit", "copilot")):
        return "A process — drafting with a tool, then verifying — is easier to follow on a short screencast than on a static page alone."
    return "The idea is a process or a distinction, and a short one-concept video can hold it still before the student opens the page."


def beat1(topic, mod, label: str) -> dict:
    tid = topic["id"]
    title = topic["title"]
    essential = " It is marked essential on the official map." if topic.get("essential") else ""
    hours = topic.get("hours")
    hours_bit = f" The official map budgets {hours:g} hour" + ("s" if hours != 1 else "") + " of study time for the page, not for this video." if isinstance(hours, (int, float)) and hours else ""
    unit = topic.get("unit") or {}
    unit_bit = ""
    if isinstance(unit, dict) and unit.get("title"):
        unit_bit = f" It sits in the unit {unit.get('id','')}: {unit.get('title')}."
    extra = ""
    if tid == "1.1":
        extra = " The site currently lists 231 topics in all; 153 of those are official topics in Modules 1 to 8. Module 9 is an optional extension and is not treated as official in this video. A twenty-item placement test is on the page. Cut scores are a human decision and are not restated here."
    nar = (
        f"This short video is Topic {tid}: {title}, in official Module {mod['n']}, {mod['title']}.{essential}{unit_bit}{hours_bit} "
        f"{label} I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, "
        f"I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision.{extra} "
        "When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract."
    )
    return {
        "screen": f"Title card: Topic {tid}: {title}. Module {mod['n']}. Label the data source. No people, no crest that would imply approval.",
        "job": "Name the official topic, label the data source, and say what the video will not do.",
        "colour": "Title in navy; source label in teal or amber; “not an institutional approval” in muted grey",
        "narration": " ".join(nar.split()),
    }


def beat_idea(topic, fr: dict) -> dict:
    tid = topic["id"]
    bridge = first_sentences(fr.get("bridge") or "", 2)
    concept = first_sentences(fr.get("concept") or "", 3)
    if not concept:
        concept = f"Topic {tid} asks you to master one idea and then check it on the site. The worked path lives on the page, not in a new claim I might add here."
    lead = f"Here is where we open. {bridge} " if bridge else ""
    nar = (
        f"{lead}The idea, in plain language, is this. {concept} "
        "Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third."
    )
    return {
        "screen": f"A short blackboard statement of the idea for Topic {tid}, paraphrased from the official page, not a verbatim extract.",
        "job": "State the teaching idea in conversational language, without reading the page verbatim.",
        "colour": "Idea in navy; “understand first, draft second, verify third” in teal",
        "narration": " ".join(nar.split()),
    }


def beat_read(fr: dict) -> dict:
    interps = fr.get("interp") or []
    if interps:
        body = " ".join(first_sentences(x, 2) for x in interps[:3])
        nar = (
            f"Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. {body} "
            "If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in."
        )
    else:
        nar = (
            "Once you have the idea, read any result slowly. Ask what the unit is, what was included, and what was left out. "
            "The official page walks the worked path in more detail than this short video. I will not invent a worked number just to fill the time."
        )
    return {
        "screen": "Two or three reading points, paraphrased, with the unit and the scope left visible.",
        "job": "Show how to read a result from this topic, without adding unsourced figures.",
        "colour": "Reading points in navy; unit and scope in teal",
        "narration": " ".join(nar.split()),
    }


def beat_example(tid: str, topic: dict, fact: dict | None, inv: dict) -> dict:
    placeholders = []
    if fact:
        nar = fact["spoken"].strip()
        return {
            "screen": fact["screen"],
            "job": fact["job"],
            "colour": fact["colour"],
            "narration": " ".join(nar.split()),
            "placeholders": fact.get("placeholders") or [],
        }
    # No official-extract card. Stay qualitative.
    row = inv.get(tid) or {}
    kind = (row.get("US_or_generic_or_already_HK") or "").strip()
    action = (row.get("action_taken_or_deferred") or "").strip()
    if tid in NAMED_CASES:
        nar = (
            "This official topic is built around a named historical or book case study. "
            "That case stays on the page, clearly labelled. This video does not relocate it to a Hong Kong official table, "
            "because no extract already in the course is a clean drop-in match, and copyright clearance is later. "
            "Use the case to practise the method — the design, the comparison, or the audit — and do not treat its book figures as official Hong Kong statistics. "
            "I will not invent a parallel official figure here."
        )
        placeholders.append("Named case figures stay on the topic page; not restated in this script.")
    elif tid in DEFERRED_KEYED or action in {"deferred", "case-study-deferred"}:
        nar = (
            "The worked numbers on this page stay on the page. Some of them still sit in a labelled textbook file, "
            "or in a design that official monthly or district series would not honestly support as an independent sample. "
            "Copyright clearance is later, and a coordinated recompute would be needed before those keys move. "
            "This video therefore stays with the method: what to count, what to check, and what not to pretend the data are. "
            "I will not invent an official Hong Kong figure as a stand-in, and I will not read a keyed book table aloud."
        )
        placeholders.append("Keyed page figures are not restated in this script; confirm them on the topic page.")
    elif kind == "already-HK" or action == "already-HK-kept":
        nar = (
            "The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. "
            "Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, "
            "and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. "
            "Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video."
        )
        placeholders.append("Synthetic Hong Kong keyed figures stay on the topic page; not restated here unless already in the official-extract card.")
    else:
        nar = (
            "The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. "
            "This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. "
            "When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. "
            "If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration."
        )
        placeholders.append("Any keyed worked figure for this topic remains on the page; not restated in this script.")
    return {
        "screen": "A clearly labelled example card: official extract, synthetic Hong Kong, or labelled book illustration, as on the page. No unsourced numbers.",
        "job": "Keep the topic’s example labelled, and refuse to invent or transcribe unsourced figures.",
        "colour": "Source label in teal or amber; “figures on the page” in navy; no green verified number unless it is an official-extract key",
        "narration": " ".join(nar.split()),
        "placeholders": placeholders,
    }


def beat_pitfalls(fr: dict) -> dict:
    pits = fr.get("pitfalls") or []
    if pits:
        body = " ".join(first_sentences(x, 2) for x in pits[:3])
        nar = (
            f"A few mistakes show up often on this topic. {body} "
            "None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion."
        )
    else:
        nar = (
            "A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. "
            "Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. "
            "If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check."
        )
    return {
        "screen": "Two or three amber caution lines, paraphrased from the official page.",
        "job": "Name the common mistakes, without introducing new figures.",
        "colour": "Cautions in amber; “not a verified number” stays off the green channel",
        "narration": " ".join(nar.split()),
    }


def beat_cross(tid: str, fr: dict) -> dict:
    summary = first_sentences(fr.get("summary") or "", 2)
    mid = f" The short close on the page is this. {summary}" if summary else ""
    nar = cross_block(tid) + mid
    return {
        "screen": "C.R.O.S.S. checklist: Count, Recompute, Other tools, Statistical principles, Sources and scope. “AI writes; you verify.”",
        "job": "Walk the verification contract and remind the student that a model is not the referee.",
        "colour": "Five ticks in teal; “AI writes; you verify” in navy; “record sources and scope” in amber",
        "narration": " ".join(nar.split()),
    }


def beat_end(topic, mod, beamer: str, osp: str) -> dict:
    tid = topic["id"]
    hash_ = topic.get("hash") or f"#t/{tid}"
    nar = (
        f"That is the one idea for Topic {tid}. Open {hash_} on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, "
        f"using {SITE_HTML} — SHA-256 {SITE_SHA} — or a later standalone if one has been issued. "
        f"The matching short Beamer deck is {beamer}. The editable OpenShot project is {osp}, still a still sequence, not a finished film. "
        f"The end-card version line is {SITE_VERSION}. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. "
        "When you are ready, go to the page, and verify."
    )
    return {
        "screen": f"End card: {hash_}; short Beamer path; OpenShot path; version line {SITE_VERSION}. No crest, no approval claim.",
        "job": "Point back to the official page, the short deck, and the OpenShot project, with no new claims.",
        "colour": "Hashes and paths in teal; version line in muted grey; last verified labels in green only if already used",
        "narration": " ".join(nar.split()),
    }


def production_notes(topic, mod, beamer: str, osp: str, fact: dict | None, placeholders: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    tid = topic["id"]
    notes = []
    if fact:
        notes.append(
            f"- Official-extract or labelled-synthetic framing for Topic {tid} follows the v10.8-dev page and the short Beamer official-data or labelled-synthetic frame. "
            "Worked numbers are FlippedStat calculations on official figures unless a line says they are official published totals. "
            "They are not to be described as official C&SD or HKO statistics when they are calculations."
        )
        if fact.get("file"):
            notes.append(f"- Student-facing file or series: `{fact['file']}`.")
    notes.append(
        "- Matching short Beamer deck (source; PDFs may be absent until a TeX engine is available) and OpenShot project "
        f"(editable stills; not a finished film): `{beamer}`; `{osp}`."
    )
    if placeholders:
        for p in placeholders:
            notes.append(f"- PLACEHOLDER: {p}")
    notes.extend(
        [
            "- Palette: navy text, teal highlights, amber warnings, red for errors, green for a verified number. High contrast. Captions live in `captions.vtt`, not burned in until access-checked.",
            "- Voice: one warm narrator, English, conversational, no jokes at students’ expense. Cantonese / Traditional Chinese versions come later.",
            "- Do not show real student data, CUHK logos in a way that implies approval, or invented policy text. Label official extracts, FlippedStat calculations, synthetic Hong Kong data, and book illustrations as such.",
            f"- If a site recording is used: record the v10.8-dev standalone (`{SITE_HTML}`, SHA-256 `{SITE_SHA}`, 20,452,306 bytes); hide any personal profile; pause before each click so captions can land. Do not invent figures that are not on the recorded page. Do not record v10.7-dev or earlier for wave-5 official-extract or labelled-synthetic parallels.",
            f"- End card version line: {SITE_VERSION}. Do not claim WCAG compliance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. Films are not finished: these files are scripts and captions only. Copyright clearance is deferred; adapt teaching points, and do not copy textbook or other third-party prose verbatim. This pass is not a legal sign-off.",
            "- Do not restate placement cut scores, certificate wording, or H1–H11 decisions.",
        ]
    )
    return notes


def build_entry(mod: dict, topic: dict, spoken: dict, inv: dict, slide_map: dict) -> dict:
    tid = topic["id"]
    fact = spoken.get(tid)
    fr = script_frames(topic)
    label = context_label(tid, inv, spoken)
    beamer = beamer_path(mod["n"], tid, topic.get("title") or tid, slide_map)
    osp = osp_path(mod["n"], tid)
    example = beat_example(tid, topic, fact, inv)
    placeholders = list(example.get("placeholders") or [])
    beats = [
        beat1(topic, mod, label),
        beat_idea(topic, fr),
        beat_read(fr),
        example,
        beat_pitfalls(fr),
        beat_cross(tid, fr),
        beat_end(topic, mod, beamer, osp),
    ]
    # Drop helper key
    for b in beats:
        b.pop("placeholders", None)
    outcome = f"Module {mod['n']} — Topic {tid}: {topic.get('title')}. One-concept topic video; official Modules 1–8 only."
    return {
        "id": f"V-T-{tid}",
        "title": f"{tid}: {topic.get('title')}",
        "module_outcome": outcome,
        "format": format_for(topic),
        "target": TARGET,
        "sources": f"Topic {tid} ({topic.get('hash') or '#'+'t/'+tid}) on {SITE_HTML}. Catalog: stage8/catalog/topic_frames.json (teaching frames extracted from v10.7-dev; wave-5 official or labelled-synthetic figures follow v10.8-dev).",
        "why": why_video(topic, fact),
        "beats": beats,
        "production": production_notes(topic, mod, beamer, osp, fact, placeholders),
        "placeholders": placeholders,
        "module": mod["n"],
        "topic_id": tid,
        "official_extract": bool(fact),
        "beamer": beamer,
        "osp": osp,
    }


def maybe_pad_or_trim(vid: dict) -> dict:
    """Keep drafts inside 3–6 minutes at 150 wpm without inventing figures."""
    words = word_count(" ".join(b["narration"] for b in vid["beats"]))
    # Under ~3:00 (450 words): add a short practice reminder to the CROSS beat.
    if words < 450:
        extra = (
            " When you open the page, do one small practice pass: write the question in your own words, "
            "name the dataset and its label, and recompute one figure that the page already shows. "
            "If you cannot point to the source of a number, leave that number out of your notes."
        )
        # CROSS is the second-to-last beat
        vid["beats"][-2]["narration"] = vid["beats"][-2]["narration"].rstrip() + extra
    words = word_count(" ".join(b["narration"] for b in vid["beats"]))
    # Over 6:00 (900 words): rare; shorten reading beat to first two sentences of narration.
    if words > 900:
        vid["beats"][2]["narration"] = first_sentences(vid["beats"][2]["narration"], 3)
        if not vid["beats"][2]["narration"].endswith("."):
            vid["beats"][2]["narration"] += "."
        vid["placeholders"] = list(vid.get("placeholders") or []) + [
            "Reading beat shortened to keep the 150 wpm draft inside 6 minutes; fuller wording stays on the topic page."
        ]
    return vid


def write_log(rows: list[dict], missing: list[str], catalog: dict) -> None:
    official_ids = []
    for m in catalog["modules"]:
        if m["n"] <= 8:
            official_ids.extend(t["id"] for t in m["topics"])
    n_off = sum(1 for r in rows if r.get("official_extract"))
    n_ph = sum(1 for r in rows if r.get("placeholders"))
    dur_lo = min((r["seconds"] for r in rows), default=0)
    dur_hi = max((r["seconds"] for r in rows), default=0)
    words_lo = min((r["words"] for r in rows), default=0)
    words_hi = max((r["words"] for r in rows), default=0)
    under = [r["id"] for r in rows if r["words"] < 450]
    over = [r["id"] for r in rows if r["words"] > 900]
    lines = [
        "# Stage 8 official topic video scripts (18 November 2026, Asia/Hong_Kong)",
        "",
        "English one-concept scripts for every official Modules 1–8 topic. Module 9 was not scripted. Films are not finished. Programme-map scripts under `stage8/scripts/V-*/` were not rewritten.",
        "",
        f"**Count:** {len(rows)} of 153 official topics written under `stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-<id>/`. Missing IDs: {', '.join(missing) if missing else 'none'}.",
        "",
        f"**Duration method:** 150 words/minute on the continuous booth script, the same method as the 32 programme-map packs (`stage8/scripts/_batch2_tools/pack.py` / `stage8/scripts/_topic_tools/pack.py`). Target length 3–6 minutes (450–900 words). Draft range: {fmt_draft(dur_lo)}–{fmt_draft(dur_hi)} ({words_lo}–{words_hi} words).",
        "",
        f"**Official-extract topics with spoken keys:** {n_off} (waves 1–4: 1.3, 2.1, 2.2, 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 6.3, 6.5, 9.7, 10.3, 10.6, 11.4, E5.2). Other topics stay qualitative or point at page figures; they do not invent official statistics.",
        "",
        f"**Placeholder notes (keyed or unsourced figures left on the page):** {n_ph} scripts. See each folder’s production notes.",
        "",
        f"**Source for facts:** `{catalog.get('source_html')}` and `stage8/catalog/topic_frames.json`. End-card version line: {SITE_VERSION}. SHA-256 of v10.7-dev: `{SITE_SHA}`. v10.8-dev was not present when these scripts were drafted.",
        "",
        "Each folder contains `BEATS.md`, `NARRATION.md`, and `captions.vtt`, and points editors at the matching short Beamer deck and OpenShot `.osp` path. Pedagogy: AI writes / student verifies (C.R.O.S.S.).",
        "",
        "Optional Module 9 topic scripts were not written in this pass.",
        "",
        "H1–H11, cut scores, and certificate wording were not changed. Copyright clearance is deferred; scripts adapt teaching points and do not copy textbook prose verbatim. This is not a legal sign-off.",
        "",
        "## Drafts outside the 3–6 minute window (after padding/trim)",
        "",
        f"- Under 3:00 after padding: {', '.join(under) if under else 'none'}",
        f"- Over 6:00 after trim: {', '.join(over) if over else 'none'}",
        "",
        "## Paths",
        "",
        "- Scripts: `stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-<id>/`",
        "- Generator: `stage8/scripts/_topic_tools/build_topic_scripts.py`",
        "- Official-extract spoken keys: `stage8/scripts/_topic_tools/official_spoken.json`",
        "- This log: `logs/stage8_topic_scripts_2026-11-18.md`",
        "",
        "## Per-topic draft lengths",
        "",
        "| video_id | Title | Words | Draft (150 wpm) | Official extract | Placeholders | Folder |",
        "|---|---|---:|---|---|---|---|",
    ]
    for r in rows:
        ph = "yes" if r.get("placeholders") else "no"
        oe = "yes" if r.get("official_extract") else "no"
        folder = f"stage8/scripts/topics/{r['id']}/"
        lines.append(
            f"| {r['id']} | {r['title']} | {r['words']} | {r['draft']} | {oe} | {ph} | `{folder}` |"
        )
    lines.append("")
    LOG.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    LOG.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf8")


def main() -> int:
    import argparse
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--only", nargs="*", default=None, help="Rebuild only these official topic ids (e.g. 5.6 7.2). Does not rewrite the all-topics log.")
    ap.add_argument("--no-log", action="store_true", help="Do not rewrite logs/stage8_topic_scripts_2026-11-18.md")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    only = set(args.only) if args.only else None
    catalog = load_catalog()
    spoken = load_spoken()
    inv = load_inventory()
    slide_map = load_slide_paths()
    OUT_ROOT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    rows = []
    written_ids = []
    for mod in catalog["modules"]:
        if mod["n"] > 8:
            continue
        for topic in mod["topics"]:
            if only is not None and topic["id"] not in only:
                continue
            vid = build_entry(mod, topic, spoken, inv, slide_map)
            vid = maybe_pad_or_trim(vid)
            folder = OUT_ROOT / vid["id"]
            rec = write_video_to(folder, vid)
            rec["official_extract"] = vid["official_extract"]
            rec["placeholders"] = vid.get("placeholders") or []
            rec["title"] = vid["title"]
            rec["folder"] = f"stage8/scripts/topics/{vid['id']}/"
            rows.append(rec)
            written_ids.append(topic["id"])
            print(f"wrote {rec['folder']} {rec['draft']} {rec['words']}w")
    official_ids = []
    for m in catalog["modules"]:
        if m["n"] <= 8:
            official_ids.extend(t["id"] for t in m["topics"])
    if only is not None:
        missing = [i for i in only if i not in written_ids]
        print(f"done {len(rows)} selected scripts; missing={missing or 'none'}")
        return 1 if missing else 0
    missing = [i for i in official_ids if i not in written_ids]
    if not args.no_log:
        write_log(rows, missing, catalog)
        print(f"done {len(rows)} scripts; missing={missing or 'none'}; log={LOG.relative_to(ROOT)}")
    else:
        print(f"done {len(rows)} scripts; missing={missing or 'none'}; log skipped")
    return 1 if missing else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/_topic_tools/pack.py ==========

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Timing, VTT packing, and folder write helpers for Stage 8 topic scripts.

Matches the programme-map house style: 150 words/minute, cue packing from
`stage8/scripts/_batch2_tools/pack.py`, and the same BEATS / NARRATION /
captions.vtt layout.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re
import textwrap
from pathlib import Path

WPM = 150
LINE_WIDTH = 42


def word_count(text: str) -> int:
    return len((text or "").split())


def secs_for(text: str) -> float:
    return word_count(text) / WPM * 60.0


def fmt_mmss(seconds: float) -> str:
    seconds = max(0, int(round(seconds)))
    m, s = divmod(seconds, 60)
    return f"{m}:{s:02d}"


def fmt_draft(seconds: float) -> str:
    m, rem = divmod(int(round(seconds)), 60)
    return f"{m}:{rem:02d}"


def fmt_vtt(seconds: float) -> str:
    if seconds < 0:
        seconds = 0
    ms_total = int(round(seconds * 1000))
    h, rem = divmod(ms_total, 3_600_000)
    m, rem = divmod(rem, 60_000)
    s, ms = divmod(rem, 1000)
    return f"{h:02d}:{m:02d}:{s:02d}.{ms:03d}"


def wrap_cue(text: str, width: int = LINE_WIDTH) -> str:
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    return "\n".join(textwrap.wrap(text, width=width, break_long_words=False, break_on_hyphens=False))


def _split_clauses(text: str) -> list[str]:
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    parts: list[str] = []
    sentences = re.split(r"(?<=[\.!?])\s+", text)
    for sent in sentences:
        sent = sent.strip()
        if not sent:
            continue
        if word_count(sent) <= 16:
            parts.append(sent)
            continue
        bits = re.split(r"(?<=[;:—,–])\s+|(?<=,)\s+", sent)
        buf = ""
        for b in bits:
            b = b.strip()
            if not b:
                continue
            cand = (buf + " " + b).strip()
            if buf and word_count(cand) > 16:
                parts.append(buf)
                buf = b
            else:
                buf = cand
        if buf:
            parts.append(buf)
    return parts


def pack_cues(text: str, target_lo: int = 8, target_hi: int = 16) -> list[str]:
    clauses = _split_clauses(text)
    cues: list[str] = []
    buf = ""
    for cl in clauses:
        cl = cl.strip()
        if not cl:
            continue
        if not buf:
            buf = cl
            continue
        cand = (buf + " " + cl).strip()
        if word_count(cand) <= target_hi:
            buf = cand
        else:
            if word_count(buf) >= 1:
                cues.append(buf)
            buf = cl
            if word_count(buf) > 21:
                words = buf.split()
                chunk = []
                for w in words:
                    chunk.append(w)
                    if len(chunk) >= target_hi:
                        cues.append(" ".join(chunk))
                        chunk = []
                buf = " ".join(chunk)
    if buf:
        cues.append(buf)
    merged: list[str] = []
    for c in cues:
        if merged and word_count(c) <= 3 and word_count(merged[-1] + " " + c) <= 21:
            merged[-1] = merged[-1] + " " + c
        else:
            merged.append(c)
    return merged


def captions_vtt(continuous: str) -> str:
    cues = pack_cues(continuous)
    t = 0.0
    out = ["WEBVTT", ""]
    for i, cue in enumerate(cues, 1):
        dur = secs_for(cue)
        start, end = t, t + dur
        out.append(str(i))
        out.append(f"{fmt_vtt(start)} --> {fmt_vtt(end)}")
        out.append(wrap_cue(cue))
        out.append("")
        t = end
    return "\n".join(out).rstrip() + "\n"


def write_video_to(folder: Path, vid: dict) -> dict:
    """Write BEATS.md, NARRATION.md and captions.vtt into folder."""
    folder = Path(folder)
    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    beats = vid["beats"]
    t = 0.0
    timed = []
    for b in beats:
        dur = secs_for(b["narration"])
        timed.append({**b, "t0": t, "t1": t + dur})
        t += dur
    total_s = t
    continuous = "\n\n".join(b["narration"].strip() for b in beats)
    total_words = word_count(continuous)
    draft = fmt_draft(total_s)
    target = vid["target"]

    rows = []
    for i, b in enumerate(timed, 1):
        rows.append(
            f"| {i} | {fmt_mmss(b['t0'])}–{fmt_mmss(b['t1'])} | {b['screen']} | {b['job']} | {b['colour']} |"
        )
    beats_md = "\n".join(
        [
            f"# {vid['id']} — beats sheet",
            "",
            f"**video_id:** {vid['id']}  ",
            f"**Title:** {vid['title']}  ",
            f"**Module / outcome:** {vid['module_outcome']}  ",
            f"**Format:** {vid['format']}  ",
            f"**Target length:** {target}  ",
            f"**Draft length (at 150 wpm):** {draft} (target {target})  ",
            f"**Source pages:** {vid['sources']}  ",
            f"**Why this is a video:** {vid['why']}  ",
            "",
            "## Beats",
            "",
            "| # | Time | What is on screen | Narration job (one sentence) | On-screen words / colour |",
            "|---|---|---|---|---|",
            *rows,
            "",
            "## Production notes",
            "",
            *vid["production"],
            "",
        ]
    )

    nar_parts = [
        f"# {vid['id']} — narration",
        "",
        f"**video_id:** {vid['id']}  ",
        f"**Title:** {vid['title']}  ",
        f"**Word count:** {total_words}  ",
        f"**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** {draft} (target {target})  ",
        "",
        "Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.",
        "",
    ]
    for i, b in enumerate(timed, 1):
        nar_parts.append(f"## Beat {i} ({fmt_mmss(b['t0'])}–{fmt_mmss(b['t1'])})")
        nar_parts.append("")
        nar_parts.append(b["narration"].strip())
        nar_parts.append("")
    nar_parts += [
        "---",
        "",
        "## Continuous script (for the recording booth)",
        "",
        continuous,
        "",
    ]
    narration_md = "\n".join(nar_parts)
    vtt = captions_vtt(continuous)

    (folder / "BEATS.md").write_text(beats_md, encoding="utf-8")
    (folder / "NARRATION.md").write_text(narration_md, encoding="utf-8")
    (folder / "captions.vtt").write_text(vtt, encoding="utf-8")

    return {
        "id": vid["id"],
        "title": vid["title"],
        "format": vid.get("format", "").split(".")[0].strip(),
        "target": target,
        "draft": draft,
        "words": total_words,
        "seconds": total_s,
        "folder": str(folder).replace("\\", "/"),
        "placeholders": vid.get("placeholders", []),
        "n_beats": len(timed),
    }

def card(kind, file, screen, colour, job, spoken, placeholders=None):
    return {
        "kind": kind,
        "file": file,
        "screen": screen,
        "colour": colour,
        "job": job,
        "spoken": spoken,
        "placeholders": list(placeholders or []),
    }


def tex_frame(title, blurb, heading, items):
    lines = [
        "\\begin{frame}{" + title + "}",
        "{\\footnotesize " + blurb + "}",
        "\\begin{block}{" + heading + "}",
        "\\begin{itemize}",
    ]
    for it in items:
        lines.append("  \\item " + it)
    lines.extend(["\\end{itemize}", "\\end{block}", "\\end{frame}", ""])
    return "\n".join(lines)


def official_frame(blurb, heading, items):
    return tex_frame("Hong Kong official-data illustration", blurb, heading, items)


def synthetic_frame(blurb, heading, items):
    return tex_frame("Hong Kong labelled-synthetic illustration", blurb, heading, items)

def merge_spoken(existing: dict) -> dict:
    """Keep wave 1-4 spoken cards; add or replace only wave-5 keys."""
    out = dict(existing)
    out.update(SPOKEN)
    return out


def merge_frames(existing: dict) -> dict:
    """Keep wave 1-4 official-data frames; add or replace only wave-5 keys."""
    out = dict(existing)
    out.update(FRAMES)
    return out

# Official topic video scripts (Modules 1–8)

One folder per official topic, named `V-T-<id>`. Each folder has the same house style as the 32 programme-map packs:

- `BEATS.md` — timed beats, on-screen action, narration job, colour notes
- `NARRATION.md` — full English narration plus a continuous booth script
- `captions.vtt` — WEBVTT at 150 words/minute

These are scripts, not finished films. Matching short Beamer decks live under `stage8/slides/topics/`, and editable OpenShot projects under `stage8/openshot/projects/M*/V-T-<id>.osp`.

Regenerate (does not touch `stage8/scripts/V-*/`):

```bash
python3 stage8/scripts/_topic_tools/build_topic_scripts.py
```

Optional Module 9 is not included. Copyright clearance is deferred; scripts adapt teaching points and do not copy textbook prose. H1–H11, cut scores, and certificate wording are not restated as approved.

========== END FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/README.md ==========

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-1.1/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-1.1 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-1.1  
**Title:** 1.1: Course map and placement  
**Word count:** 749  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:00 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–1:16)

This short video is Topic 1.1: Course map and placement, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It sits in the unit W1: Starting Out: Statistical Questions and an AI Workbench. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. The site currently lists 231 topics in all; 153 of those are official topics in Modules 1 to 8. Module 9 is an optional extension and is not treated as official in this video. A twenty-item placement test is on the page. Cut scores are a human decision and are not restated here. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (1:16–1:51)

Here is where we open. Welcome. Before any statistics, here is the routine you will follow in every one of the 231 topics on this site. The idea, in plain language, is this. FlippedStat runs every topic through the same seven-stage learning loop: question → concept → worked example → AI assistance → human verification → interpretation → practice. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:51–2:36)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. You meet new ideas on your own first, then spend class time doing statistics while help is nearby. That is what “flipped” means. The order is the point. You frame the question and understand the idea before you ask AI anything, so you have something to compare its answer with. Notice where the time goes in the chart below: human verification is the biggest slice. In this course checking is not an extra; it is the main skill. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:36–3:14)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (3:14–3:41)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Treating the AI stage as the 'answer' stage. In FlippedStat it is a drafting stage. Skipping the question stage because it feels obvious — most analysis errors start with a vague question. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:41–4:26)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Seven stages, always in the same order. Understand first, ask AI second, verify third.

# V-T-1.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-1.2  
**Title:** 1.2: What statistics is  
**Word count:** 693  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:37 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:57)

This short video is Topic 1.2: What statistics is, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W1: Starting Out: Statistical Questions and an AI Workbench. The official map budgets 1.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:57–1:34)

Here is where we open. Imagine you are deciding what question the data can answer — before anyone has opened a file. The idea, in plain language, is this. A statistical question is one you expect to answer with data that vary . “How tall am I?” has one answer. “How long do CUHK first-years commute?” has a different answer for every student. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:34–2:19)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. A good statistical question names who (the group), what (the variable) and often compared with what . “Do hall residents sleep more than students who live at home?” names all three. Vague questions make vague analyses. “Is social media bad?” cannot be analysed until you decide: bad for which outcome, for whom, measured how, compared with whom? Sharpening the question is a human job. AI can suggest versions; only you know what decision the answer must support. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:19–2:57)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:57–3:24)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Writing a question that contains no group (who?) — you cannot decide what data to collect. Hiding a causal claim inside the question ('Does X cause Y?') when only observational data are possible. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:24–4:04)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Statistical questions expect variability. Name who, what and compared with what.

## Beat 7 (4:04–4:37)

That is the one idea for Topic 1.2. Open #t/1.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M1/T-1.2_What_statistics_is.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M1/V-T-1.2.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. # V-T-1.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-1.3  
**Title:** 1.3: Variables and measurement  
**Word count:** 729  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:52 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic 1.3: Variables and measurement, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W1: Starting Out: Statistical Questions and an AI Workbench. The official map budgets 2.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:29)

Here is where we open. Imagine you must classify a variable before summarising it: is “year of study, 1–4” a number to average or a label to count? The idea, in plain language, is this. Variables come in four scales: nominal (names, no order), ordinal (ordered, gaps unknown), interval (equal gaps, no true zero) and ratio (equal gaps and a true zero). Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:29–2:16)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Faculty is nominal: Science is not “more” than Arts. Satisfaction 1–5 is ordinal: 4 beats 3, but the step 3→4 need not equal 1→2. Temperature in °C is interval: 20 °C is not “twice as hot” as 10 °C. Commute minutes is ratio: 60 minutes really is twice 30. The scale decides which summaries make sense. A mean of faculty codes (1–5) is meaningless — a classic H2 wrong-method error that AI tools make when categories are stored as numbers. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:16–3:15)

The student-facing classification example is now an official extract: the file hk_district_profile_2016_2025.csv, built from Census and Statistics Department tables 110-02001 and 130-06806, retrieved on 18 November 2026. There is one row for each of the 18 District Council districts. The column region_en is categorical and nominal: Hong Kong Island, Kowloon, or the New Territories. district_en is a name, and district_code is a label, not a number to average. Mid-year land population is numerical, and discrete in origin — a count, published in thousands. The 2025 median monthly household income, in Hong Kong dollars, is numerical on a ratio scale, but it is a district median, not one household’s income. A derived flag, population_gained, is a FlippedStat calculation, not an official C and SD field. OpenIntro’s US-county typings, including median education, remain on the page as a labelled book illustration, because this extract has no official ordinal education variable.

## Beat 5 (3:15–3:40)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Averaging codes for nominal categories. Saying '30 °C is twice as hot as 15 °C'. Treating typhoon signals or exam grades (A, B, C) as equally spaced numbers. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:40–4:18)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio — order matters, gaps matter, zero matters. The scale decides which summaries are allowed.

## Beat 7 (4:18–4:52)

That is the one idea for Topic 1.3. Open #t/1.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M1/T-1.3_Variables_and_measurement.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M1/V-T-1.3.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-1.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-1.4  
**Title:** 1.4: AI tools at CUHK  
**Word count:** 623  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:09 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:51)

This short video is Topic 1.4: AI tools at CUHK, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It sits in the unit W1: Starting Out: Statistical Questions and an AI Workbench. The official map budgets 0.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract (course referee file) on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:51–1:32)

Here is where we open. Imagine you can now frame a question and type your variables. Next: the AI tools you will use to help — and their limits. The idea, in plain language, is this. Copilot Chat (signed in with your CUHK account) is the standard tool in this course. Some versions can write and run code ; others only generate text . Your first job is to know which you are using. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:32–2:18)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Microsoft 365 Copilot (where licensed) works inside Word, Excel, Outlook and Teams and can draw on your own work files; availability depends on your licence. Features change often. When a lab depends on a feature (file upload, code execution), check the current behaviour yourself — don't trust last term's notes, or this page. The chart sorts typical tasks by whether a tool can really do them. “Compute a mean exactly” needs code execution; text alone only guesses . If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:18–2:44)

Official Census and Statistics Department and Hong Kong Observatory teaching extracts bundled in this course — for example the file hk_district_profile_2016_2025.csv — are course files you may use in labs. An AI summary of an official extract is not itself an official statistic. Formal rights clearance of third-party sources remains deferred and is not claimed as done. The checks on this page were not changed.

## Beat 5 (2:44–3:03)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Assuming every Copilot surface can see the same files or run code. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:03–3:36)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Copilot Chat with CUHK sign-in is the course tool. Look for code + output before trusting a number.

## Beat 7 (3:36–4:09)

That is the one idea for Topic 1.4. Open #t/1.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M1/T-1.4_AI_tools_at_CUHK.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M1/V-T-1.4.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-1.5 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-1.5  
**Title:** 1.5: How a language model produces a number  
**Word count:** 704  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:42 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–1:00)

This short video is Topic 1.5: How a language model produces a number, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W1: Starting Out: Statistical Questions and an AI Workbench. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (1:00–1:40)

Here is where we open. Imagine you now know what to upload. Next, what actually happens when a chatbot gives you a number. The idea, in plain language, is this. A language model writes text by predicting a likely next piece of text (a token). A number written that way is generated , not computed. Some assistants can also execute code — and a number from executed code is computed. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:40–2:20)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. From outside the two look the same. Your clue is a code block with output , or a note that an analysis was run. Even executed code can be wrong: the wrong column, blanks treated as zeros. Execution removes arithmetic guessing; it does not remove judgement errors . So the rule for this course: demand code, read the code, check one number yourself . If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:20–2:58)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:58–3:26)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:26–4:08)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Generated ≠ computed. Look for code and output.

## Beat 7 (4:08–4:42)

That is the one idea for Topic 1.5. Open #t/1.5 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. # V-T-1.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-1.6  
**Title:** 1.6: Excel verification workbench  
**Word count:** 608  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:03 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:51)

This short video is Topic 1.6: Excel verification workbench, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It sits in the unit W1: Starting Out: Statistical Questions and an AI Workbench. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract (Excel referee file) on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:51–1:24)

Here is where we open. To catch errors you need a referee. In this course that referee is Excel, because every formula is visible. The idea, in plain language, is this. Five functions give the reference values you will check AI against: =COUNT, =AVERAGE, =MEDIAN, =STDEV.S and =MIN/=MAX — plus =COUNTBLANK for missing cells. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–2:00)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. =COUNT counts numbers only: text and blanks are skipped. Compare it with the number of rows you expected — that is your n check. =STDEV.S is the sample SD (divides by n − 1). =STDEV.P divides by n. Put each formula in its own labelled cell, so anyone can see exactly what was computed. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:00–2:29)

A concrete referee file for the Excel verification workbench is hk_district_profile_2016_2025.csv: it has 18 district rows. Confirm that a count of the district-name column returns 18, and recompute a labelled teaching key from the codebook — for example Pearson r = minus 0.38 on the 2025 median income and density columns. Do not treat a blank as zero. Those teaching keys are FlippedStat calculations on official columns, not official C and SD statistics.

## Beat 5 (2:29–2:49)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Using STDEV.P on a sample. Not noticing that numbers stored as text are skipped. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (2:49–3:30)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. COUNT, AVERAGE, MEDIAN, STDEV.S, MIN/MAX, COUNTBLANK. STDEV.S (n − 1) is the sample SD.

## Beat 7 (3:30–4:03)

That is the one idea for Topic 1.6. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

Here is where we open. To catch errors you need a referee. In this course that referee is Excel, because every formula is visible. The idea, in plain language, is this. Five functions give the reference values you will check AI against: =COUNT, =AVERAGE, =MEDIAN, =STDEV.S and =MIN/=MAX — plus =COUNTBLANK for missing cells. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. =COUNT counts numbers only: text and blanks are skipped. Compare it with the number of rows you expected — that is your n check. =STDEV.S is the sample SD (divides by n − 1). =STDEV.P divides by n. Put each formula in its own labelled cell, so anyone can see exactly what was computed. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

A concrete referee file for the Excel verification workbench is hk_district_profile_2016_2025.csv: it has 18 district rows. Confirm that a count of the district-name column returns 18, and recompute a labelled teaching key from the codebook — for example Pearson r = minus 0.38 on the 2025 median income and density columns. # V-T-1.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-1.7  
**Title:** 1.7: Running code in R or Python  
**Word count:** 678  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:31 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:57)

This short video is Topic 1.7: Running code in R or Python, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It sits in the unit W1: Starting Out: Statistical Questions and an AI Workbench. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:57–1:34)

Here is where we open. Excel is the referee. Code is how you will handle larger files — and you don't need to install anything. The idea, in plain language, is this. A notebook mixes text and code in cells you run one at a time, with output under each. Google Colab or Jupyter (Python) and Posit Cloud (R) all run in a browser. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:34–2:15)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. In this course AI drafts code; in Week 1 your job is to read the draft and understand what each line intends. Running and debugging come next. A notebook is also a record: question, code, output and comments in one place — exactly what your reproducibility log needs. Run cells top to bottom . Running them out of order is the commonest cause of “it worked yesterday”. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:15–2:53)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:53–3:21)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:21–3:58)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Notebooks: text + code + output, in a browser. AI drafts; you read and understand first.

## Beat 7 (3:58–4:31)

That is the one idea for Topic 1.7. # V-T-1.8 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-1.8  
**Title:** 1.8: Capability probe  
**Word count:** 643  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:17 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:55)

This short video is Topic 1.8: Capability probe, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It sits in the unit W1: Starting Out: Statistical Questions and an AI Workbench. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:55–1:32)

Here is where we open. Imagine you have the habits. Now test the tool on a file where you already know every answer. The idea, in plain language, is this. A capability probe is a test file with known answers. The probe has 20 rows, an ID column and one numeric column 'score' with one blank — so the true n is 19. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:32–2:06)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. You upload the file to Copilot Chat (CUHK sign-in), paste the prompt contract first, and record what happens. Did the upload succeed? Did it report 20 rows, 2 columns and 1 missing value correctly? Note the date and tool version in your log — capabilities change from term to term. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:06–2:44)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:44–3:12)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:12–3:44)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Test tools on files with known answers. Probe: 20 rows, 1 blank, true n = 19.

## Beat 7 (3:44–4:17)

That is the one idea for Topic 1.8. Open #t/1.8 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M1/T-1.8_Capability_probe.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M1/V-T-1.8.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.
