# V-T-1.9 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-1.9  
**Title:** 1.9: Prompt contract, C.R.O.S.S. and the log  
**Word count:** 718  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:47 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–1:00)

This short video is Topic 1.9: Prompt contract, C.R.O.S.S. and the log, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W1: Starting Out: Statistical Questions and an AI Workbench. The official map budgets 0.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (1:00–1:36)

Here is where we open. Everything that went wrong this week can be prevented — or at least exposed — by five sentences at the top of each prompt. The idea, in plain language, is this. The prompt contract has five clauses: (1) data check , (2) show code , (3) separate results, interpretation and assumptions, (4) limits , (5) handover checks. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:36–2:21)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. 1: use only the attached file; report rows, columns and missing values first. 2: show the code or formula for every number; say if code was not executed. 3: keep computed results, interpretation and assumptions in separate sections. 4: no causal language unless treatment was assigned; no outside thresholds, sources or figures. 5: end with three checks a human should perform. The contract does not make the AI correct; it makes its errors easier to see. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:21–2:59)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:59–3:27)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:27–4:14)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Five clauses at the top of every lab prompt. Data check · code · separate · limits · handover.

## Beat 7 (4:14–4:47)

That is the one idea for Topic 1.9. Open #t/1.9 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M1/T-1.9_Prompt_contract_C_R_O_S_S_and_the_log.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M1/V-T-1.9.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:51–1:31)

Here is where we open. Week 4 described a scatterplot with r. Week 10 fits a line you can use: for prediction, for comparison, and with uncertainty. The idea, in plain language, is this. Simple linear regression models how the average of y changes with x: y = β₀ + β₁x + ε. β₀, β₁ are parameters ; ε is the error — how far an individual sits from the line. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:31–2:00)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. The line describes the mean of y at each x; individuals scatter around it. Estimates b₀, b₁ come from the data; inference (10.4) asks how close they are to β₀, β₁. Observational data → association language. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:00–3:00)

For the 18 official 2025 district median monthly household incomes and official 2025 densities in hk_district_profile_2016_2025.csv, the least-squares line is median income in Hong Kong dollars approximately 34,283 minus 0.121 times density, or about 121 Hong Kong dollars lower district median income for each additional 1,000 persons per square kilometre. The intercept is the line’s value at density 0, which is not a real district. R-squared is about 0.14, already used on Topic 10.3. These are FlippedStat calculations on official pairs, not an official C and SD regression, not a household-level slope, and not a causal claim. The 18 districts are a census of areas, not a random sample, so this line is a descriptive summary of these official pairs. Slope inference is taken up in Topic 10.4, with a design caution. The keyed course fit from revision_quiz.csv, and labelled book illustrations such as the possum data, remain on the page.

## Beat 5 (3:00–3:20)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Treating the line as describing every individual. Checking conditions after reporting p-values — check first. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:20–4:03)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Line for the mean of y. Individuals scatter (ε).

# V-T-10.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-10.2  
**Title:** 10.2: Least squares  
**Word count:** 607  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:03 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:47)

This short video is Topic 10.2: Least squares, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W10: Simple Linear Regression. The official map budgets 2.1667 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:47–1:18)

Here is where we open. Many lines pass through a cloud. Which is “best”? The idea, in plain language, is this. Least squares chooses b₀, b₁ to minimise the sum of squared residuals (SSE). Formulas: b₁ = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)/Σ(x − x̄)², b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:18–1:43)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Squaring makes big misses count more and gives a unique answer. The line always passes through (x̄, ȳ). b₁ = r × s_y/s_x links slope and correlation. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:43–2:23)

The official-data line on Topic 10.1 is a least-squares fit: among straight lines through the 18 official density and median-income pairs, it minimises the sum of squared vertical residuals. The slope, minus 0.121 Hong Kong dollars per person per square kilometre, is that fitted number, not a law for every district. Sai Kung lies well above the line and Kwun Tong a little below it, as Topics 4.1, 4.2 and 10.6 already noted. Because the 18 districts are all the official areas, the fitted slope is a summary of this official scatter, not an estimate from a sample of districts.

## Beat 5 (2:23–2:51)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:51–3:29)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Minimise squared residuals. Line passes through (x̄, ȳ).

## Beat 7 (3:29–4:03)

That is the one idea for Topic 10.2. Open #t/10.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Minimise squared residuals. Line passes through (x̄, ȳ).

That is the one idea for Topic 10.2. # V-T-10.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-10.3  
**Title:** 10.3: Residuals and R-squared  
**Word count:** 595  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 3:58 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:50)

This short video is Topic 10.3: Residuals and R-squared, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W10: Simple Linear Regression. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:50–1:21)

Here is where we open. For a 6-hour student the line predicts 63.8. What does that number represent? The idea, in plain language, is this. The fitted value ŷ = b₀ + b₁x estimates the mean y for units with that x — not one individual's exact score. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:21–1:46)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Every observation has a fitted value on the line. ŷ is a statistic: it has an SE (10.4.4). Individuals with the same x still vary (ε). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:46–2:22)

R-squared is just r squared, on a simple line. With r of minus 0.38, R-squared is about 0.14: the line accounts for about 14% of the variation in these 18 official district median incomes. Most of the variation is residual. That is a FlippedStat calculation, not an official C and SD R-squared, and it is not a household-level fit. The keyed sleep and grumpiness spreadsheet, the Elmhurst aid figure, and the Guided Practice check with r of minus 0.97 stay as labelled book illustrations; those numbers are not replaced here.

## Beat 5 (2:22–2:50)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:50–3:24)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. ŷ = estimated mean at x. Not one person's score.

## Beat 7 (3:24–3:58)

That is the one idea for Topic 10.3. Open #t/10.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M5/T-10.3_Residuals_and_R_squared.tex. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-10.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-10.4  
**Title:** 10.4: Inference for the slope  
**Word count:** 609  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:04 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

This short video is Topic 10.4: Inference for the slope, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W10: Simple Linear Regression. The official map budgets 2.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:16)

Here is where we open. A different sample of 120 students would give a different slope. How much would it wobble? The idea, in plain language, is this. The slope b₁ has a sampling distribution. Its standard error SE(b₁) = s_e/√Σ(x − x̄)². Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:16–1:44)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. SE is smaller when residual scatter is small, n is large, and x is spread out. A wide range of x pins the slope down better. The bootstrap (resampling students) shows the wobble directly. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:44–2:34)

The official income-on-density slope from Topics 10.1 and 10.2 describes all 18 official districts. A t-test or confidence interval for that slope would treat the 18 rows as a random sample from a larger population of districts, which they are not. One can still compute the usual residual standard deviation and a formula standard error of about 0.075, with t about minus 1.62 if the 18 rows were independent and identically distributed, but that number would not be a sampling standard error for these official areas, and this page does not treat it as a test result. Use the official line as a descriptive summary; use the Elmhurst and unemployment examples on this topic to practise slope inference on data that are presented as samples.

## Beat 5 (2:34–3:02)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:02–3:30)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. SE(b₁) = s_e/√Sxx. Spread-out x helps.

## Beat 7 (3:30–4:04)

That is the one idea for Topic 10.4. Open #t/10.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M5/T-10.4_Inference_for_the_slope.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M5/V-T-10.4.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

This short video is Topic 10.5: Residual diagnostics and transformations, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W10: Simple Linear Regression. The official map budgets 3 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. ## Beat 2 (0:55–1:28)

Here is where we open. Imagine you are told the line fits well, and nobody has looked at the residuals. The idea, in plain language, is this. A residual plot puts residuals against fitted values (or x) with a line at 0. Removing the trend magnifies what's left. Good: a patternless horizontal band . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–1:51)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Curve (smile/frown) → wrong form (10.5.3). Funnel → unequal spread (10.5.2). Isolated far points → outliers or influential points (10.6). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:51–2:28)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:28–2:56)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:56–3:38)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Residuals vs fitted. Want a patternless band.

# V-T-10.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-10.6  
**Title:** 10.6: Outliers, leverage and influence  
**Word count:** 644  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:18 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

This short video is Topic 10.6: Outliers, leverage and influence, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W10: Simple Linear Regression. The official map budgets 0.9167 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:21)

Here is where we open. 119 students revised 0–12 hours; one revised 30. That student sits far from everyone in x. The idea, in plain language, is this. Leverage hᵢ = 1/n + (xᵢ − x̄)²/Σ(x − x̄)² measures how unusual a point's x is. Average 2/n; above about 4/n to 6/n is high. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:21–1:43)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Leverage depends only on x, not y. High-leverage points can pull the line strongly. Potential influence, not yet actual influence. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:43–2:39)

Leverage is not the same as influence. On the simple line of official 2025 median income on official 2025 density, the average hat-value is 2 over 18, about 0.11. Kwun Tong, with official density 59,400 persons per square kilometre, has hat-value 0.31: above the two-times guide, a little under the three-times guide, so high leverage by the page’s two-times rule. The Islands district, official density 1,090, has hat-value 0.11, about average. Central and Western has the largest ordinary residual, but a small hat-value of 0.06. Cook’s distances are 0.04 for Kwun Tong, and 0.15 for Central and Western, the largest of the 18. Both are well below the page’s rule that a Cook’s D greater than 1 is large. These are FlippedStat calculations, not official C and SD diagnostics. The parenthood summary and book residual plots were not changed.

## Beat 5 (2:39–3:07)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:07–3:44)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Leverage = unusual x. Average 2/n.

## Beat 7 (3:44–4:18)

That is the one idea for Topic 10.6. Open #t/10.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M5/T-10.6_Outliers_leverage_and_influence.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M5/V-T-10.6.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. # V-T-10.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-10.7  
**Title:** 10.7: Copilot lab: fit, interpret, reproduce  
**Word count:** 634  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:14 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic 10.7: Copilot lab: fit, interpret, reproduce, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W10: Simple Linear Regression. The official map budgets 1.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:30)

Here is where we open. Copilot lab: Copilot fits the regression and writes “More revision leads to higher scores. The model explains the data well.” The idea, in plain language, is this. Ask Copilot (with the contract) to fit the regression showing code, the full coefficient table (estimate, SE, t, p, CI), n, R², s_e and a residual plot — then read its wording critically. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:30–2:00)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Copilot executes; you read the code and audit output and wording (10.7.2). Expect causal verbs ( H4 ) and “explains the data well” for R² = 0.09. Ask for a plain-language interpretation of slope and R² separately. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:00–2:38)

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

## Beat 5 (2:38–3:06)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:06–3:40)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Full table + n + R² + s_e. Residual plot.

## Beat 7 (3:40–4:14)

That is the one idea for Topic 10.7. Open #t/10.7 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M5/T-10.7_Copilot_lab_fit_interpret_reproduce.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M5/V-T-10.7.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-10.8 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-10.8  
**Title:** 10.8: Audit lab: two numbers and one extreme row  
**Word count:** 588  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 3:55 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:55)

This short video is Topic 10.8: Audit lab: two numbers and one extreme row, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W10: Simple Linear Regression. The official map budgets 1.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:55–1:26)

Here is where we open. Audit lab. AI: “Revision hours explain 61% of quiz performance.” Open the output. The idea, in plain language, is this. Count (n = 120, no missing), Recompute (slope 0.610, R² 0.094), then name the error: slope digits given R²'s meaning — H2/H3 . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:26–1:48)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. The true share of variation is about 9%. “Explain” also implies cause (H4). Memo line 5 refuses the 61% claim. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:48–2:26)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:26–2:54)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:54–3:22)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Count, recompute, name. Slope ≠ R².

## Beat 7 (3:22–3:55)

That is the one idea for Topic 10.8. Open #t/10.8 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M5/T-10.8_Audit_lab_two_numbers_and_one_extreme_row.tex. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:47)

This short video is Topic 11.1: Multiple regression, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W11: Multiple Regression and Adjustment. The official map budgets 2.9167 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:47–1:23)

Here is where we open. Week 10 used one explanatory variable. But senior students both exercise more and have higher GPAs. The idea, in plain language, is this. Multiple regression uses several predictors: ŷ = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + .... Each slope is an adjusted association: the association with that predictor after accounting for the others in the model. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:23–1:49)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. The simple slope mixes a predictor's own association with those of anything correlated with it. Adding a related variable separates them. Still association — adjustment is not randomisation (11.3.3). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:49–2:48)

A descriptive multiple regression of the 18 official 2025 district median monthly household incomes on official 2025 density and region — Hong Kong Island as the reference, with indicators for Kowloon and the New Territories — can be written, in Hong Kong dollars, as median income approximately 43,380 minus 0.230 times density minus 5,127 times Kowloon minus 10,982 times New Territories, with R-squared about 0.59. These are FlippedStat calculations, not official C and SD coefficients. n = 18 with four parameters is a thin fit, the intercept at density 0 is not a real district, and region differences here are differences among means of official district medians, not official regional median incomes. The official Hong Kong median in 2025 is 30,000 Hong Kong dollars. The 18 rows are a census of areas, so coefficient p-values would not be sampling p-values and are not reported as test results here.

## Beat 5 (2:48–3:10)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Reading an adjusted slope as causal. Comparing a simple and an adjusted slope without saying which is which. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:10–3:49)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Several predictors at once. Each slope adjusted for the others.

## Beat 7 (3:49–4:22)

That is the one idea for Topic 11.1. # V-T-11.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-11.2  
**Title:** 11.2: Indicator variables and interaction  
**Word count:** 677  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:31 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

This short video is Topic 11.2: Indicator variables and interaction, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W11: Multiple Regression and Adjustment. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:22)

Here is where we open. Faculty has five categories. You can't multiply “Arts” by a slope. The idea, in plain language, is this. An indicator (dummy) is 1 if a unit is in a category, 0 otherwise. A variable with k levels needs k − 1 indicators ; the omitted level is the reference . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:22–1:48)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Each indicator's coefficient = mean difference from the reference, holding other predictors fixed. Including all k indicators plus an intercept is perfect collinearity (11.4.1). ANOVA (8.6) is regression on indicators. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:48–2:54)

The three-level region factor in Topic 11.1 is the same idea as a new-versus-used indicator, with two dummy columns instead of one. Holding official 2025 density fixed in that descriptive fit, official 2025 district median incomes on Hong Kong Island sit higher, on the fitted plane, than those in Kowloon — about 5,100 Hong Kong dollars lower — and the New Territories — about 11,000 Hong Kong dollars lower. That is a comparison of official district medians after a linear density adjustment, not a causal effect of region, and not an official C and SD region effect. For context only, the unadjusted means of the official 2025 district medians are 39,425 Hong Kong dollars on Hong Kong Island, with n = 4; 27,420 in Kowloon, with n = 5; and 30,933 in the New Territories, with n = 9. Those means of medians are themselves FlippedStat summaries, not official regional medians. The Mario Kart new-versus-used illustration, and any checks on this page, were not changed.

## Beat 5 (2:54–3:22)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:22–3:57)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. k levels → k − 1 indicators. Coefficient = difference from reference.

## Beat 7 (3:57–4:31)

That is the one idea for Topic 11.2. Open #t/11.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M5/T-11.2_Indicator_variables_and_interaction.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M5/V-T-11.2.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Those means of medians are themselves FlippedStat summaries, not official regional medians. The Mario Kart new-versus-used illustration, and any checks on this page, were not changed.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. k levels → k − 1 indicators. Coefficient = difference from reference.

That is the one idea for Topic 11.2. Open #t/11.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M5/T-11.2_Indicator_variables_and_interaction.tex. # V-T-11.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-11.3  
**Title:** 11.3: Confounding in regression  
**Word count:** 627  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:11 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:57)

This short video is Topic 11.3: Confounding in regression, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W11: Multiple Regression and Adjustment. The official map budgets 0.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:57–1:34)

Here is where we open. Adding one variable can shrink a coefficient, grow it, or flip its sign. Which happens depends on how it relates to x and y. The idea, in plain language, is this. A confounder relates to both x and y. Left out, its association leaks into x's slope. Positively related to both → simple slope too large ; adjusting shrinks it. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:34–2:02)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Positively related to one and negatively to the other → simple slope too small or wrong-signed. Unrelated to x → slope barely changes (precision may improve). Direction of bias: sign(x–z relation) × sign(z–y relation). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:02–2:40)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:40–3:08)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:08–3:37)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Confounder → biased simple slope. Direction = product of signs.

## Beat 7 (3:37–4:11)

That is the one idea for Topic 11.3. Open #t/11.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-11.4/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-11.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-11.4  
**Title:** 11.4: Multicollinearity  
**Word count:** 643  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:17 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:47)

This short video is Topic 11.4: Multicollinearity, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W11: Multiple Regression and Adjustment. The official map budgets 0.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:47–1:21)

Here is where we open. A model includes study hours and library hours, which almost always move together. The fit is fine; the coefficients make no sense. The idea, in plain language, is this. Multicollinearity: strongly correlated predictors leave little information about each one's separate association. Symptoms: large SEs, unstable slopes, significant F with no significant slope. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:21–1:49)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Perfect collinearity (cm and inches; all k dummies + intercept) makes estimation impossible. It doesn't bias predictions within range or lower R²; it harms interpreting individual coefficients. Look at predictor correlations and VIFs (11.4.3). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:49–2:34)

Multicollinearity is sometimes just a definition asked twice. Official 2025 density is defined from mid-year land population and land area, in table 110-02001. On the log scale, log density equals log population minus log area, up to rounding. A regression of official log density on those two logs, for the 18 districts, has R-squared of 1.000 to three decimal places; official density and population divided by area differ by under 0.2%, and the leftover is published-figure rounding. Putting all three columns into one linear model asks the official definition twice. These are FlippedStat observations, not an official C and SD regression. The parenthood correlation matrix and VIF figures stay labelled book illustrations.

## Beat 5 (2:34–3:02)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:02–3:44)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Correlated predictors. Big SEs, unstable slopes.

## Beat 7 (3:44–4:17)

That is the one idea for Topic 11.4. Open #t/11.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M5/T-11.4_Multicollinearity.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M5/V-T-11.4.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-11.5 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-11.5  
**Title:** 11.5: Model comparison  
**Word count:** 618  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:07 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic 11.5: Model comparison, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W11: Multiple Regression and Adjustment. The official map budgets 2 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:24)

Here is where we open. Imagine you add ten columns of random noise to a model and R² goes up. The idea, in plain language, is this. R² never decreases when a predictor is added — even pure noise. Adjusted R² penalises extra predictors and can fall. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–1:50)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Adjusted R² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − p − 1). It rises only if a predictor helps more than chance would. Neither replaces out-of-sample checks (Week 12). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:50–2:28)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:28–2:56)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:56–3:34)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. R² always rises. Adjusted R² can fall.

## Beat 7 (3:34–4:07)

That is the one idea for Topic 11.5. Open #t/11.5 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Count reporters. Compare with non-reporters.

That is the one idea for Topic 11.6. Open #t/11.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M5/T-11.6_Audit_lab_the_verb_and_the_missing_rows.tex. # V-T-11.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-11.7  
**Title:** 11.7: Capstone: analysis plan  
**Word count:** 594  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 3:58 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 11.7: Capstone: analysis plan, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W11: Multiple Regression and Adjustment. The official map budgets 1.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:24)

Here is where we open. Write the analysis plan before asking AI anything. It's the best protection against forking paths. The idea, in plain language, is this. Your analysis plan fixes in writing: target quantity, unit of analysis, data, primary model, missing-data handling, checks, sensitivity analyses, and reporting. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–1:50)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Target: e.g. the adjusted association of exercise with sleep quality. Model and reference categories chosen from the question, not the results. Anything added later is labelled exploratory (8.8.3). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:50–2:28)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:28–2:56)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:56–3:24)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Plan before analysis. Target, model, missing, checks, sensitivity.

## Beat 7 (3:24–3:58)

That is the one idea for Topic 11.7. Open #t/11.7 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M5/T-11.7_Capstone_analysis_plan.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M5/V-T-11.7.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-11.8 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-11.8  
**Title:** 11.8: Block D exam practice  
**Word count:** 634  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:14 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 11.8: Block D exam practice, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W11: Multiple Regression and Adjustment. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:24)

Here is where we open. Block D so far by hand: interpretation, residuals, inference, adjustment, indicators and model comparison. The idea, in plain language, is this. Exam-format items on Weeks 9.7–11: write the model; interpret coefficients with units and “holding fixed”; check conditions; refuse unsupported claims. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–1:51)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Two items require refusing a claim — a slope read as a percentage, or a causal verb on observational data. About 6 minutes per item. Week 12 adds prediction and validation. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:51–2:28)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:28–2:56)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:56–3:40)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Model → units → holding fixed → association. Refuse when needed.

## Beat 7 (3:40–4:14)

That is the one idea for Topic 11.8. Open #t/11.8 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. # V-T-12.1 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-12.1  
**Title:** 12.1: Prediction versus explanation  
**Word count:** 635  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:14 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:57)

This short video is Topic 12.1: Prediction versus explanation, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W12: Prediction, Validation and Fairness. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:57–1:32)

Here is where we open. Weeks 10–11 explained relationships. Week 12 asks a different question: how well can we guess an outcome for someone new? The idea, in plain language, is this. A prediction task judges a model by accuracy on new units. A loss function scores each error: squared error → RMSE ; absolute error → MAE . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:32–2:01)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Squared error punishes big misses much more; RMSE ≥ MAE always. The gap between RMSE and MAE grows when a few errors are large. Choose the loss that matches the cost of errors in the decision. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:01–2:38)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:38–3:06)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:06–3:40)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Prediction = accuracy on new data. RMSE vs MAE.

## Beat 7 (3:40–4:14)

That is the one idea for Topic 12.1. # V-T-12.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-12.2  
**Title:** 12.2: Validation and leakage  
**Word count:** 609  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:04 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic 12.2: Validation and leakage, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W12: Prediction, Validation and Fairness. The official map budgets 1.8333 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:29)

Here is where we open. Before building anything, lock 20% of the data in a drawer. Open it once, at the very end. The idea, in plain language, is this. Holdout validation: split into a training set (build and tune) and a test set (evaluate once). The test set must stay untouched during building. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:29–1:55)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Typical splits: 70/30 or 80/20. No peeking, no tuning, no choosing variables on the test set — otherwise it becomes training data. Report the test error as the honest estimate. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:55–2:33)

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

## Beat 5 (2:33–3:01)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:01–3:30)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Lock a test set first. Never tune on it.

## Beat 7 (3:30–4:04)

That is the one idea for Topic 12.2. Open #t/12.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-12.3/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-12.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-12.3  
**Title:** 12.3: Baselines and metrics  
**Word count:** 628  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:11 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 12.3: Baselines and metrics, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W12: Prediction, Validation and Fairness. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:23)

Here is where we open. Only 2% of students drop out. Predicting “stays” for everyone is 98% accurate. The idea, in plain language, is this. A baseline is the simplest sensible prediction without the model's predictors: majority class for classification, mean for a numerical outcome. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:23–1:50)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Majority baseline accuracy = share of the commonest class. Mean baseline RMSE ≈ SD of y. A model is useful only if it beats the baseline on the measure that matters. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:50–2:28)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:28–2:56)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:56–3:38)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Always report a baseline. Majority / mean.

## Beat 7 (3:38–4:11)

That is the one idea for Topic 12.3. Open #t/12.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M5/T-12.3_Baselines_and_metrics.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M5/V-T-12.3.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.
