# V-T-12.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-12.4  
**Title:** 12.4: Audit lab: 98% accurate  
**Word count:** 618  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:07 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 12.4: Audit lab: 98% accurate, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W12: Prediction, Validation and Fairness. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:27)

Here is where we open. Audit lab. AI: “The dropout model is 98% accurate, so it works.” First check: how rare is dropping out? The idea, in plain language, is this. Count: 5,000 students, 100 dropouts — base rate 2%. With such class imbalance , predicting “stays” for everyone is already 98% accurate. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:27–1:51)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. So “98% accurate” carries almost no information. Memo line 1: the base rate. Then look at the features (12.4.2) and the right metrics (12.4.3). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:51–2:28)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:28–2:56)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:56–3:34)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Base rate 2%. Baseline already 98%.

## Beat 7 (3:34–4:07)

That is the one idea for Topic 12.4. Open #t/12.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. # V-T-12.5 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-12.5  
**Title:** 12.5: Fairness definitions  
**Word count:** 616  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:06 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 12.5: Fairness definitions, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W12: Prediction, Validation and Fairness. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:27)

Here is where we open. A tool flags students at risk of failing. Among truly at-risk students, does it catch the same share in every group? The idea, in plain language, is this. Equal sensitivity (“equal opportunity”): the true-positive rate is the same in each group. Equalised odds adds an equal false-positive rate. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:27–1:53)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Intuition: people in the same true situation are treated the same, whatever their group. Check with per-group confusion matrices. Report group sizes and uncertainty — small groups give noisy rates. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:53–2:31)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:31–2:59)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:59–3:33)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Equal TPR across groups. Equalised odds adds equal FPR.

## Beat 7 (3:33–4:06)

That is the one idea for Topic 12.5. Open #t/12.5 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. This short video is Topic 12.5: Fairness definitions, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W12: Prediction, Validation and Fairness. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

Here is where we open. A tool flags students at risk of failing. Among truly at-risk students, does it catch the same share in every group? The idea, in plain language, is this. Equal sensitivity (“equal opportunity”): the true-positive rate is the same in each group. Equalised odds adds an equal false-positive rate. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Intuition: people in the same true situation are treated the same, whatever their group. Check with per-group confusion matrices. Report group sizes and uncertainty — small groups give noisy rates. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Equal TPR across groups. Equalised odds adds equal FPR.

That is the one idea for Topic 12.5. Open #t/12.5 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M8/T-12.5_Fairness_definitions.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M8/V-T-12.5.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-12.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-12.6  
**Title:** 12.6: Bias in data and models  
**Word count:** 664  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:26 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 12.6: Bias in data and models, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W12: Prediction, Validation and Fairness. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract plus named case kept on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:22)

Here is where we open. A model trained on learning-app users is deployed to all students. Who wasn't in the training data? The idea, in plain language, is this. Sampling bias carries into models: under-represented groups get less accurate predictions. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:22–1:48)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Examples: face-recognition systems less accurate on darker-skinned faces; health models trained in one hospital failing in another. Compare training composition with the deployment population. Report performance by group, with n. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:48–2:55)

A bias of interpretation sits in official area-level figures. Topics 4.1 and 4.2 already report Pearson r = minus 0.38 between the 18 official 2025 district median household incomes and official 2025 densities. That is an ecological association among district aggregates. Reading it as “households in denser neighbourhoods have lower incomes,” or as a causal effect of density, would go beyond what the official pairs show. The Boston and Chicago résumé-callback experiment remains the named study on this page, and for case study C4.8; its figures are not replaced and are not Hong Kong official statistics. The same teaching point applies in a Hong Kong hiring setting: a name, a residential district, or another field that is correlated with a protected characteristic can act as a proxy in a model trained on past decisions, even if the protected characteristic itself is never entered. This video does not invent a local audit’s callback rates. Any real Hong Kong field study would need its own design, sample, and cited results.

## Beat 5 (2:55–3:23)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:23–3:52)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Training mix ≠ deployment mix. Under-represented → worse accuracy.

## Beat 7 (3:52–4:26)

That is the one idea for Topic 12.6. Open #t/12.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M8/T-12.6_Bias_in_data_and_models.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M8/V-T-12.6.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-12.7/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-12.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-12.7  
**Title:** 12.7: Audit lab: equally accurate, therefore fair?  
**Word count:** 645  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:18 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic 12.7: Audit lab: equally accurate, therefore fair?, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W12: Prediction, Validation and Fairness. The official map budgets 1.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:33)

Here is where we open. Audit lab. AI: “The tool is equally accurate in both groups (0.89 vs 0.90), therefore fair.” Separate design from data first. The idea, in plain language, is this. The README gives the design: sensitivity 0.85, specificity 0.90 in both groups; base rates 20% (A) and 5.3% (B). The data file is a finite sample whose counts differ slightly by chance. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:33–1:57)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Always say whether you report design or file figures. Recompute file figures from the counts yourself. Don't treat small sample differences as design differences. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:57–2:35)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:35–3:03)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:03–3:44)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Design vs file. Recompute from counts.

## Beat 7 (3:44–4:18)

That is the one idea for Topic 12.7. Open #t/12.7 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M8/T-12.7_Audit_lab_equally_accurate_therefore_fair.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M8/V-T-12.7.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-12.8 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-12.8  
**Title:** 12.8: Block D post-check  
**Word count:** 602  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:01 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 12.8: Block D post-check, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W12: Prediction, Validation and Fairness. The official map budgets 0.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:24)

Here is where we open. Block D post-check: regression, adjustment, prediction and fairness. The idea, in plain language, is this. The post-check is parallel to the Block D pre-check from Week 9. Compare item types — slope vs R², adjusted vs simple, accuracy vs baseline, fairness metrics. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–1:45)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Tag misses by lesson. Revisit two lessons before the capstone weeks. Attempts are saved in this browser. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:45–2:23)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:23–2:51)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:51–3:27)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Parallel post-check. Tag misses.

## Beat 7 (3:27–4:01)

That is the one idea for Topic 12.8. Open #t/12.8 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:14–3:43)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Six codes, six checks. Several codes per answer is normal.

Six H-codes name every AI failure in this course — and each has a check that catches it: H1 misread data (Count), H2 wrong method (Statistical principles), H3 calculation (Recompute), H4 over-reach, H5 fabrication, H6 biased framing (Sources and scope). Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. A single sentence can carry several codes; log them all. Naming errors quickly makes audits faster and logs comparable across students and tools. The codes describe outputs, not intentions — a fluent answer can still be H1. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Six codes, six checks. Several codes per answer is normal.

That is the one idea for Topic 13.1. Open #t/13.1 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M8/T-13.1_How_generative_AI_fails_at_statistics.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M8/V-T-13.1.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. # V-T-13.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-13.2  
**Title:** 13.2: Copilot lab: agreement is not proof  
**Word count:** 659  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:24 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:58)

This short video is Topic 13.2: Copilot lab: agreement is not proof, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W13: Responsible Practice and Capstone Analysis. The official map budgets 1.1667 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:58–1:34)

Here is where we open. Imagine three AI tools agree on n = 228 and you are tempted to stop checking. The idea, in plain language, is this. Give the same file and the same neutral prompt to three tools; ask each for n used, missing counts, median and mean, with code. Fill a three-tool log with your Excel column as referee. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:34–2:02)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Agreement between tools is weak evidence if they share a default. Your column must be computed independently, with settings you can see. Disagreement is a gift: it shows exactly where to look. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:02–2:40)

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

## Beat 5 (2:40–3:08)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:08–3:50)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Same file, same neutral prompt. Excel as referee.

## Beat 7 (3:50–4:24)

That is the one idea for Topic 13.2. Open #t/13.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M8/T-13.2_Copilot_lab_agreement_is_not_proof.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M8/V-T-13.2.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-13.3/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-13.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-13.3  
**Title:** 13.3: Reproducibility, provenance and disclosure  
**Word count:** 635  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:14 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:58)

This short video is Topic 13.3: Reproducibility, provenance and disclosure, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W13: Responsible Practice and Capstone Analysis. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:58–1:31)

Here is where we open. Six weeks from now your tutor asks where 0.116 came from. Can you show it in five minutes? The idea, in plain language, is this. A result is reproducible if someone with your files can regenerate it. Keep five things: prompts, outputs, code, data versions, checks . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:31–1:57)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Prompts: exact text, date, tool. Outputs and code: saved, with seeds and package versions. Data: file name and version, never edited by hand; checks: what you recomputed and the result. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:57–2:35)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:35–3:03)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:03–3:40)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Prompts, outputs, code, data, checks. Version everything.

## Beat 7 (3:40–4:14)

That is the one idea for Topic 13.3. Open #t/13.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M8/T-13.3_Reproducibility_provenance_and_disclosure.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M8/V-T-13.3.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-13.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-13.4  
**Title:** 13.4: Communicating uncertainty  
**Word count:** 636  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:14 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 13.4: Communicating uncertainty, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W13: Responsible Practice and Capstone Analysis. The official map budgets 0.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:29)

Here is where we open. Imagine your result: 95% CI 1.2 to 8.8 marks. The principal asks: “So did it work?” The idea, in plain language, is this. Lead with the estimate and range in plain words , with units; say what the range rules out and what it doesn't; connect it to the decision threshold . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:29–2:00)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Too technical: “Δ = 5.0, CI [1.2, 8.8], p = 0.012.” Overstated: “The method improves scores by 5 marks.” Clear and honest: “Scores were about 5 marks higher, plausibly between 1 and 9. A drop is unlikely; a very small gain is possible.” If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:00–2:38)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:38–3:06)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:06–3:41)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Estimate + range + units. What it rules in and out.

## Beat 7 (3:41–4:14)

That is the one idea for Topic 13.4. Open #t/13.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M8/T-13.4_Communicating_uncertainty.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M8/V-T-13.4.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Six checks, each with finding and action. Expectations first.

# V-T-13.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-13.6  
**Title:** 13.6: Hallucination quiz and confidence survey  
**Word count:** 631  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:12 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:59)

This short video is Topic 13.6: Hallucination quiz and confidence survey, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W13: Responsible Practice and Capstone Analysis. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:59–1:27)

Here is where we open. Ten statements an AI might write. Most contain an error you can now catch. The idea, in plain language, is this. The hallucination quiz: decide whether each statement can be accepted, and if not, which H-code applies. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:27–1:51)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Items draw on every block: misread data, wrong methods, slips, over-reach, fabrication, framing. Answer without AI or notes. Your score is saved for comparison. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:51–2:29)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:29–2:57)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:57–3:39)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Accept or code each statement. No AI.

## Beat 7 (3:39–4:12)

That is the one idea for Topic 13.6. Open #t/13.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-13.7/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-13.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-13.7  
**Title:** 13.7: Capstone: exploration  
**Word count:** 630  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:12 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 13.7: Capstone: exploration, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W13: Responsible Practice and Capstone Analysis. The official map budgets 2 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:27)

Here is where we open. Before modelling, look. Careful description often reveals more than any p-value. The idea, in plain language, is this. Exploration: one variable at a time (n, missing, median, IQR, mean, SD, histogram), then the outcome by the main explanatory variable, then threats to the plan (skew, outliers, sparse groups). Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:27–1:55)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Every number in exploration is checkable later. Note anything that changes the plan as a planned sensitivity, not a silent fix. Don't test hypotheses you formed while exploring on the same data (8.9.2). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:55–2:32)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:32–3:00)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:00–3:38)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Describe before modelling. Turn surprises into planned checks.

## Beat 7 (3:38–4:12)

That is the one idea for Topic 13.7. Open #t/13.7 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M8/T-13.7_Capstone_exploration.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M8/V-T-13.7.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

This short video is Topic 14.1: Capstone: main analysis, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W14: Capstone Completion. The official map budgets 2.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:26)

Here is where we open. Plan written (11.7), data audited (13.5), exploration done (13.7). Now run the analysis — exactly as planned. The idea, in plain language, is this. Run the main analysis as planned , using methods from at least two blocks, logging each step: recount the sample, fit, check, interpret. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:26–1:53)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Recount: n in file → n complete for the model → reasons rows were dropped. Fit the planned model; record estimate, CI, n. Check residuals, leverage, VIF; then interpret with association wording. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:53–2:31)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:31–2:59)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:59–3:40)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Run as planned. Recount n first.

# V-T-14.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-14.2  
**Title:** 14.2: Capstone: verification and sensitivity  
**Word count:** 627  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:11 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 14.2: Capstone: verification and sensitivity, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W14: Capstone Completion. The official map budgets 2.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:26)

Here is where we open. Every number in your report must be traceable and checked. Not most numbers. The idea, in plain language, is this. A verification log has one row per reported number: as reported · where · how produced · independent check · result · H-code if any. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:26–1:54)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Apply C.R.O.S.S. to the key numbers: Count, Recompute, Other tool, Statistical principles, Sources and scope. Small numbers matter: n in a table, a percentage in the abstract. The log is graded evidence of verification. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:54–2:31)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:31–2:59)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:59–3:37)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. One row per number. Independent check for each.

## Beat 7 (3:37–4:11)

That is the one idea for Topic 14.2. Open #t/14.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-14.3/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-14.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-14.3  
**Title:** 14.3: Capstone: report  
**Word count:** 618  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:07 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic 14.3: Capstone: report, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W14: Capstone Completion. The official map budgets 1.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:30)

Here is where we open. Imagine you must fit the whole study into two pages that a non-specialist can check. The idea, in plain language, is this. The two-page IMRaD report: Introduction (question and why), Methods (data, n, model, checks), Results (estimate + CI + n in words, one figure), Discussion (meaning, limits, scope) — plus the five-line memo and AI appendix. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:30–1:55)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Every number in the report appears in the verification log. Use association wording for observational data; state the population. One clear figure beats three busy ones (4.4.2). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:55–2:32)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:32–3:00)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:00–3:34)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. IMRaD in two pages. Every number logged.

## Beat 7 (3:34–4:07)

That is the one idea for Topic 14.3. Open #t/14.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M8/T-14.3_Capstone_report.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M8/V-T-14.3.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

## Continuous script (for the recording booth)

This short video is Topic 14.3: Capstone: report, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W14: Capstone Completion. The official map budgets 1.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

Here is where we open. Imagine you must fit the whole study into two pages that a non-specialist can check. The idea, in plain language, is this. The two-page IMRaD report: Introduction (question and why), Methods (data, n, model, checks), Results (estimate + CI + n in words, one figure), Discussion (meaning, limits, scope) — plus the five-line memo and AI appendix. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Every number in the report appears in the verification log. Use association wording for observational data; state the population. One clear figure beats three busy ones (4.4.2). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. # V-T-14.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-14.4  
**Title:** 14.4: Peer review  
**Word count:** 606  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:02 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic 14.4: Peer review, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W14: Capstone Completion. The official map budgets 1.0833 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:25)

Here is where we open. Imagine you've audited AI output for thirteen weeks. Now audit a classmate's report — fairly, specifically and kindly. The idea, in plain language, is this. Score each rubric criterion 0–4 with evidence ; check at least three numbers yourself; give one strength and the highest-priority fix. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:25–1:56)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Read once for the story, then with the rubric. Verification (25) and interpretation (20) carry the most weight; the full rubric with 0–4 descriptors is the next subtopic. Comment on the work, not the person; quote the sentence you discuss. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:56–2:33)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:33–3:01)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:01–3:29)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Score with evidence. Check three numbers.

## Beat 7 (3:29–4:02)

That is the one idea for Topic 14.4. Open #t/14.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-14.5 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-14.5  
**Title:** 14.5: Oral briefing  
**Word count:** 628  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:11 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic 14.5: Oral briefing, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W14: Capstone Completion. The official map budgets 0.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:26)

Here is where we open. A department head has five minutes and no statistics training. What do they need to hear? The idea, in plain language, is this. Structure five minutes around one message: question → data → finding (estimate and range in plain words) → uncertainty → limitation → so what. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:26–1:50)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. One chart, one number with its range. Name the main limitation in one sentence. End with what you'd recommend and what would change your mind. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:50–2:28)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:28–2:56)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:56–3:38)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. One message. Estimate + range in words.

## Continuous script (for the recording booth)

This short video is Topic 14.5: Oral briefing, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W14: Capstone Completion. The official map budgets 0.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

Here is where we open. A department head has five minutes and no statistics training. What do they need to hear? The idea, in plain language, is this. Structure five minutes around one message: question → data → finding (estimate and range in plain words) → uncertainty → limitation → so what. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. One chart, one number with its range. Name the main limitation in one sentence. End with what you'd recommend and what would change your mind. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. One message. Estimate + range in words.

# V-T-14.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-14.6  
**Title:** 14.6: Revision, reflection and exit survey  
**Word count:** 616  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:06 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 14.6: Revision, reflection and exit survey, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W14: Capstone Completion. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:26)

Here is where we open. Imagine your reviewer flagged four things. You needn't accept all — but you must answer all. The idea, in plain language, is this. A response to review answers each comment with “Changed: what and where” or “Not changed: reason”, prioritising correctness (numbers, verbs, scope) over style. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:26–1:50)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Re-verify any number you changed; update the log and AI appendix. Polite disagreement with evidence is fine. Keep the response with the final report. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:50–2:28)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:28–2:56)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:56–3:33)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Answer every comment. Correctness first.

## Beat 7 (3:33–4:06)

That is the one idea for Topic 14.6. Open #t/14.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued.
