========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-2.1/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-2.1 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-2.1  
**Title:** 2.1: Data rectangles and encoding  
**Word count:** 713  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:45 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

This short video is Topic 2.1: Data rectangles and encoding, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It sits in the unit W2: Where Data Come From. The official map budgets 1.4167 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:27)

Here is where we open. Week 1 ended with you uploading a file. This week asks: where did that file come from, and is it in a shape any tool can read? The idea, in plain language, is this. Tidy data follow three rules: each row is one observation, each column is one variable, each cell holds one value. OpenIntro calls this rectangle a data matrix . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:27–2:17)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Almost every statistical tool — Excel, R, Python, Copilot — expects a rectangle. Tidy layout is not about looks: it turns filtering, grouping and charting into one-line operations. Messy files break the rules in typical ways: values hidden in column headers (Mon, Tue, Wed), several values in one cell (“Chan 7/10”), rows that are days instead of people. Most mess can be fixed by splitting cells, stacking columns into rows (wide → long) or spreading rows into columns. AI drafts reshaping code well once you describe the target layout. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:17–3:02)

When you import a file in this topic, start with hk_district_profile_2016_2025.csv, not with a messy spreadsheet. It is a tidy rectangle: one row per District Council district, 18 data rows plus a header, UTF-8 and comma-separated. Official mid-year land population and density come from C and SD table 110-02001. Official median monthly household income comes from table 130-06806. Derived columns — population change, and the gained-or-lost flag — are labelled FlippedStat calculations, not official statistics. The older file booksales.csv stays on the page as a labelled textbook illustration. Do not treat that book file as an official Hong Kong table, and do not treat the derived flags as if the Department published them.

## Beat 5 (3:02–3:31)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Merged cells and colour-coding — they carry meaning that disappears on export. Several tables stacked on one sheet with blank rows between them. Totals typed as extra rows inside the data (they get averaged in later!). None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:31–4:12)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Row = observation, column = variable, cell = value. Values in headers → stack them.

## Beat 7 (4:12–4:45)

That is the one idea for Topic 2.1. Open #t/2.1 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M1/T-2.1_Data_rectangles_and_encoding.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M1/V-T-2.1.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-2.2 — beats sheet

**video_id:** V-T-2.2  
**Title:** 2.2: Importing and checking  
**Module / outcome:** Module 1 — Topic 2.2: Importing and checking. One-concept topic video; official Modules 1–8 only.  
**Format:** motion-graphics (digital blackboard allowed). No live-action people.

# V-T-2.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-2.2  
**Title:** 2.2: Importing and checking  
**Word count:** 650  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:20 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

This short video is Topic 2.2: Importing and checking, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It sits in the unit W2: Where Data Come From. The official map budgets 1.0833 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:24)

Here is where we open. Imagine you've saved the file in a good format. The first check after any import takes ten seconds. The idea, in plain language, is this. Do the row and column counts match what you expected? Expectations come from the README, the data dictionary or the survey platform — and you write them down before opening the file. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–2:04)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. One row short: the header was read as data (or a data row as header), or a final line was lost. One column extra: an unnamed index column, or a trailing comma at the end of each line. Far more rows: a bad join multiplied them or files were stacked. Far fewer: a filter, or a line broken by a quote mark inside text. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:04–2:44)

Importing is only the first check. On the official extract, try a simple filter: keep the rows whose region_en is New Territories. That should leave 9 of the 18 official districts. Then go back to the codebook and confirm the count, rather than trusting a preview pane. The page still includes a Night Garden illustration with a keyed toy count of 10 utterances. That n equals 10 belongs to the labelled textbook illustration, not to this official extract. If a tool reports 10 when you are working the official 18-row file, you have the wrong dataset in the workspace.

## Beat 5 (2:44–3:12)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:12–3:46)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Write expected rows × columns first. Compare after every import.

## Beat 7 (3:46–4:20)

That is the one idea for Topic 2.2. Open #t/2.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M1/T-2.2_Importing_and_checking.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M1/V-T-2.2.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-2.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-2.3  
**Title:** 2.3: Types of study  
**Word count:** 630  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:12 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic 2.3: Types of study, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W2: Where Data Come From. The official map budgets 3.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:31)

Here is where we open. A clean file still can't tell you what it can prove. That depends on how the data were collected. The idea, in plain language, is this. Four designs: a census measures everyone; a sample survey measures a sample to describe a population; an experiment assigns treatments; an observational study records what units already do. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:31–2:08)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Hong Kong runs a population census every ten years and a by-census in between: no sampling error, but costly — and still exposed to non-response and measurement error. Experiments: clinical trials, A/B tests of web pages. Observational studies: most health, social-science and business data. Quick test: who decided which treatment each unit got? The researcher → experiment. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:08–2:46)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:46–3:08)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Calling a study an 'experiment' because it was done carefully or in a lab — assignment is what matters. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:08–3:38)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. ## Continuous script (for the recording booth)

This short video is Topic 2.3: Types of study, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W2: Where Data Come From. The official map budgets 3.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

Here is where we open. A clean file still can't tell you what it can prove. That depends on how the data were collected. The idea, in plain language, is this. Four designs: a census measures everyone; a sample survey measures a sample to describe a population; an experiment assigns treatments; an observational study records what units already do. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Hong Kong runs a population census every ten years and a by-census in between: no sampling error, but costly — and still exposed to non-response and measurement error. Experiments: clinical trials, A/B tests of web pages. Observational studies: most health, social-science and business data. Quick test: who decided which treatment each unit got? The researcher → experiment. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Calling a study an 'experiment' because it was done carefully or in a lab — assignment is what matters. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. # V-T-2.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-2.4  
**Title:** 2.4: Populations, frames and sampling  
**Word count:** 662  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:25 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic 2.4: Populations, frames and sampling, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It sits in the unit W2: Where Data Come From. The official map budgets 2.0833 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:24)

Here is where we open. Generalising needs a population. Defining it precisely is harder than it sounds. The idea, in plain language, is this. The target population is the group you want conclusions about. The study population is the group you can actually reach. Gaps between them are coverage problems. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–2:01)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. “CUHK students” is not precise enough. “Full-time undergraduates enrolled at CUHK in Term 1, 2026–27” is. Students on exchange may be in the target but unreachable; graduates with active accounts may be reachable but not in the target. Write both definitions down. Your conclusion should match the study population, and the gap should be discussed. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:01–2:38)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:38–3:06)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:06–3:51)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Target = who you want; study = who you can reach. Define both precisely.

## Beat 7 (3:51–4:25)

That is the one idea for Topic 2.4. Open #t/2.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-2.5/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-2.5 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-2.5  
**Title:** 2.5: Bias  
**Word count:** 648  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:19 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic 2.5: Bias, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W2: Where Data Come From. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:28)

Here is where we open. The voluntary sample was wrong in a consistent direction. That kind of error has a name. The idea, in plain language, is this. Bias is a systematic error: it pushes results one way and does not shrink with a bigger sample. Random error does shrink. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–2:08)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Selection bias: how units enter the sample relates to the outcome. Undercoverage: part of the population can't be selected. Response bias: answers are shaded — social desirability, fear, poor recall. Measurement bias: the instrument is off — a miscalibrated scale, a tracker that undercounts steps. Each needs its own fix: better frame, follow-up of non-responders, anonymity, validated instruments. No formula repairs a biased design afterwards. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:08–2:46)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:46–3:06)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Believing a bigger sample fixes bias. Using one word 'bias' without naming which kind. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:06–3:46)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Bias = systematic; random error = noise. Selection, undercoverage, non-response, response, measurement.

## Beat 7 (3:46–4:19)

That is the one idea for Topic 2.5. Open #t/2.5 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M1/T-2.5_Bias.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M1/V-T-2.5.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-2.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-2.6  
**Title:** 2.6: Proportions and margin of error  
**Word count:** 651  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:20 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic 2.6: Proportions and margin of error, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It sits in the unit W2: Where Data Come From. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:24)

Here is where we open. Imagine you've designed a fair survey. Now report its main number properly. The idea, in plain language, is this. A sample proportion is count ÷ total: p̂ = x / n . It is a statistic that estimates the population proportion p . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–2:04)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Always report the count and n: “35.0% (42 of 120)”. A percentage without n hides how much evidence there is. A proportion is the mean of a 0/1 variable: code gym users 1 and others 0; the column average is p̂. This link drives Weeks 6–8. p̂ is almost never exactly p. How far off it is likely to be is the next lesson. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:04–2:42)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:42–3:10)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:10–3:47)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. p̂ = x / n; report x and n. A proportion is the mean of 0/1 data.

## Beat 7 (3:47–4:20)

That is the one idea for Topic 2.6. Open #t/2.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M1/T-2.6_Proportions_and_margin_of_error.tex. # V-T-2.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-2.7  
**Title:** 2.7: Ethics, privacy and data protection  
**Word count:** 648  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:19 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:55)

This short video is Topic 2.7: Ethics, privacy and data protection, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It sits in the unit W2: Where Data Come From. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:55–1:30)

Here is where we open. Good data come from people. Before you collect any, they must agree — properly. The idea, in plain language, is this. Informed consent: before taking part, people know the purpose, what is collected, how it is used and stored, who sees it, any risks, and that they may refuse or withdraw without penalty. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:30–2:10)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Consent must be voluntary . A lecturer surveying their own students must make clear grades are unaffected; power differences make “voluntary” harder. Consent is specific: data collected for a course project should not later be uploaded to an AI tool or shared unless participants were told. Research involving people at CUHK normally needs ethics review — check before collecting. Minors and vulnerable groups need extra protection. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:10–2:48)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:48–3:16)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:16–3:46)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Purpose, data, use, storage, risks, right to withdraw. Voluntary and specific.

## Beat 7 (3:46–4:19)

## Continuous script (for the recording booth)

This short video is Topic 2.7: Ethics, privacy and data protection, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It sits in the unit W2: Where Data Come From. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

Here is where we open. Good data come from people. Before you collect any, they must agree — properly. The idea, in plain language, is this. Informed consent: before taking part, people know the purpose, what is collected, how it is used and stored, who sees it, any risks, and that they may refuse or withdraw without penalty. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Consent must be voluntary . A lecturer surveying their own students must make clear grades are unaffected; power differences make “voluntary” harder. Consent is specific: data collected for a course project should not later be uploaded to an AI tool or shared unless participants were told. Research involving people at CUHK normally needs ethics review — check before collecting. Minors and vulnerable groups need extra protection. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Purpose, data, use, storage, risks, right to withdraw. Voluntary and specific.

That is the one idea for Topic 2.7. # V-T-2.8 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-2.8  
**Title:** 2.8: Copilot lab: survey overview and bias check  
**Word count:** 655  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:22 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 2.8: Copilot lab: survey overview and bias check, in official Module 1, Statistical Thinking and AI-Assisted Analysis. It sits in the unit W2: Where Data Come From. The official map budgets 1.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:27)

Here is where we open. Everything this week comes together in the lab. First question: what is in this file? The idea, in plain language, is this. Before “what does the survey show?”, ask “what is in this file?”: a data overview of rows, columns and a one-line description of each variable. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:27–2:00)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Paste the prompt contract, upload the synthetic student survey (300 rows) and its README. Ask for rows, columns, column names and a description of each from the README. Verify rows and columns in Excel and compare every description with the README. Log mismatches (H1) and invented descriptions (H5). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:00–2:38)

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

## Beat 5 (2:38–3:06)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:06–3:48)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Overview before analysis. Verify rows, columns, descriptions.

## Beat 7 (3:48–4:22)

That is the one idea for Topic 2.8. Open #t/2.8 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-3.1/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-3.1 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-3.1  
**Title:** 3.1: Tables, rates and percentages  
**Word count:** 731  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:52 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

This short video is Topic 3.1: Tables, rates and percentages, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It sits in the unit W3: Describing One Variable. The official map budgets 2 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:27)

Here is where we open. Week 2 gave you a clean, tidy file. Week 3 asks the first honest question about any variable: what values occur, and how often? The idea, in plain language, is this. A frequency is a count of units in a category; a relative frequency is that count divided by the total n. A frequency table lists every category, the total, and any missing. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:27–2:02)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Relative frequencies let you compare groups of different sizes: 28 of 60 and 140 of 300 are both 46.7%. Always show n and a missing row if there is one. Dropping non-responses silently inflates every percentage. For ordered categories add a cumulative column — “two-thirds rated 3 or lower” comes straight from it. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:02–3:18)

Counts of districts are not population rates. Of the 18 official districts, 4 are on Hong Kong Island, 5 in Kowloon, and 9 in the New Territories — that is 22.2%, 27.8%, and 50.0% of the districts. Official 2025 mid-year land population region totals, from table 110-02001, are 1,162.4 thousand on Hong Kong Island, 2,242.7 thousand in Kowloon, and 4,092.7 thousand in the New Territories, against an official Hong Kong total of 7,497.8 thousand. FlippedStat shares of that official total, rounded to one decimal place, are 15.5%, 29.9%, and 54.6%. So Hong Kong Island is 22.2% of districts but only 15.5% of the official mid-year land population; the New Territories is half the districts but 54.6% of the population. Use those official region and Hong Kong totals, not a sum of the 18 rounded district figures, which add to 7,497.9 thousand — one tenth of a thousand above the official total, because of published rounding. The contingency table on the page is region by the derived gained-or-lost flag. Row percentages ask, within each region, what share of districts gained. Column percentages ask, of the districts that gained, where were they.

## Beat 5 (3:18–3:43)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Percentages that add to more than 100% because respondents could choose several options — say so explicitly. Dropping 'no answer' from the denominator without mentioning it. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:43–4:19)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Frequency = count; relative frequency = count ÷ n. Show n and missing.

## Beat 7 (4:19–4:52)

That is the one idea for Topic 3.1. Open #t/3.1 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M2/T-3.1_Tables_rates_and_percentages.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M2/V-T-3.1.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-3.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-3.2  
**Title:** 3.2: Distribution shapes  
**Word count:** 611  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:04 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:52)

This short video is Topic 3.2: Distribution shapes, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It sits in the unit W3: Describing One Variable. The official map budgets 2 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:52–1:28)

Here is where we open. Categories need tables. A numerical variable like clinic wait time needs a picture of its whole distribution. The idea, in plain language, is this. A histogram splits the number line into bins and draws touching bars whose height is the count (or proportion) in each bin. The bin width is a choice that can change the story. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–2:03)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Too narrow: jagged noise, every bump looks meaningful. Too wide: real features — like a long tail — vanish. Try several widths, keep features that are stable, and report the width you used. Rules like Sturges or Freedman–Diaconis are starting points. Histogram ≠ bar chart: bars touch because the scale is continuous. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:03–2:41)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:41–3:01)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Accepting the software's default bins without trying others. Gaps between bars on a continuous histogram. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:01–3:31)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Bins split the scale; bars touch. Bin width changes the picture.

## Beat 7 (3:31–4:04)

That is the one idea for Topic 3.2. Open #t/3.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-3.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-3.3  
**Title:** 3.3: Measures of centre  
**Word count:** 644  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:18 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:51)

This short video is Topic 3.3: Measures of centre, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W3: Describing One Variable. The official map budgets 2.1667 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:51–1:21)

Here is where we open. With the shape named, the next sentence is “a typical value is...”. There are five candidates. The idea, in plain language, is this. Mean = sum ÷ n (the balance point). Median = middle value when sorted. Mode = most frequent value. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:21–1:54)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. The mean uses every value, so one huge value pulls it. The median barely moves. The mode is the only centre for nominal data (“most common mode: MTR”). Weighted means appear everywhere: GPA weights grades by credits; a portfolio return weights assets by money invested. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:54–2:42)

Centre is easy to misread when the rows are area aggregates. Take the 18 official 2025 district median monthly household incomes. The unweighted mean of those 18 district medians is 31,844 Hong Kong dollars. The median of those 18 district medians is 31,000. Neither of those is an official C and SD statistic, and neither is the official all-household median, which table 130-06806 gives as 30,000 Hong Kong dollars in 2025. The mean sitting a little above the median of medians is a mild right-skew signature, but it is a signature of 18 area medians, not of household incomes. Existing MTR, AFL and loan examples and their keys stay on the page; this official parallel sits beside them, clearly labelled.

## Beat 5 (2:42–3:01)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Reporting a mean for nominal codes. Forgetting to sort before taking the median. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:01–3:44)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Mean pulled by extremes; median resistant. Mode for categories.

## Beat 7 (3:44–4:18)

That is the one idea for Topic 3.3. # V-T-3.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-3.4  
**Title:** 3.4: Position and the boxplot  
**Word count:** 674  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:30 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:51)

This short video is Topic 3.4: Position and the boxplot, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W3: Describing One Variable. The official map budgets 1.1667 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:51–1:25)

Here is where we open. The median is the 50th percentile. Other percentiles describe other positions. The idea, in plain language, is this. The p-th percentile is a value with about p% of the data at or below it. Percentile rank goes the other way: given a value, what % are at or below it? Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:25–1:56)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Percentiles describe position, not quality: the 90th percentile of waits is a bad wait. Q1 = 25th, median = 50th, Q3 = 75th. Service standards often use them: “90% of visits seen within X minutes”. Like the median, percentiles resist outliers. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:56–2:49)

The primary five-number and box-plot example is the 18 official 2025 district median monthly household incomes, using the exclusive-halves quartile method: for even n, the two halves do not overlap. The figures, which are FlippedStat calculations and not official C and SD quartiles, are a minimum of 24,900 Hong Kong dollars in Kwun Tong, a first quartile of 26,200, a median of 31,000, a third quartile of 34,200, and a maximum of 45,000 in Central and Western. The interquartile range is 8,000. Tukey fences sit at 14,200 and 46,200, and no district is a Tukey outlier. These are 18 area aggregates, not household incomes. Software percentile algorithms may differ slightly at n equals 18; say which rule you used. The OpenIntro loan box plot, which does have outliers, remains a labelled book illustration.

## Beat 5 (2:49–3:17)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:17–3:56)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Percentile: value with p% at or below. Percentile rank: the reverse.

## Beat 7 (3:56–4:30)

That is the one idea for Topic 3.4. Open #t/3.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-3.5/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-3.5 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-3.5  
**Title:** 3.5: Measures of spread  
**Word count:** 689  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:36 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:51)

This short video is Topic 3.5: Measures of spread, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W3: Describing One Variable. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:51–1:29)

Here is where we open. Two groups can share a centre and live completely different lives. Spread is the missing half of the description. The idea, in plain language, is this. Spread measures how far values are from each other or from the centre: range (max − min), IQR (middle half), variance (average squared deviation) and standard deviation (its square root, back in the original units). Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:29–2:13)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Deviations (value − mean) always add to zero, so their plain average is useless. Squaring makes them all positive and gives big deviations more weight. Variance has squared units (minutes²). The SD is in minutes: roughly “a typical distance from the mean”. Divide by n − 1 for a sample: the mean was fitted to the same data, so deviations from it are a bit too small; n − 1 corrects that. Excel: STDEV.S. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:13–2:59)

Spread, on the same 18 official 2025 district median incomes, can be told three ways. The range is 20,100 Hong Kong dollars. The interquartile range is 8,000. The sample standard deviation, using divisor n minus 1, to match R’s sd function and jamovi, is 6,121, around a mean of 31,844. Eleven of the 18 values, about 61%, lie within one sample standard deviation of the mean, and 17 of 18 lie within two. The familiar 68 and 95 percent rule is only a rough guide here: n is 18, and the values are mildly right-skewed. These are FlippedStat calculations, not official C and SD statistics. Existing MTR, AFL and loan spread examples stay on the page.

## Beat 5 (2:59–3:25)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Using STDEV.P on sample data. Reporting variance in a plain-language report (units squared). Reporting mean ± SD for strongly skewed data (e.g. 12 ± 15 minutes implies negative waits). None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:25–4:02)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Range, IQR, variance, SD. SD = typical distance from the mean; divide by n − 1.

## Beat 7 (4:02–4:36)

That is the one idea for Topic 3.5. Open #t/3.5 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M2/T-3.5_Measures_of_spread.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M2/V-T-3.5.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-3.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-3.6  
**Title:** 3.6: Standardisation and shape  
**Word count:** 654  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:22 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

This short video is Topic 3.6: Standardisation and shape, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It sits in the unit W3: Describing One Variable. The official map budgets 2.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:21)

Here is where we open. An SD gives a natural ruler. Measure any value with it and you can compare across completely different scales. The idea, in plain language, is this. A z-score counts how many SDs a value is above (+) or below (−) its mean: z = (x − mean) ÷ SD. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:21–1:58)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. z-scores are unit-free, so you can compare marks from different tests, or heights with weights. For roughly bell-shaped data |z| > 2 is unusual (about 5%) and |z| > 3 rare. For skewed data that rule fails: the longest clinic wait has z = 5.97 — extreme on a bell curve, but not shocking for a long-tailed wait. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:58–2:51)

Hong Kong dollars and persons per square kilometre are not comparable in raw units. Standardise first. Using z equals x minus the mean, divided by the sample standard deviation of the 18 official district values, Central and Western’s 2025 median income has z of plus 2.15, and Kwun Tong’s has z of minus 1.13. On official 2025 density, Kwun Tong has z of plus 2.07, and the Islands district has z of minus 1.00. Those z-scores are relative to 18 area aggregates, not to households. Skewness of the official incomes is described on the page only in words; a software skewness figure from the AFL walk-through remains a labelled book illustration, because conventions are not treated as interchangeable at n equals 18. SAT and ACT examples also stay labelled book illustrations.

## Beat 5 (2:51–3:19)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:19–3:48)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. z = (x − mean) ÷ SD. Compare across scales.

## Beat 7 (3:48–4:22)

That is the one idea for Topic 3.6. Open #t/3.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M2/T-3.6_Standardisation_and_shape.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M2/V-T-3.6.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-3.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-3.7  
**Title:** 3.7: Missing data as a decision  
**Word count:** 662  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:25 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic 3.7: Missing data as a decision, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W3: Describing One Variable. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:28)

Here is where we open. Every summary this week used the recorded waits. How many rows is that, really? The idea, in plain language, is this. Rows in the file ≠ rows in the analysis. Report both, with a ledger that accounts for every row: used + excluded = total. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–2:02)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Rows drop out through missing values, filters, exclusions and joins — often silently. Write it: “199 of 230 visits had a recorded wait (31 missing, 13.5%).” Then ask who is missing. If patients who gave up and left are the blanks, the recorded waits understate the clinic's slowness. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:02–2:40)

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

## Beat 5 (2:40–3:08)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:08–3:51)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Report file rows and analysis rows. Used + excluded = total.

## Beat 7 (3:51–4:25)

That is the one idea for Topic 3.7. Open #t/3.7 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M2/T-3.7_Missing_data_as_a_decision.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M2/V-T-3.7.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

## Continuous script (for the recording booth)

This short video is Topic 3.7: Missing data as a decision, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W3: Describing One Variable. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

Here is where we open. Every summary this week used the recorded waits. How many rows is that, really? The idea, in plain language, is this. Rows in the file ≠ rows in the analysis. Report both, with a ledger that accounts for every row: used + excluded = total. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Rows drop out through missing values, filters, exclusions and joins — often silently. Write it: “199 of 230 visits had a recorded wait (31 missing, 13.5%).” Then ask who is missing. If patients who gave up and left are the blanks, the recorded waits understate the clinic's slowness. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Report file rows and analysis rows. Used + excluded = total.

That is the one idea for Topic 3.7. # V-T-3.8 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-3.8  
**Title:** 3.8: Copilot lab: summaries from three tools  
**Word count:** 652  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:21 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic 3.8: Copilot lab: summaries from three tools, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It sits in the unit W3: Describing One Variable. The official map budgets 2.0833 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:34)

Here is where we open. Imagine you hand the same clinic file to three AI tools and get three different answers for n. The idea, in plain language, is this. Send the same neutral prompt (with the contract) to Copilot Chat and two other tools, each in a fresh chat, with the same file. Ask for n, missing, mean, median, SD, Q1, Q3 and a code-generated histogram with the bin width stated. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:34–2:02)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Fill a comparison table: one row per statistic, one column per tool, plus your Excel column as referee. For charts: same bin width? axis labels with units? Expect differences. The next lesson is about naming them. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:02–2:40)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:40–3:08)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:08–3:47)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Same prompt, same file, fresh chats. Excel column is the referee.

## Beat 7 (3:47–4:21)

That is the one idea for Topic 3.8. Open #t/3.8 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M2/T-3.8_Copilot_lab_summaries_from_three_tools.tex.
