# V-T-4.1 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-4.1  
**Title:** 4.1: Comparing groups  
**Word count:** 642  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:17 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

This short video is Topic 4.1: Comparing groups, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It sits in the unit W4: Comparing, Relating and Displaying. The official map budgets 1.1667 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:20)

Here is where we open. Imagine you compare MTR and bus commutes and an AI reports only the two means. The idea, in plain language, is this. Side-by-side boxplots draw one boxplot per group on a shared axis , so centre, spread, skew and outliers can be compared at a glance. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:20–1:54)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Order groups meaningfully (by median, or a natural order), and always show n under each box. Overlay the points when n is small or moderate: a box hides two-peaked groups. Read in order: centre → spread → shape → outliers → n. Then write one sentence that mentions centre and spread. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:54–2:49)

To compare groups, the page splits the 18 official districts by whether mid-year land population rose or fell from 2016 to 2025. Ten districts gained; eight lost; none were unchanged. That flag is a FlippedStat calculation on official figures from tables 110-02001 and 130-06806. Now look at 2025 official district median monthly household incomes in those two groups. The median of those district medians is 30,350 Hong Kong dollars in the gained group, and 33,800 in the lost group. The centre goes the other way from OpenIntro’s US-county illustration, which remains labelled on the page. The interquartile ranges are 5,600 versus 11,650. This is observational only: districts that lost population are not a random treatment group. And a median of district medians is not the official Hong Kong median, which is 30,000 Hong Kong dollars in 2025.

## Beat 5 (2:49–3:14)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Different y-axis scales for each group. Comparing medians without mentioning spread. No n shown — a tiny group's box looks as reliable as a big one. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:14–3:43)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. One box per group, shared axis. Show n; overlay points.

## Beat 7 (3:43–4:17)

That is the one idea for Topic 4.1. Open #t/4.1 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M2/T-4.1_Comparing_groups.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M2/V-T-4.1.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-4.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-4.2  
**Title:** 4.2: Two numerical variables  
**Word count:** 619  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:08 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

This short video is Topic 4.2: Two numerical variables, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It sits in the unit W4: Comparing, Relating and Displaying. The official map budgets 1.4167 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:18)

Here is where we open. Comparing groups uses one categorical and one numerical variable. Now both variables are numbers. The idea, in plain language, is this. A scatterplot shows two numerical variables on the same units: one dot per unit, x = explanatory, y = response. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:18–1:50)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Label both axes with units. Unlike bar charts, scatterplot axes need not start at zero. Overplotting hides density: use transparency, smaller dots, or slight jitter for rounded values. A third variable can be colour or shape — only if the chart stays readable. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:50–2:23)

Plot official 2025 district median monthly household income, in Hong Kong dollars, against official 2025 population density, for the 18 districts. Pearson’s r is minus 0.38: a weak-to-moderate negative association. That r is a FlippedStat calculation on 18 official pairs, not an official C and SD statistic. Eighteen area-level points are not 18 households, so this is an ecological association, not a household law. Look at the scatter before you trust the single number. OpenIntro’s US income-and-poverty scatter remains a labelled book illustration.

## Beat 5 (2:23–2:51)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:51–3:34)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. One dot per unit. Explanatory on x, response on y.

## Beat 7 (3:34–4:08)

That is the one idea for Topic 4.2. Open #t/4.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M2/T-4.2_Two_numerical_variables.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M2/V-T-4.2.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-4.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-4.3  
**Title:** 4.3: Transformations  
**Word count:** 668  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:27 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:47)

This short video is Topic 4.3: Transformations, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It sits in the unit W4: Comparing, Relating and Displaying. The official map budgets 0.9167 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:47–1:25)

Here is where we open. Some variables, like income, are so skewed that most of the data are squashed into one corner. A transformation can unsquash them. The idea, in plain language, is this. A transformation applies the same function to every value: order is kept, distances change. Log turns multiplication into addition and pulls in long right tails; square root is gentler; reciprocal is strongest. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:25–1:59)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Ladder of powers: x² → x → √x → log x → −1/√x → −1/x. Moving down pulls in right tails more. Logs need positive values. log(x + 1) handles zeros but changes interpretation — say so. Square root is common for counts; log for money, sizes and rates. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:59–2:46)

Transformations earn their keep on a skewed official series. The page uses official daily rainfall at the Hong Kong Observatory, from 2016 to 2025. Trace rainfall, meaning less than 0.05 millimetres, is kept as an official token, not recoded as a number. On the 1,477 measurable wet days, the raw positive totals run from 0.1 millimetres to 425.0 millimetres on 8 September 2023, with a mean of 16.73 millimetres and a median of 4.3 — strongly right-skewed. After a log10 transform, the mean is 0.58, the median is 0.63, and the Pearson skew is minus 0.14: nearly symmetric. Those are FlippedStat calculations on official figures, not official Observatory statistics. OpenIntro’s US-county histograms remain a labelled book illustration.

## Beat 5 (2:46–3:14)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:14–3:54)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Transform = same function on every value. Log pulls in right tails.

## Beat 7 (3:54–4:27)

That is the one idea for Topic 4.3. Open #t/4.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M2/T-4.3_Transformations.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M2/V-T-4.3.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-4.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-4.4  
**Title:** 4.4: Visual encoding and chart choice  
**Word count:** 665  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:26 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:52)

This short video is Topic 4.4: Visual encoding and chart choice, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W4: Comparing, Relating and Displaying. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:52–1:26)

Here is where we open. Every chart turns numbers into something visual. Some visual codes are read far more accurately than others. The idea, in plain language, is this. Charts encode values as position, length, angle, area or colour. People judge position on a common scale best, then length, then angle, then area, then colour. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:26–2:00)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. So: dot plots and bar charts for precise comparison; pies only for 2–3 parts of a whole; colour for categories, not exact values. Area traps: scale a circle's radius by the value and its area grows with the square — differences look huge. Avoid 3-D: it distorts length and angle. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:00–2:49)

Chart choice includes a decision about what you are allowed to copy. C and SD maps and graphics are excluded from the general reuse permission, so this course does not reproduce official map artwork. Instead, you read the official figures from a ranked table of the 18 districts. The highest 2025 district median monthly household incomes are Central and Western at 45,000 Hong Kong dollars, and Wan Chai at 43,300. The lowest are Kwun Tong at 24,900 and Sham Shui Po at 25,000. The highest official density is Kwun Tong, at 59,400 persons per square kilometre. OpenIntro’s US-county maps remain labelled book illustrations. The teaching point is what stands out in the official table, not a choropleth copied from a government publication.

## Beat 5 (2:49–3:17)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:17–3:52)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Position and length are read best. Angle and area are poor for comparison.

## Beat 7 (3:52–4:26)

That is the one idea for Topic 4.4. Open #t/4.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M2/T-4.4_Visual_encoding_and_chart_choice.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M2/V-T-4.4.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. The highest 2025 district median monthly household incomes are Central and Western at 45,000 Hong Kong dollars, and Wan Chai at 43,300. The lowest are Kwun Tong at 24,900 and Sham Shui Po at 25,000. The highest official density is Kwun Tong, at 59,400 persons per square kilometre. OpenIntro’s US-county maps remain labelled book illustrations. The teaching point is what stands out in the official table, not a choropleth copied from a government publication.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Position and length are read best. Angle and area are poor for comparison.

That is the one idea for Topic 4.4. Open #t/4.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M2/T-4.4_Visual_encoding_and_chart_choice.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M2/V-T-4.4.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-4.5 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-4.5  
**Title:** 4.5: Misleading and accessible charts  
**Word count:** 630  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:12 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic 4.5: Misleading and accessible charts, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W4: Comparing, Relating and Displaying. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:30)

Here is where we open. Good encodings can still be abused. The commonest trick is the axis. The idea, in plain language, is this. In a bar chart the bar's length encodes the value, so the axis must start at zero . Line charts and dot plots encode position and may start elsewhere — clearly labelled. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:30–2:02)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. A truncated axis turns a 2-point gap into a fake 3× difference. Watch for broken axes, uneven tick spacing, and charts meant to be compared that use different axis ranges. Checking trick: read the actual numbers off the axis and compute the real ratio. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:02–2:40)

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

## Beat 5 (2:40–3:08)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:08–3:38)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Bars start at zero. Lines and dots may not — label clearly.

## Beat 7 (3:38–4:12)

That is the one idea for Topic 4.5. Open #t/4.5 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M2/T-4.5_Misleading_and_accessible_charts.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M2/V-T-4.5.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-4.6/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-4.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-4.6  
**Title:** 4.6: Joining and reshaping tables  
**Word count:** 658  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:23 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 4.6: Joining and reshaping tables, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It sits in the unit W4: Comparing, Relating and Displaying. The official map budgets 1.3333 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:25)

Here is where we open. Real data arrive in several tables. Keys tell the computer which rows belong together. The idea, in plain language, is this. A key identifies rows. A primary key is unique in its own table; a foreign key in another table refers to it. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:25–2:00)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Check before joining: unique where it should be? Same type in both tables (text '0123' vs number 123)? Names are bad keys: duplicates (two “Chan Tai Man”), spelling variants and privacy issues. Use IDs. A composite key, such as (student_id, course), can be the primary key when no single column is unique. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:00–2:38)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:38–3:06)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:06–3:50)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Keys link tables. Primary key unique; foreign key refers to it.

## Beat 7 (3:50–4:23)

That is the one idea for Topic 4.6. Open #t/4.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M2/T-4.6_Joining_and_reshaping_tables.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M2/V-T-4.6.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-4.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-4.7  
**Title:** 4.7: Reading AI-written code  
**Word count:** 642  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:17 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic 4.7: Reading AI-written code, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It sits in the unit W4: Comparing, Relating and Displaying. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:25)

Here is where we open. AI writes the code; you read it. The most dangerous lines are the settings you can't see. The idea, in plain language, is this. Every function has default arguments — choices someone made for you. Defaults for missing values, SD divisor and quantile method change results. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:25–1:58)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. pandas .mean() skips missing values; R mean() returns NA unless na.rm=TRUE . pandas .std() divides by n − 1; numpy np.std() divides by n. Habit: for each call, ask “what settings did it use that I can't see?” — then ask AI to write them explicitly: df['x'].std(ddof=1) . If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:58–2:36)

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

## Beat 5 (2:36–3:04)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:04–3:43)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Defaults are hidden choices. NA handling, SD divisor, quantile type.

## Beat 7 (3:43–4:17)

That is the one idea for Topic 4.7. Open #t/4.7 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. Count first: rows in the file, blanks, recorded values — and who the blanks might be. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–2:03)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. File: 230 scheduled visits. Blank wait_min: 31. Blanks in a clinic log often mean the patient left before being seen — the long waits are the ones likely to be missing . You can't prove why from the file alone, but you must name the risk: line 2 of your memo. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:03–2:40)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:40–3:08)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:08–3:44)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Count: 230 rows, 31 blank, 199 recorded. Ask who the blanks are.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Count: 230 rows, 31 blank, 199 recorded. Ask who the blanks are.

That is the one idea for Topic 4.8. Open #t/4.8 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M2/T-4.8_Audit_lab_the_tail_and_the_blanks.tex. # V-T-4.9 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-4.9  
**Title:** 4.9: Block A exam practice and post-check  
**Word count:** 615  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:06 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:55)

This short video is Topic 4.9: Block A exam practice and post-check, in official Module 2, Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualisation. It sits in the unit W4: Comparing, Relating and Displaying. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:55–1:29)

Here is where we open. Block A is done. Can you still do it with a calculator and no AI? The idea, in plain language, is this. Exam-format items cover Weeks 1–4: questions and variables, sampling and bias, margins of error, tables and rates, distributions, centre, spread, boxplots, z-scores, missing data, scatterplots and correlation, chart choice. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:29–1:58)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Show method: formula, substitution, answer with units, one-line interpretation. Two items ask you to refuse an unsupported claim — “cannot be concluded because...” is a full-mark answer when it's right. Time yourself: about 6 minutes per item. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:58–2:36)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:36–3:04)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:04–3:32)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Formula, substitution, answer, interpretation. Refusing can be correct.

## Beat 7 (3:32–4:06)

That is the one idea for Topic 4.9. Open #t/4.9 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-5.1/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-5.1 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-5.1  
**Title:** 5.1: Block B pre-check  
**Word count:** 648  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:19 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:52)

This short video is Topic 5.1: Block B pre-check, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It sits in the unit W5: Probability and Conditioning. The official map budgets 0.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:52–1:23)

Here is where we open. Block A described data you have. Block B is about the process that produces data — chance. The idea, in plain language, is this. The Block B pre-check is ten short items on chance, risk and conditional statements. It is a baseline, not a grade. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:23–1:57)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Two items present a confident claim (a medical test, a “hot streak”) and ask whether it follows. “It does not follow, because...” can be the best answer. Intuition about probability is famously unreliable — even among doctors and lawyers. A low score is normal. Answer without notes or AI. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:57–2:35)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:35–3:03)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:03–3:46)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Baseline, not a grade. Intuition about chance is unreliable.

## Beat 7 (3:46–4:19)

That is the one idea for Topic 5.1. Open #t/5.1 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M3/T-5.1_Block_B_pre_check.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M3/V-T-5.1.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-5.10 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-5.10  
**Title:** 5.10: Audit lab: two conditionals  
**Word count:** 644  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:18 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 5.10: Audit lab: two conditionals, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It sits in the unit W5: Probability and Conditioning. The official map budgets 1.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:27)

Here is where we open. Audit lab. An AI wrote: “This test is 90% accurate, so a positive result means you are 90% certain to have the condition.” Check it with numbers. The idea, in plain language, is this. Count and Recompute: build the 1,000-person table at 4% prevalence and at 20%, then compute PPV. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:27–1:55)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. 4%: TP = 0.90 × 40 = 36; FP = 0.08 × 960 = 76.8; PPV ≈ 0.32. 20%: TP 180, FP 64 → PPV ≈ 0.74. Use the lab panel to confirm both. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:55–2:33)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:33–3:01)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:01–3:44)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Build the table. PPV 0.32 at 4%; 0.74 at 20%.

## Beat 7 (3:44–4:18)

That is the one idea for Topic 5.10. # V-T-5.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-5.2  
**Title:** 5.2: Experiments, sample spaces and events  
**Word count:** 645  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:18 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:52)

This short video is Topic 5.2: Experiments, sample spaces and events, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It sits in the unit W5: Probability and Conditioning. The official map budgets 1.6667 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:52–1:27)

Here is where we open. To talk about chance precisely you need a list of everything that could happen. The idea, in plain language, is this. A random experiment has an uncertain result. Each possible result is an outcome ; the list of all outcomes is the sample space S. Choose outcomes that are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:27–2:03)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. For two dice, treat them as first and second: 36 ordered pairs (1,1) ... (6,6), all equally likely for fair dice. Listing sums 2–12 gives 11 outcomes that are not equally likely: one way to get 2, six ways to get 7. Choosing the right level of detail is the first skill of probability. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:03–2:41)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:41–3:04)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Treating outcomes as equally likely when they aren't (sums of dice, 'rain or no rain'). Forgetting outcomes (e.g. a draw in football). None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:04–3:44)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Sample space = all outcomes. Pick outcomes that are equally likely when you can.

## Beat 7 (3:44–4:18)

That is the one idea for Topic 5.2. # V-T-5.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-5.3  
**Title:** 5.3: Interpretations and axioms  
**Word count:** 624  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:10 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic 5.3: Interpretations and axioms, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It sits in the unit W5: Probability and Conditioning. The official map budgets 2 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:28)

Here is where we open. Imagine you toss a coin ten times and get seven heads. Is the coin biased, or is ten tosses just too few? The idea, in plain language, is this. Three interpretations: classical (equally likely outcomes by symmetry), frequency (long-run proportion over repetitions) and subjective (a coherent degree of belief, updated with evidence). Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–2:02)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. The law of large numbers links classical and frequency: as repetitions grow, the observed proportion settles near the true probability. But short runs wander a lot . 10 tosses giving 7 heads is ordinary. A forecaster is well calibrated if it rains on about 70% of the days they say “70%”. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:02–2:40)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:40–3:02)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. The gambler's fallacy: thinking short-run deviations must 'correct'. The law of large numbers works by swamping, not compensating. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:02–3:36)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Classical, frequency, subjective. LLN: proportions settle in the long run.

## Beat 7 (3:36–4:10)

That is the one idea for Topic 5.3. Open #t/5.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M3/T-5.3_Interpretations_and_axioms.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M3/V-T-5.3.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-5.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-5.4  
**Title:** 5.4: Counting  
**Word count:** 612  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:05 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:52)

This short video is Topic 5.4: Counting, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It sits in the unit W5: Probability and Conditioning. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:52–1:25)

Here is where we open. Equally likely outcomes mean probability = count ÷ count. So you need fast counting. The idea, in plain language, is this. Multiplication principle: k stages with n₁, n₂, ..., nₖ choices give n₁ × n₂ × ... × nₖ ways. Addition principle: choosing from separate groups, add. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:25–1:58)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. A tree shows why: each branch splits into the same number of sub-branches. 4 teas or 5 coffees → 9 drinks (add). 3 sizes and 9 drinks → 27 orders (multiply). The stages must not change each other's number of choices — or you need a different count. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:58–2:36)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:36–3:04)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:04–3:31)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Stages multiply. Separate groups add.

## Beat 7 (3:31–4:05)

That is the one idea for Topic 5.4. Open #t/5.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M3/T-5.4_Counting.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M3/V-T-5.4.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

Here is where we open. Back to “or”. Adding two probabilities is almost right — the error is in the overlap. The idea, in plain language, is this. Addition law: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Adding counts the overlap twice; subtract it once. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:23–1:51)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. You need P(A ∩ B) from data, a table, or an assumption (e.g. independence: P(A)P(B)). Rearranged: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B). The Venn diagram makes the double-counting visible. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:51–2:29)

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

## Beat 5 (2:29–2:57)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:57–3:40)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Add, then subtract the overlap. Need P(A ∩ B) from somewhere.

## Beat 7 (3:40–4:14)

# V-T-5.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-5.6  
**Title:** 5.6: Multiplication law and conditional probability  
**Word count:** 786  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 5:14 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:51)

This short video is Topic 5.6: Multiplication law and conditional probability, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W5: Probability and Conditioning. The official map budgets 1.9167 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:51–1:28)

Here is where we open. Knowing one thing about a person can change the probability of another. That is conditioning. The idea, in plain language, is this. Conditional probability P(A | B) is the probability of A when we restrict attention to cases where B happened: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B). In counts: both ÷ number in B. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–1:58)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Conditioning shrinks the sample space to B. Multiplication law: P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B). Use it to build joint probabilities step by step. Everyday language hides conditioning: “among smokers”, “of the flagged cases”, “if it rains”. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:58–3:34)

The student-facing official illustration on this topic is a two-way table built from the official 2025 mid-year land population in hk_district_profile_2016_2025.csv, classed by region and by a FlippedStat flag for whether official mid-year land population was higher in 2025 than in 2016. The figures come from C and SD table 110-02001. Weighting each district by its official 2025 mid-year land population gives a table of people in those official district figures, not a sample of households. The 18 published district figures sum to 7,497.9 thousand; the official Hong Kong total in the same table is 7,497.8 thousand, and the table notes that figures may not add because of rounding. Of that 7,497.9 thousand, 4,831.0 thousand live in a gained-population district, so P of gained is 4,831.0 over 7,497.9, or 64.4 percent. Given region: P of gained given Hong Kong Island is 0 percent — all four official Island districts lost population; P of gained given Kowloon is 1,535.3 over 2,242.7, or 68.5 percent; and P of gained given the New Territories is 3,295.7 over 4,092.8, or 80.5 percent. The other way around is a different number: P of Kowloon given gained is 1,535.3 over 4,831.0, or 31.8 percent, not 68.5. These percentages are FlippedStat calculations on official figures and a derived grouping, not official C and SD probabilities. A labelled course illustration on the same page still uses 1,000 students and a vape-and-asthma table to show the same swap.

## Beat 5 (3:34–4:02)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (4:02–4:41)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Conditioning shrinks the world.

## Beat 7 (4:41–5:14)

That is the one idea for Topic 5.6. Open #t/5.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M3/T-5.6_Multiplication_law_and_conditional_probability.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M3/V-T-5.6.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

The other way around is a different number: P of Kowloon given gained is 1,535.3 over 4,831.0, or 31.8 percent, not 68.5. These percentages are FlippedStat calculations on official figures and a derived grouping, not official C and SD probabilities. A labelled course illustration on the same page still uses 1,000 students and a vape-and-asthma table to show the same swap.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Conditioning shrinks the world.

That is the one idea for Topic 5.6. Open #t/5.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. # V-T-5.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-5.7  
**Title:** 5.7: Independence  
**Word count:** 671  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:28 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:46)

This short video is Topic 5.7: Independence, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It sits in the unit W5: Probability and Conditioning. The official map budgets 0.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:46–1:17)

Here is where we open. Sometimes knowing B tells you nothing about A. That special case has a name. The idea, in plain language, is this. A and B are independent if P(A | B) = P(A) — equivalently P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:17–1:53)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Independence is symmetric: if B tells you nothing about A, A tells you nothing about B. Physically separate processes (a coin and a die, draws with replacement) give independence. In data, independence is checked or assumed , never taken for granted. Repeated measures on the same student, classmates, consecutive days — usually not independent. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:53–2:54)

Independence would require that P of gained given region equals the marginal P of gained, for every region. Using the same official 2025 mid-year land-population figures and FlippedStat gained-or-lost flag as Topic 5.6, P of gained is 64.4 percent, but P of gained given Hong Kong Island is 0 percent, P of gained given Kowloon is 68.5 percent, and P of gained given the New Territories is 80.5 percent. Learning the region changes the probability, so the events “lives in a gained-population district” and “lives on Hong Kong Island” are not independent. If the two classifications were independent, the expected official 2025 population in gained-population districts on Hong Kong Island would be 1,162.4 times 4,831.0 over 7,497.9, or about 749 thousand; the observed figure is 0. That comparison describes these official aggregates. It is not a chi-square test of a random sample, and it is not an official C and SD finding.

## Beat 5 (2:54–3:22)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:22–3:55)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Independent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). Symmetric.

## Beat 7 (3:55–4:28)

That is the one idea for Topic 5.7. Open #t/5.7 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M3/T-5.7_Independence.tex. # V-T-5.8 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-5.8  
**Title:** 5.8: Total probability and Bayes' theorem  
**Word count:** 614  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:06 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic 5.8: Total probability and Bayes' theorem, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W5: Probability and Conditioning. The official map budgets 2.1667 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:28)

Here is where we open. Overall rates are built from group rates. The rule that combines them comes next. The idea, in plain language, is this. Law of total probability: if B₁, ..., Bₖ split S into non-overlapping pieces, P(A) = Σ P(A | Bᵢ) P(Bᵢ) — a weighted average of group rates. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–1:57)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Partitions: Machine A/B; disease/no disease; Year 1/2/3/4. It is exactly “add the tree paths that end in A”. Overall rates depend on both within-group rates and group sizes — the root of Simpson's paradox (11.3.2). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:57–2:34)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:34–3:02)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:02–3:32)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Overall = weighted average of group rates. Weights = group sizes.

## Beat 7 (3:32–4:06)

That is the one idea for Topic 5.8. Open #t/5.8 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued.
