# V-T-5.9 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-5.9  
**Title:** 5.9: Screening and base rates  
**Word count:** 627  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:11 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic 5.9: Screening and base rates, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W5: Probability and Conditioning. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:26)

Here is where we open. Natural frequencies give the four counts of every screening table. Each has a name. The idea, in plain language, is this. Sensitivity = P(+ | condition); specificity = P(− | no condition). PPV = P(condition | +); NPV = P(no condition | −). Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:26–1:53)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Sensitivity and specificity condition on the true status (columns); PPV and NPV condition on the test result (rows). Patients care about PPV and NPV. False-positive rate = 1 − specificity. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:53–2:31)

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

## Beat 5 (2:31–2:55)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Telling a patient 'the test is 90% accurate, so you have a 90% chance'. Using 'accuracy' (TP+TN)/n — dominated by the large healthy group. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (2:55–3:37)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Sens/spec: given true status. PPV/NPV: given test result.

## Beat 7 (3:37–4:11)

That is the one idea for Topic 5.9. # V-T-6.1 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-6.1  
**Title:** 6.1: Discrete random variables  
**Word count:** 660  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:24 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:52)

This short video is Topic 6.1: Discrete random variables, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It sits in the unit W6: Random Variables, Models and Simulation. The official map budgets 1.8333 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:52–1:32)

Here is where we open. Week 5 gave probabilities to events. Week 6 attaches numbers to outcomes, so we can average and measure spread — of chance itself. The idea, in plain language, is this. A random variable X assigns a number to each outcome. A discrete X has a list of values; its pmf gives P(X = x) and its CDF F(x) = P(X ≤ x) adds them up. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:32–2:05)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. pmf rules: each probability between 0 and 1; all add to 1. Use the pmf for “exactly”, the CDF for “at most”; “at least k” = 1 − F(k − 1). Keep apart the random variable X (before the experiment) and an observed value x (after). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:05–2:42)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:42–3:10)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:10–3:50)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Random variable = number per outcome. pmf for exactly; CDF for at most.

## Continuous script (for the recording booth)

This short video is Topic 6.1: Discrete random variables, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It sits in the unit W6: Random Variables, Models and Simulation. The official map budgets 1.8333 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

Here is where we open. Week 5 gave probabilities to events. Week 6 attaches numbers to outcomes, so we can average and measure spread — of chance itself. The idea, in plain language, is this. A random variable X assigns a number to each outcome. A discrete X has a list of values; its pmf gives P(X = x) and its CDF F(x) = P(X ≤ x) adds them up. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. pmf rules: each probability between 0 and 1; all add to 1. Use the pmf for “exactly”, the CDF for “at most”; “at least k” = 1 − F(k − 1). Keep apart the random variable X (before the experiment) and an observed value x (after). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Random variable = number per outcome. pmf for exactly; CDF for at most.

That is the one idea for Topic 6.1. Open #t/6.1 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. # V-T-6.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-6.2  
**Title:** 6.2: Binomial distribution  
**Word count:** 642  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:17 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:55)

This short video is Topic 6.2: Binomial distribution, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W6: Random Variables, Models and Simulation. The official map budgets 3.9167 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:55–1:29)

Here is where we open. The simplest random variable has two values: 1 for success, 0 for failure. The idea, in plain language, is this. A Bernoulli trial has two outcomes, coded 1 (“success” — whatever you count) with probability p, and 0 with 1 − p. Mean = p; variance = p(1 − p) . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:29–2:01)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. “Success” can be “defective” or “infected”; it's just the outcome you count. Variance p(1 − p) is largest at p = 0.5 — why 1/√n is the worst-case margin of error (2.6.2). The sample proportion p̂ is the average of many Bernoulli 0/1 values. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:01–2:39)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:39–3:07)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:07–3:43)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Bernoulli: 1 with p, 0 with 1 − p. Mean p, variance p(1 − p).

## Beat 7 (3:43–4:17)

That is the one idea for Topic 6.2. Open #t/6.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. # V-T-6.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-6.3  
**Title:** 6.3: Poisson distribution and rare events  
**Word count:** 669  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:28 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:49)

This short video is Topic 6.3: Poisson distribution and rare events, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It sits in the unit W6: Random Variables, Models and Simulation. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:49–1:26)

Here is where we open. Some counts have no fixed number of trials — calls just arrive. They need a different model. The idea, in plain language, is this. The Poisson distribution models counts of events in a fixed interval when events happen independently at a constant average rate λ: P(X = k) = e^(−λ) λᵏ ÷ k!. Mean = variance = λ. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:26–1:56)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Examples: calls per hour, typos per page, goals per match, admissions per night. Scale λ to the interval: 3 per hour → 6 per 2 hours. Assumptions: independent events, constant rate , no two at exactly the same instant. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:56–2:56)

A Poisson model needs a count with a reasonably stable rate. The page does not throw daily lightning stroke totals into that role, because strokes cluster in storms and are strongly overdispersed. Instead, for each June, July and August from 2016 to 2025, count the days with at least one official cloud-to-ground lightning record over Hong Kong territory. That is 30 months, and the monthly counts are a FlippedStat derivation from official daily totals. The mean is 17.17 days, the sample variance is 18.35, and variance over mean is 1.07. A Poisson rate of 17.17 is a starting model, not a claim that nature is exactly Poisson. Official monthly live births, from table 115-01012A, have a changing rate — the official annual total fell from 60,856 in 2016 to 31,053 in 2025 — so they are a caution, not the worked example. The New York AMI figure remains a labelled book illustration.

## Beat 5 (2:56–3:24)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:24–3:54)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Counts at a constant rate λ. Mean = variance = λ.

## Beat 7 (3:54–4:28)

That is the one idea for Topic 6.3. Open #t/6.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M3/T-6.3_Poisson_distribution_and_rare_events.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M3/V-T-6.3.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-6.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-6.4  
**Title:** 6.4: Continuous random variables  
**Word count:** 658  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:23 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 6.4: Continuous random variables, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It sits in the unit W6: Random Variables, Models and Simulation. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:27)

Here is where we open. Counts take separate values. Times and heights take any value in a range — and that changes how probability works. The idea, in plain language, is this. For a continuous X, single values have probability 0; probability lives in intervals , as the area under a density curve f(x). Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:27–2:01)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Density rules: f(x) ≥ 0 and total area = 1. A density's height is not a probability — it can exceed 1. Only areas are probabilities. P(X < b) = P(X ≤ b) for continuous X. A density-scaled histogram approximates the curve as n grows and bins shrink. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:01–2:38)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:38–3:06)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:06–3:50)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Probability = area under the density. Height is not probability.

## Beat 7 (3:50–4:23)

That is the one idea for Topic 6.4. Open #t/6.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. # V-T-6.5 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-6.5  
**Title:** 6.5: The normal distribution  
**Word count:** 671  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:28 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:51)

This short video is Topic 6.5: The normal distribution, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W6: Random Variables, Models and Simulation. The official map budgets 2.1667 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:51–1:24)

Here is where we open. One continuous shape appears everywhere averages and sums appear: the normal. The idea, in plain language, is this. A normal N(μ, σ) is a symmetric bell centred at μ with SD σ. Standardising Z = (X − μ)/σ turns any normal into the standard normal N(0, 1). Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–1:55)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. 68–95–99.7: about 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 (1.96 exactly), 99.7% within 3. Sums and averages of many small independent effects tend to be normal — the CLT (Week 7). Incomes, waits and counts of rare events are usually not normal (3.6.2). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:55–2:48)

The normal curve is a model, not a medal. The official June to August daily mean temperatures at the Hong Kong Observatory, 2016 to 2025, give 920 days. The mean is 29.23 degrees Celsius, the median is 29.50, and the sample standard deviation is 1.35, with a mild left skew of minus 0.75. 633 of those 920 days, 68.8%, lie within one sample standard deviation of the mean; 875, or 95.1%, within two; and 918, or 99.8%, within three. That is a reasonably mound-shaped official measurement, and a fair course illustration. It is not a claim that the official series is exactly normal. The full-year series is a poor normal model because of the seasonal cycle, and it is used only as a contrast. SAT and US height figures remain labelled book illustrations.

## Beat 5 (2:48–3:16)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:16–3:55)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Bell centred at μ, width σ. Standardise with z.

This short video is Topic 6.5: The normal distribution, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W6: Random Variables, Models and Simulation. The official map budgets 2.1667 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

Here is where we open. One continuous shape appears everywhere averages and sums appear: the normal. The idea, in plain language, is this. A normal N(μ, σ) is a symmetric bell centred at μ with SD σ. Standardising Z = (X − μ)/σ turns any normal into the standard normal N(0, 1). Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. 68–95–99.7: about 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 (1.96 exactly), 99.7% within 3. Sums and averages of many small independent effects tend to be normal — the CLT (Week 7). Incomes, waits and counts of rare events are usually not normal (3.6.2). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

The normal curve is a model, not a medal. The official June to August daily mean temperatures at the Hong Kong Observatory, 2016 to 2025, give 920 days. The mean is 29.23 degrees Celsius, the median is 29.50, and the sample standard deviation is 1.35, with a mild left skew of minus 0.75. 633 of those 920 days, 68.8%, lie within one sample standard deviation of the mean; 875, or 95.1%, within two; and 918, or 99.8%, within three. That is a reasonably mound-shaped official measurement, and a fair course illustration. It is not a claim that the official series is exactly normal. The full-year series is a poor normal model because of the seasonal cycle, and it is used only as a contrast. SAT and US height figures remain labelled book illustrations.

# V-T-6.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-6.6  
**Title:** 6.6: Simulation and the law of large numbers  
**Word count:** 716  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:46 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic 6.6: Simulation and the law of large numbers, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W6: Random Variables, Models and Simulation. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:24)

Here is where we open. When the formula is hard, let a computer play the game many times. The idea, in plain language, is this. Monte Carlo simulation: write down the random process, repeat it R times, count how often the event happens. The proportion estimates the probability. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–2:02)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Steps: (1) define the model and assumptions; (2) simulate once; (3) repeat R times; (4) summarise; (5) report the Monte Carlo error. It works for queues, sports seasons, insurance portfolios, sampling distributions (Week 7) and permutation tests (Week 8). A simulation is only as good as its model . “The computer said so” is never a justification — the assumptions are. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:02–3:12)

The official 2025 mid-year land population of Hong Kong is 7,497.8 thousand, of whom 4,092.7 thousand live in the New Territories, from C and SD table 110-02001. The FlippedStat share is 4,092.7 over 7,497.8, or 54.6 percent, already used as a regional share in Topic 3.1. That official share can play the role of a known population proportion p. If simple random samples of residents were drawn from this official mid-year land population, the sample proportion living in the New Territories would wander around 54.6 percent. The law of large numbers says that as the sample size grows, that sample proportion gets closer to the official 54.6 percent. The samples themselves are FlippedStat teaching draws, not an official C and SD survey, and the official table is a census-style mid-year count, not a poll. The page’s birthday illustration remains: in a tutorial of 23 people, the exact probability of a shared birthday is 0.507. Keep that classic illustration labelled, and do not treat official daily weather or monthly birth series as independent draws.

## Beat 5 (3:12–3:40)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:40–4:13)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Define, simulate, repeat, summarise. Report MC error.

## Beat 7 (4:13–4:46)

That is the one idea for Topic 6.6. Open #t/6.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-6.7/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-6.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-6.7  
**Title:** 6.7: Copilot lab: rare-event risk by simulation  
**Word count:** 678  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:31 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:50)

This short video is Topic 6.7: Copilot lab: rare-event risk by simulation, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It sits in the unit W6: Random Variables, Models and Simulation. The official map budgets 1.8333 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract (rare-event contrast) on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:50–1:28)

Here is where we open. Copilot lab: get an AI to write and run a seeded simulation — properly. The idea, in plain language, is this. Ask Copilot (with the contract) to write and execute a seeded simulation: R = 10,000 batches of 1,000 runs, failure probability 0.001, report P(X ≥ 3), its MC SE, the seed and the code — and list the model assumptions . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–1:59)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Read the drafted code against the checklist before looking at the number. Check: ≥ 3, not > 3; p = 0.001, not 0.01; n = 1,000 per batch; seed set once at the top. Assumptions to expect: independent runs, constant p. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:59–3:00)

The keyed lab on this page is unchanged. Each of 1,000 independent runs fails with probability 0.001, and the exact probability of three or more failures is 0.0802. That 0.0802 remains the referee for the simulation. Beside it, a parallel official-share illustration — not a replacement for the p = 0.001 lab — uses the official 2025 mid-year land population of the Islands district: 198.4 thousand out of 7,497.8 thousand, or about 2.65 percent, from C and SD table 110-02001. That is uncommon, but not as rare as p = 0.001. If 50 residents were drawn independently from that official population, the probability of at least one Islands resident is 1 minus (1 minus 198.4 over 7,497.8) to the power 50, or about 74 percent. That is a FlippedStat calculation on an official share, not an official survey probability. Do not swap the 0.0802 lab key for the 74 percent contrast.

## Beat 5 (3:00–3:28)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:28–3:58)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Seeded, executed code with MC SE. Read the code before the number.

## Beat 7 (3:58–4:31)

That is the one idea for Topic 6.7. Open #t/6.7 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M3/T-6.7_Copilot_lab_rare_event_risk_by_simulation.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M3/V-T-6.7.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-6.8/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-6.8 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-6.8  
**Title:** 6.8: Block B exam practice and post-check  
**Word count:** 642  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:17 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:55)

This short video is Topic 6.8: Block B exam practice and post-check, in official Module 3, Probability, Distributions and Simulation. It sits in the unit W6: Random Variables, Models and Simulation. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:55–1:23)

Here is where we open. Block B by hand: probability rules, conditioning, Bayes, counting, distributions. No AI. The idea, in plain language, is this. Exam-format items on Weeks 5–6. Show the rule, the substitution and the answer with a one-line interpretation. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:23–1:54)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Two items ask you to refuse an unsupported claim (e.g. “90% accurate so a positive is 90% certain”). About 6 minutes per item. Watch for the three classic slips: wrong conditional direction, disjoint vs independent, “at least one” without the complement. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:54–2:32)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:32–3:00)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:00–3:43)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Rule → substitution → answer → interpretation. Refusing can be correct.

## Beat 7 (3:43–4:17)

That is the one idea for Topic 6.8. Open #t/6.8 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M3/T-6.8_Block_B_exam_practice_and_post_check.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M3/V-T-6.8.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

**video_id:** V-T-7.1

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 7.1: Block C pre-check, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W7: From Samples to Populations: Estimation. The official map budgets 0.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:31)

Here is where we open. Block B taught you how chance behaves when you know the rules. Block C turns it round: you see one sample and must say something about the rules. The idea, in plain language, is this. The Block C pre-check is ten items on sampling variability, standard errors, confidence intervals and tests. It is a baseline, not a grade. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:31–2:07)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Two items give a confident claim — for example “there is a 95% chance the true mean is in this interval” — and ask whether it is worded correctly. Most people's first intuition about intervals is subtly wrong. That is normal; this week builds the right picture by simulation. Answer without notes or AI. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:07–2:44)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:44–3:12)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:12–3:45)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Baseline only. Watch for interval wording.

# V-T-7.10 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-7.10  
**Title:** 7.10: Sample size  
**Word count:** 612  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:05 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

This short video is Topic 7.10: Sample size, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W7: From Samples to Populations: Estimation. The official map budgets 2.6667 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:22)

Here is where we open. The library wants a ±3-point estimate before anyone is surveyed. How many students? The idea, in plain language, is this. Plan sample size from the margin E you need. Proportion: n = (z*/E)² × p(1 − p) (p = 0.5 if unknown). Mean: n = (z*σ/E)² , with a guess of σ. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:22–1:47)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Round up, then divide by the expected response rate. Underestimating σ gives too small a sample. Sample-size formulas assume random sampling; they don't protect against bias . If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:47–2:28)

Suppose we wanted a 95 percent margin of error of 3 percentage points for a simple random sample that estimates the New Territories share of mid-year land population, and we used the official 2025 share, 54.6 percent, as a planning value. Then n is about 1.96 squared times 4,092.7 over 7,497.8 times 1 minus that share, over 0.03 squared, which is about 1,058.1, and rounds up to 1,059. Using the conservative planning value p = 0.5 instead would give n = 1,068. These are FlippedStat planning calculations, not an official sample-size recommendation, and not a claim that C and SD samples this way.

## Beat 5 (2:28–2:56)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:56–3:31)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. n = (z*/E)² p(1 − p). Round up; adjust for response.

## Beat 7 (3:31–4:05)

That is the one idea for Topic 7.10. Open #t/7.10 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-7.10_Sample_size.tex. Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Round up, then divide by the expected response rate. Underestimating σ gives too small a sample. Sample-size formulas assume random sampling; they don't protect against bias . If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

Suppose we wanted a 95 percent margin of error of 3 percentage points for a simple random sample that estimates the New Territories share of mid-year land population, and we used the official 2025 share, 54.6 percent, as a planning value. Then n is about 1.96 squared times 4,092.7 over 7,497.8 times 1 minus that share, over 0.03 squared, which is about 1,058.1, and rounds up to 1,059. Using the conservative planning value p = 0.5 instead would give n = 1,068. These are FlippedStat planning calculations, not an official sample-size recommendation, and not a claim that C and SD samples this way.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. n = (z*/E)² p(1 − p). Round up; adjust for response.

That is the one idea for Topic 7.10. Open #t/7.10 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-7.10_Sample_size.tex. # V-T-7.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-7.2  
**Title:** 7.2: Sampling distributions  
**Word count:** 689  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:36 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:51)

This short video is Topic 7.2: Sampling distributions, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W7: From Samples to Populations: Estimation. The official map budgets 2.5833 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:51–1:25)

Here is where we open. Two classmates survey 25 random students each and get different mean sleep. Neither made a mistake. The idea, in plain language, is this. A statistic varies from sample to sample — sampling variability . The distribution of a statistic over all possible samples of the same size is its sampling distribution . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:25–2:09)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. In real life you get one sample; the sampling distribution is a thought experiment — but it tells you how far your one statistic is likely to be from the truth. Three things to know: its centre (does it aim at the parameter? — bias), its spread (the standard error), its shape (often normal, by the CLT). Simulation lets you see it: draw thousands of samples from a known population and plot the statistic. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:09–3:06)

The same construction works with a Hong Kong official share in place of the page’s 88 percent solar-support course illustration. If simple random samples of n = 400 were drawn from the official 2025 mid-year land population, and each sample recorded the share living in the New Territories, the sampling distribution of p-hat would be centred at the official share 4,092.7 over 7,497.8, or 54.6 percent. The standard error is the square root of p times 1 minus p, over n, which is about 0.0249, or about 2.5 percentage points — a FlippedStat calculation, not an official C and SD standard error. A typical 95 percent margin of error would be about 4.9 percentage points. These imagined samples are teaching draws; they are not a C and SD survey, and the 18 districts themselves are not a random sample of people.

## Beat 5 (3:06–3:32)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Confusing the spread of the data (SD) with the spread of the statistic (SE). Thinking a 'bad' sample means the method failed — some samples are always far off by chance. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:32–4:02)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Statistics vary from sample to sample. Sampling distribution: centre, spread, shape.

## Beat 7 (4:02–4:36)

That is the one idea for Topic 7.2. Open #t/7.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-7.2_Sampling_distributions.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M4/V-T-7.2.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. # V-T-7.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-7.3  
**Title:** 7.3: Central limit theorem  
**Word count:** 712  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:45 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

This short video is Topic 7.3: Central limit theorem, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W7: From Samples to Populations: Estimation. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:24)

Here is where we open. Sampling distributions keep looking like bells, even when the data don't. That's no accident. The idea, in plain language, is this. Central Limit Theorem: for a random sample of n independent observations from a population with mean μ and finite SD σ, x̄ is approximately normal with mean μ and SD σ/√n when n is large enough. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–1:58)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Intuition: averaging cancels extremes. One big spender is offset by ordinary ones. The same holds for sums and for proportions (averages of 0/1 values). It is why normal-based intervals and tests work for so many kinds of data — the bridge from Week 6 to Weeks 7–8. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:58–2:59)

Return to n = 400 and the official 2025 New Territories mid-year land-population share, p = 54.6 percent. If the draws are a simple random sample, the independence condition is the design we are imagining, not a property of the official table. The success-failure counts are n p about 218 and n times 1 minus p about 182, both far above 10, so the normal approximation for p-hat is reasonable. Combined with a standard error of about 0.0249 from Topic 7.2, about 95 percent of such teaching samples would have p-hat within 1.96 times 0.0249, or about 4.9 percentage points, of the official 54.6 percent. These are FlippedStat calculations on an official population share, not official survey estimates, and not a licence to treat official daily weather or monthly birth series as independent draws. The page’s Hong Kong dollar spending illustration of skew and the central limit theorem remains a labelled course illustration.

## Beat 5 (2:59–3:27)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:27–4:11)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Means of many independent values → normal. SD of the mean = σ/√n.

## Beat 7 (4:11–4:45)

That is the one idea for Topic 7.3. Open #t/7.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-7.3_Central_limit_theorem.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M4/V-T-7.3.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-7.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-7.4  
**Title:** 7.4: t, chi-square and F distributions  
**Word count:** 654  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:22 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic 7.4: t, chi-square and F distributions, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W7: From Samples to Populations: Estimation. The official map budgets 0.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:32)

Here is where we open. Three new curves appear in every table from here on: t, χ² and F. Where do they come from? The idea, in plain language, is this. t: a bell with heavier tails, for means standardised with the estimated s. χ²: positive, right-skewed — sums of squared normals, for tables of counts. F: a ratio of variance estimates, for ANOVA and regression. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:32–2:02)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Each is a family indexed by degrees of freedom. As df grows, t → normal and χ² becomes more symmetric. You rarely need their formulas; you need to know which one a method uses and read values from software. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:02–2:40)

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

## Beat 5 (2:40–3:08)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:08–3:48)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. t for means, χ² for counts, F for variance ratios. Families indexed by df.

## Beat 7 (3:48–4:22)

That is the one idea for Topic 7.4. Open #t/7.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-7.4_t_chi_square_and_F_distributions.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M4/V-T-7.4.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-7.5 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-7.5  
**Title:** 7.5: Point estimation  
**Word count:** 629  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:12 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:52)

This short video is Topic 7.5: Point estimation, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W7: From Samples to Populations: Estimation. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:52–1:25)

Here is where we open. “The average” is a recipe. “6.6 hours” is the dish. The idea, in plain language, is this. An estimator is a rule for computing a guess at a parameter from a sample; it is a random variable. An estimate is the number you get from your actual data. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:25–1:58)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Notation: parameter θ (e.g. μ), estimator θ̂ (X̄), estimate θ̂ = 6.6. Several reasonable estimators may target the same parameter: mean, median, trimmed mean all estimate the centre of a symmetric population. We judge estimators by their sampling distributions: bias (7.5.2), variance (7.5.3), MSE (7.5.4). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:58–2:36)

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

## Beat 5 (2:36–3:04)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:04–3:38)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Estimator = recipe; estimate = number. Several estimators per parameter.

This short video is Topic 7.5: Point estimation, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W7: From Samples to Populations: Estimation. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

Here is where we open. “The average” is a recipe. “6.6 hours” is the dish. The idea, in plain language, is this. An estimator is a rule for computing a guess at a parameter from a sample; it is a random variable. An estimate is the number you get from your actual data. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Notation: parameter θ (e.g. μ), estimator θ̂ (X̄), estimate θ̂ = 6.6. Several reasonable estimators may target the same parameter: mean, median, trimmed mean all estimate the centre of a symmetric population. We judge estimators by their sampling distributions: bias (7.5.2), variance (7.5.3), MSE (7.5.4). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. # V-T-7.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-7.6  
**Title:** 7.6: Confidence intervals and coverage  
**Word count:** 675  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:30 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:52)

This short video is Topic 7.6: Confidence intervals and coverage, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W7: From Samples to Populations: Estimation. The official map budgets 3.4167 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:52–1:26)

Here is where we open. “95% confident the mean is between 6.2 and 7.0.” Does that mean a 95% probability μ is in [6.2, 7.0]? The idea, in plain language, is this. A confidence interval is estimate ± critical value × SE. The 95% describes the method: about 95% of intervals built this way contain the parameter. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:26–2:06)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. For your one interval, μ is either inside or not; it's a fixed unknown number. “Confident” expresses trust in the procedure . Correct: “We are 95% confident the mean is between 6.2 and 7.0 hours.” Wrong: “95% of students sleep between 6.2 and 7.0” (that's individuals); “95% chance the next sample mean is in it”; “ 95% probability μ is in it ”. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:06–2:59)

In the teaching experiment of Topics 7.2 and 7.3, the parameter is known: the official 2025 New Territories mid-year land-population share is 54.6 percent. If we repeatedly drew simple random samples of n = 400 and built a 95 percent Wald interval, p-hat plus or minus 1.96 times the square root of p-hat times 1 minus p-hat over n, each time, the coverage claim is about that procedure: in the long run, about 95 percent of those intervals would contain 54.6 percent. Any single interval either does or does not contain the official share. The official share is not itself an interval, and these intervals would not be official C and SD estimates. The page’s keyed picture of 25 simulated solar polls, with a population proportion of 0.88, remains a labelled course illustration.

## Beat 5 (2:59–3:27)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:27–3:56)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. 95% describes the method. One interval either contains μ or not.

## Beat 7 (3:56–4:30)

That is the one idea for Topic 7.6. Open #t/7.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-7.6_Confidence_intervals_and_coverage.tex.
