========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-7.7/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-7.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-7.7  
**Title:** 7.7: Interval for a mean  
**Word count:** 683  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:33 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:49)

This short video is Topic 7.7: Interval for a mean, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W7: From Samples to Populations: Estimation. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled labelled synthetic teaching table on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:49–1:14)

Here is where we open. Put it all together: a 95% interval for mean sleep from 16 students. The idea, in plain language, is this. One-sample t interval: x̄ ± t*ₙ₋₁ × s/√n. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:14–1:50)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Steps: (1) x̄, s, n; (2) SE = s/√n; (3) df = n − 1, find t*; (4) margin = t* × SE; (5) interval; (6) interpret with units. Excel: margin = CONFIDENCE.T(0.05, s, n). Report: “95% CI 5.96 to 7.24 h (n = 16)”. Round to one or two decimals more than the data. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:50–2:50)

Official district medians and official daily weather series are not a random sample of people, so they are a poor object for a t interval for a mean. A small FlippedStat teaching sample is used instead, and it is labelled synthetic: it is not official CUHK data and not a C and SD survey. Six students on a quiet hostel floor have midterm quiz scores 78, 74, 81, 69, 75 and 77. The sample mean is 75.67 and the sample standard deviation is 4.08, with divisor n minus 1. With 5 degrees of freedom, t-star for 95 percent is 2.571, so the interval is 75.67 plus or minus 2.571 times 4.08 over the square root of 6, or about 71.4 to 80.0 points. n = 6 is small, and the interval is wide, as the formula says it should be. Labelled book illustrations on the page were not changed.

## Beat 5 (2:50–3:18)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:18–4:00)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. x̄ ± t* s/√n. Six steps.

## Beat 7 (4:00–4:33)

That is the one idea for Topic 7.7. Open #t/7.7 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-7.7_Interval_for_a_mean.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M4/V-T-7.7.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-7.8 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-7.8  
**Title:** 7.8: Interval for a proportion  
**Word count:** 662  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:25 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

This short video is Topic 7.8: Interval for a proportion, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W7: From Samples to Populations: Estimation. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:22)

Here is where we open. 2 of 20 students failed. The textbook formula gives a 95% interval of −3% to 23%. The idea, in plain language, is this. The Wald interval p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) works when n is large and p̂ isn't near 0 or 1. It fails otherwise — even going below 0. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:22–1:55)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Condition: np̂ ≥ 10 and n(1 − p̂) ≥ 10. When p̂ = 0 or 1, the SE is 0 and the interval collapses to a point — absurd certainty. Many AI tools and spreadsheets use Wald by default. Check np̂ whenever you see one. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:55–2:42)

For planning, the official 2025 New Territories share, 54.6 percent, can be used as a known population proportion. In a simple random teaching sample of n = 400, the Wald standard error is about 0.0249 and a 95 percent margin of error is about 4.9 percentage points, as in Topics 7.2 and 7.3. In a real sample we would plug in p-hat instead of the official p; the official table is the population in this illustration, not the sample. Official daily weather and monthly birth series were not used here, because those observations are time-ordered and serially dependent. When success-failure fails, the page still points to a Clopper-Pearson or Wilson interval, and those textbook worked examples were not changed.

## Beat 5 (2:42–3:10)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:10–3:51)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Wald = margin of error from Week 2. Fails for small n or extreme p̂.

## Beat 7 (3:51–4:25)

That is the one idea for Topic 7.8. Open #t/7.8 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-7.8_Interval_for_a_proportion.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M4/V-T-7.8.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

**Title:** 7.9: Intervals for differences  
**Word count:** 647  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:19 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:49)

This short video is Topic 7.9: Intervals for differences, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W7: From Samples to Populations: Estimation. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled labelled synthetic teaching table on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:49–1:23)

Here is where we open. Tutorial A averages 72, tutorial B 66. Is the 6-mark gap real or sampling noise? The idea, in plain language, is this. For two independent groups estimate μ₁ − μ₂ with x̄₁ − x̄₂. SE = √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). The Welch t interval doesn't assume equal SDs — the safe default. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:23–1:55)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Variances add because both means vary independently (6.1.3). If the interval excludes 0, the data support a difference in that direction; if it includes 0, zero is plausible — not proven. Judge the difference's own interval ; overlapping individual intervals don't imply no difference. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:55–2:43)

On the same labelled synthetic teaching sample as Topic 7.7, the six quiet-floor quiz scores have mean 75.67, and the six social-floor scores — 60, 64, 58, 66, 61, 63 — have mean 62.00. The difference of means is 13.67 points. A Welch 95 percent interval, not assuming equal standard deviations, is about 9.0 to 18.3 points, with a standard error of about 2.04 and about 9.0 degrees of freedom. The interval lies entirely above 0, so in this teaching sample the quiet-floor mean is higher. This is not a randomised experiment, not official CUHK data, and not a claim about every hostel. The two randomised experiments on this page remain the labelled book illustrations; their checks were not changed.

## Beat 5 (2:43–3:11)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:11–3:45)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Difference ± t* × √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Welch by default.

## Beat 7 (3:45–4:19)

That is the one idea for Topic 7.9. Open #t/7.9 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-7.9_Intervals_for_differences.tex. # V-T-8.1 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-8.1  
**Title:** 8.1: Anatomy of a hypothesis test  
**Word count:** 609  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:04 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:55)

This short video is Topic 8.1: Anatomy of a hypothesis test, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W8: Hypothesis Testing. The official map budgets 2.3333 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already has a Hong Kong example or official extract beside a labelled textbook or overseas illustration. Keep those labels visible. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:55–1:30)

Here is where we open. Week 7 asked “how big, give or take?”. Week 8 asks a sharper question: “could this just be chance?”. The idea, in plain language, is this. A hypothesis test compares two statements about a population or process: the null H₀ (“nothing special”, with an equals sign) and the alternative H₁ (what you suspect). Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:30–2:00)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Hypotheses are never about the sample — you can see the sample. H₀ needs a specific value so we can compute what data look like “if nothing were going on”. Write the parameter in words first, then H₀ and H₁. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:00–2:38)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:38–3:00)

A few mistakes show up often on this topic. Writing hypotheses about sample statistics (x̄, p̂) instead of parameters. Choosing H₁'s direction after seeing which way the data went. None of those is a small slip if it moves a number you later quote. Mark them in amber, and fix them before you write a conclusion.

## Beat 6 (3:00–3:30)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. H₀: no effect, with an equals sign. H₁: what you suspect.

## Beat 7 (3:30–4:04)

That is the one idea for Topic 8.1. Open #t/8.1 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-8.2/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-8.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-8.2  
**Title:** 8.2: What p-values do not mean  
**Word count:** 671  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:28 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic 8.2: What p-values do not mean, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W8: Hypothesis Testing. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a synthetic Hong Kong example, labelled synthetic on the page. It is not an official C and SD table. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:34)

Here is where we open. “p = 0.03, so there's a 97% chance the treatment works.” Almost everyone has heard this. It's wrong. The idea, in plain language, is this. The p-value is P(data at least this extreme | H₀) . It is not P(H₀ | data), not the chance the result is “due to chance”, and 1 − p is not the probability the effect is real. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:34–2:04)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. P(H₀ | data) needs Bayes and a prior (5.8) — the confusion of the inverse again. A p-value says nothing about effect size or importance (8.2.2). Under H₀ p-values are uniform: 5% fall below 0.05 by design. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:04–2:42)

The worked example on this page is already a Hong Kong situation, and it is labelled synthetic where the data were built for teaching. Keep that label visible. Synthetic Hong Kong data can teach a method well, but they are not an official C and SD or Observatory table, and they must not be cited as if they were. If the page also keeps a labelled book illustration, leave it labelled. Open the file on the site, count the rows, and recompute the page’s figures there. I will not invent extra statistics in this video.

## Beat 5 (2:42–3:10)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:10–3:55)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. p = P(data | H₀), not P(H₀ | data). Not the size of the effect.

## Beat 7 (3:55–4:28)

That is the one idea for Topic 8.2. Open #t/8.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-8.2_What_p_values_do_not_mean.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M4/V-T-8.2.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-8.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-8.3  
**Title:** 8.3: Errors, power and effect size  
**Word count:** 686  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:34 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:51)

This short video is Topic 8.3: Errors, power and effect size, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W8: Hypothesis Testing. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:51–1:26)

Here is where we open. A smoke alarm can fail two ways: screaming with no fire, or silent during one. Tests fail the same two ways. The idea, in plain language, is this. Type I error: reject H₀ when it's true (false alarm), probability α. Type II error: fail to reject when H₀ is false (missed effect), probability β. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:26–1:58)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Truth (H₀ true/false) × decision (reject/not) gives four cells — two correct, two errors. Lowering α reduces Type I errors but increases Type II, unless you collect more data. Which error is worse depends on context: convicting the innocent vs missing a disease. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:58–2:54)

Suppose a study planned to test H nought: p = 0.50 — that New Territories residents are not a majority of mid-year land population — against a two-sided alternative at alpha = 0.05, with n = 1,000, and that the true p were the official 2025 share, 54.6 percent. A normal approximation gives power of about 0.83. Under the null, the 5 percent critical values sit at 0.50 plus or minus 1.96 times the square root of 0.25 over 1,000; under the official share, the chance of crossing the upper critical value is about 83 percent, and the lower tail is negligible. That is a FlippedStat planning calculation on an official population share, not an official power analysis, and not a hypothesis test carried out on the official table itself — the official table already is the population in this illustration.

## Beat 5 (2:54–3:22)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:22–4:01)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Type I: false alarm (α). Type II: missed effect (β).

## Beat 7 (4:01–4:34)

That is the one idea for Topic 8.3. Open #t/8.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-8.3_Errors_power_and_effect_size.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M4/V-T-8.3.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-8.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-8.4  
**Title:** 8.4: t-tests  
**Word count:** 635  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:14 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:47)

This short video is Topic 8.4: t-tests, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W8: Hypothesis Testing. The official map budgets 1.3333 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled labelled synthetic teaching table on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:47–1:17)

Here is where we open. Three questions, three t-tests: a mean vs a value, two independent groups, before vs after. The idea, in plain language, is this. One-sample t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n). Welch t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/√(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Paired: one-sample t on the differences. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:17–1:45)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Each pairs with its Week 7 interval: report estimate, CI, t, df and p together. Choose by design, not by which gives the smallest p. Welch is the safe default for two independent groups. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:45–2:38)

The same labelled synthetic teaching sample as Topics 7.7 and 7.9 can be used for a t-test. Quiet floor, n = 6: scores 78, 74, 81, 69, 75, 77, mean 75.67, sample standard deviation 4.08. Social floor, n = 6: 60, 64, 58, 66, 61, 63, mean 62.00, sample standard deviation 2.90. A Welch two-sample test of equal means gives t about 6.69, about 9.0 degrees of freedom, and p about 0.00009. A one-sample test that the quiet-floor mean equals 70 gives t = 3.40, 5 degrees of freedom, p about 0.019, with a 95 percent interval about 71.4 to 80.0, as in Topic 7.7. These are FlippedStat calculations on a labelled synthetic teaching sample, not official CUHK scores, and not a randomised experiment. Textbook worked examples on the page were not changed.

## Beat 5 (2:38–3:06)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:06–3:40)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. One-sample, Welch, paired. Report estimate, CI, t, df, p.

## Beat 7 (3:40–4:14)

That is the one idea for Topic 8.4. Open #t/8.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. # V-T-8.5 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-8.5  
**Title:** 8.5: Chi-square and exact tests  
**Word count:** 608  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:03 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:47)

This short video is Topic 8.5: Chi-square and exact tests, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W8: Hypothesis Testing. The official map budgets 3.4167 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:47–1:17)

Here is where we open. From means to counts. A die is rolled 120 times. The idea, in plain language, is this. The χ² goodness-of-fit test checks whether counts in one categorical variable match H₀'s proportions: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E, df = categories − 1. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:17–1:40)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Expected count Eᵢ = n × pᵢ from H₀. Each term measures one category's departure, scaled by E. Right-tail p-value from χ². If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:40–2:32)

Topic 5.7 already showed that, in the official 2025 mid-year land-population figures, “lives in a gained-population district” and region are not independent: P of gained given Hong Kong Island is 0 percent, against a marginal 64.4 percent. Under independence, the expected official 2025 population in gained-population districts on Hong Kong Island would be about 749 thousand; the observed figure is 0. That comparison is a useful description of these official aggregates and a FlippedStat grouping. A chi-square test of independence would be the wrong tool for this table: the figures are official mid-year counts of all 18 districts, not a random sample of people, and a p-value would not be a sampling p-value. Official daily weather and monthly birth series were not used as if they were independent trials either.

## Beat 5 (2:32–3:00)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:00–3:30)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. df = k − 1.

## Beat 7 (3:30–4:03)

That is the one idea for Topic 8.5. ## Continuous script (for the recording booth)

This short video is Topic 8.5: Chi-square and exact tests, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W8: Hypothesis Testing. The official map budgets 3.4167 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

Here is where we open. From means to counts. A die is rolled 120 times. The idea, in plain language, is this. The χ² goodness-of-fit test checks whether counts in one categorical variable match H₀'s proportions: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E, df = categories − 1. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Expected count Eᵢ = n × pᵢ from H₀. Each term measures one category's departure, scaled by E. Right-tail p-value from χ². If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

Topic 5.7 already showed that, in the official 2025 mid-year land-population figures, “lives in a gained-population district” and region are not independent: P of gained given Hong Kong Island is 0 percent, against a marginal 64.4 percent. Under independence, the expected official 2025 population in gained-population districts on Hong Kong Island would be about 749 thousand; the observed figure is 0. That comparison is a useful description of these official aggregates and a FlippedStat grouping. A chi-square test of independence would be the wrong tool for this table: the figures are official mid-year counts of all 18 districts, not a random sample of people, and a p-value would not be a sampling p-value. Official daily weather and monthly birth series were not used as if they were independent trials either.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. df = k − 1.

That is the one idea for Topic 8.5. Open #t/8.5 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-8.5_Chi_square_and_exact_tests.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M4/V-T-8.5.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-8.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-8.6  
**Title:** 8.6: One-way ANOVA  
**Word count:** 649  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:20 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:47)

This short video is Topic 8.6: One-way ANOVA, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W8: Hypothesis Testing. The official map budgets 4.5833 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled labelled synthetic teaching table on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:47–1:17)

Here is where we open. Three revision methods. Could three random groups of students differ this much by chance? The idea, in plain language, is this. One-way ANOVA compares three or more means in one test by splitting total variation into between-groups and within-groups parts. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:17–1:44)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. If H₀ (all means equal) holds, between-group variation is just noise and comparable to within-group variation. Why not many t-tests? Each adds Type I risk (8.8). SS_T = SS_B + SS_W. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:44–2:36)

Add a third, mixed floor to the labelled synthetic teaching sample: scores 70, 68, 73, 65, 71, 67, with mean 69.00 and sample standard deviation 2.90, alongside quiet, mean 75.67, and social, mean 62.00, with n = 6 on each floor. A one-way ANOVA of quiz score by floor gives SSB about 560.4, SSW about 167.3, MSB about 280.2, MSW about 11.16, F about 25.12 on 2 and 15 degrees of freedom, p about 0.000016, and eta-squared about 0.77. These are FlippedStat calculations on a labelled synthetic teaching sample, not official CUHK or hostel data, and not a claim that floor assignment caused the scores. The three floors are a teaching design, not a random sample of students. The clinical-trial mood-gain illustration on the page remains a labelled book example.

## Beat 5 (2:36–3:04)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:04–3:46)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Between vs within. One test for k groups.

## Beat 7 (3:46–4:20)

That is the one idea for Topic 8.6. Open #t/8.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-8.6_One_way_ANOVA.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M4/V-T-8.6.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-8.7/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-8.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-8.7  
**Title:** 8.7: Choosing a test  
**Word count:** 623  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:09 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic 8.7: Choosing a test, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W8: Hypothesis Testing. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:25)

Here is where we open. Imagine you now have many tests. Choosing among them takes three questions. The idea, in plain language, is this. Choose a test by: (1) outcome type (numerical or categorical); (2) number of groups ; (3) independent or paired . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:25–1:52)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Numerical: one-sample t; Welch t; paired t; ANOVA (+ Tukey). Categorical: goodness-of-fit χ²; χ² of independence (Fisher if small); McNemar for paired (E2). Let design choose the test before seeing data. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:52–2:30)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:30–2:58)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:58–3:36)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Outcome → groups → pairing. Design before data.

## Beat 7 (3:36–4:09)

That is the one idea for Topic 8.7. Open #t/8.7 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-8.7_Choosing_a_test.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M4/V-T-8.7.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-8.8 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-8.8  
**Title:** 8.8: Multiple comparisons  
**Word count:** 627  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:11 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:47)

This short video is Topic 8.8: Multiple comparisons, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W8: Hypothesis Testing. The official map budgets 0.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled labelled synthetic teaching table on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:47–1:22)

Here is where we open. A researcher measures 20 outcomes, tries 3 outlier rules and analyses with and without covariates. Something is bound to be “significant”. The idea, in plain language, is this. Every analysis choice is a fork; taking forks after seeing data — the garden of forking paths — inflates false positives even without bad intent. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:22–1:53)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. m independent tests of true nulls at 0.05: P(at least one false positive) = 1 − 0.95ᵐ. 10 tests → 0.40; 20 → 0.64; 50 → 0.92. Data snooping — deciding what to test after looking — is the core problem. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:53–2:35)

On the same synthetic three-floor quiz scores as Topic 8.6, Tukey’s Honestly Significant Difference, at 95 percent family-wise, finds all three pairwise mean differences significant: quiet versus mixed about 6.67 points, with a 95 percent interval 1.66 to 11.68, p about 0.009; mixed versus social 7.00 points, 1.99 to 12.01, p about 0.007; and quiet versus social 13.67 points, 8.66 to 18.68, p less than 0.001. With a large overall F, this is the case where the pairs agree with the omnibus test. The figures are FlippedStat calculations on the teaching sample, not official statistics. The textbook worked examples on this page were not changed.

## Beat 5 (2:35–3:03)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:03–3:37)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Every choice is a fork. 1 − 0.95ᵐ grows fast.

## Beat 7 (3:37–4:11)

That is the one idea for Topic 8.8. Open #t/8.8 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. # V-T-8.9 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-8.9  
**Title:** 8.9: Research integrity  
**Word count:** 609  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:04 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:48)

This short video is Topic 8.9: Research integrity, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W8: Hypothesis Testing. The official map budgets 0.9167 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract (course referee file) on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:48–1:19)

Here is where we open. “p = 0.052. Let me just drop that odd participant... The idea, in plain language, is this. p-hacking: trying analyses until p < 0.05 and reporting only the one that worked. Each step feels reasonable; together they make the reported p meaningless. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:19–1:44)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Forms: selective outlier removal, adding/dropping covariates, many outcomes, splitting groups, optional stopping. Consequences: false findings, wasted resources, failed replications. Defence: pre-specify; report every analysis you ran. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:44–2:31)

Research integrity also applies to official tables. The course file hk_district_profile_2016_2025.csv is a teaching join of C and SD tables 110-02001 and 130-06806: 18 district rows, plus a codebook that already reports FlippedStat calculations such as Pearson r = minus 0.38, and the official regional totals 1,162.4, 2,242.7, 4,092.7 and 7,497.8 thousand. A basic integrity check is to recompute a published teaching key from the file, and to keep official figures distinct from derived columns — the gained-or-lost flag — and from any AI paraphrase of the table. An AI summary of an official extract is not itself an official statistic, and formal rights clearance of third-party sources remains a later-stage task. It is not claimed as done here.

## Beat 5 (2:31–2:59)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:59–3:30)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Trying until p < 0.05 invalidates p. Optional stopping ≈ 19% false positives here.

## Continuous script (for the recording booth)

This short video is Topic 8.9: Research integrity, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It sits in the unit W8: Hypothesis Testing. The official map budgets 0.9167 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract (course referee file) on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

Here is where we open. “p = 0.052. Let me just drop that odd participant... The idea, in plain language, is this. p-hacking: trying analyses until p < 0.05 and reporting only the one that worked. Each step feels reasonable; together they make the reported p meaningless. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Forms: selective outlier removal, adding/dropping covariates, many outcomes, splitting groups, optional stopping. Consequences: false findings, wasted resources, failed replications. Defence: pre-specify; report every analysis you ran. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

Research integrity also applies to official tables. The course file hk_district_profile_2016_2025.csv is a teaching join of C and SD tables 110-02001 and 130-06806: 18 district rows, plus a codebook that already reports FlippedStat calculations such as Pearson r = minus 0.38, and the official regional totals 1,162.4, 2,242.7, 4,092.7 and 7,497.8 thousand. A basic integrity check is to recompute a published teaching key from the file, and to keep official figures distinct from derived columns — the gained-or-lost flag — and from any AI paraphrase of the table. An AI summary of an official extract is not itself an official statistic, and formal rights clearance of third-party sources remains a later-stage task. It is not claimed as done here.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Trying until p < 0.05 invalidates p. Optional stopping ≈ 19% false positives here.

That is the one idea for Topic 8.9. Open #t/8.9 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M8/T-8.9_Research_integrity.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M8/V-T-8.9.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-9.1 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-9.1  
**Title:** 9.1: Copilot lab: a three-arm trial  
**Word count:** 662  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:25 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic 9.1: Copilot lab: a three-arm trial, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W9: Inference in Practice and the Capstone Question. The official map budgets 1.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:36)

Here is where we open. Week 8 gave you the tests. Now an AI runs one for you — on the same three-arm trial you analysed in 8.6. The idea, in plain language, is this. Ask Copilot to recommend before it runs: outcome type, number of groups, independence → a test with reasons. Then run it showing code, group n/mean/SD, the full ANOVA table , η², Tukey comparisons and assumption checks. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:36–2:03)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Paste the prompt contract; upload the trial file and README. Record everything: recommendation, code, every number, anything not shown. Watch for an over-reaching ranking (“C is best”) that Tukey doesn't support (H4). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:03–2:40)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:40–3:08)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:08–3:51)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Recommend, then run. Full table + Tukey + assumptions.

## Beat 7 (3:51–4:25)

That is the one idea for Topic 9.1. Open #t/9.1 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-9.2/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-9.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-9.2  
**Title:** 9.2: Audit lab: the age gap  
**Word count:** 717  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:47 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:50)

This short video is Topic 9.2: Audit lab: the age gap, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W9: Inference in Practice and the Capstone Question. The official map budgets 2.3333 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled labelled synthetic teaching table on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:50–1:25)

Here is where we open. Audit lab. An AI says District A scores 9.3 points higher than B (p = 0.004), “so living in A raises scores”. The idea, in plain language, is this. A crude comparison mixes the group effect with a composition effect . Direct standardisation compares groups as if both had the same age mix. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:25–1:56)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. District A is young (125 of 200 aged 18–34); B is old (125 of 200 aged 55+). Scores fall with age, so A's crude mean is inflated by its age mix. Within every age band A − B = 1.1 points. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:56–3:06)

The 1973 Berkeley postgraduate admissions tables remain the named historical illustration on this page; they are not replaced, and their checks were not changed. A FlippedStat teaching table, labelled as synthetic and not Hospital Authority or official statistics, shows the same reversal in a local setting. Clinic A treats mostly lower-need patients: 210 of 300 lower-need recover, or 70 percent, and 10 of 50 higher-need recover, or 20 percent, so 220 of 350 overall, or 62.9 percent. Clinic B treats mostly higher-need patients: 80 of 100 lower-need recover, or 80 percent, and 90 of 300 higher-need recover, or 30 percent, so 170 of 400 overall, or 42.5 percent. Clinic B has the higher recovery rate in each need group, but the lower pooled rate, because it sees a larger share of higher-need patients. As with Berkeley, which table answers your question depends on the question: clinic performance given need, or the mixed caseload as a whole. No official extract already in the course is a clean three-way reversal table, so this parallel is synthetic by design.

## Beat 5 (3:06–3:34)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:34–4:13)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Crude comparisons mix in composition. Standardise to a common mix.

## Beat 7 (4:13–4:47)

That is the one idea for Topic 9.2. Open #t/9.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M4/T-9.2_Audit_lab_the_age_gap.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M4/V-T-9.2.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-9.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-9.3  
**Title:** 9.3: Fabricated sources  
**Word count:** 645  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:18 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:58)

This short video is Topic 9.3: Fabricated sources, in official Module 8, Responsible and Ethical AI-Assisted Statistical Analysis. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W9: Inference in Practice and the Capstone Question. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:58–1:34)

Here is where we open. Copilot gives three perfect-looking references for your capstone. Authors, journal, volume, pages. The idea, in plain language, is this. Language models can produce references that look real but don't exist (H5). Three failures: the source doesn't exist; it exists but doesn't say what's claimed ; it's real and relevant but misdescribed (wrong year, population, number). Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:34–2:04)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. The second type is the most dangerous: it survives a quick search. Check each one: library database or Google Scholar; open the DOI; check authors, year, venue; find the exact passage. Treat AI-suggested references as search leads, not sources. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:04–2:42)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:42–3:10)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:10–3:44)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. References can be fabricated or misattributed. Open and find the passage.

## Beat 7 (3:44–4:18)

That is the one idea for Topic 9.3. Open #t/9.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M8/T-9.3_Fabricated_sources.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M8/V-T-9.3.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-9.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-9.4  
**Title:** 9.4: Capstone: question and source scan  
**Word count:** 615  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:06 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic 9.4: Capstone: question and source scan, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W9: Inference in Practice and the Capstone Question. The official map budgets 1.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:31)

Here is where we open. Imagine your capstone starts with one sentence. If the sentence is vague, nothing after it can be precise. The idea, in plain language, is this. A good capstone question is a statistical question: it names a population, one or two variables, a comparison or relationship — and it fits the data and design available. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:31–1:58)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Data: course synthetic files or approved open data — no personal data. Design: observational data support association; causal wording needs random assignment. Methods from at least two blocks (e.g. description + regression). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:58–2:36)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:36–3:04)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:04–3:32)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Population + variables + comparison. Fits data and design.

# V-T-9.5 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-9.5  
**Title:** 9.5: Block C exam practice and post-check  
**Word count:** 642  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:17 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic 9.5: Block C exam practice and post-check, in official Module 4, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing. It sits in the unit W9: Inference in Practice and the Capstone Question. The official map budgets 1.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:26)

Here is where we open. Block C by hand: sampling distributions, intervals, tests, effect sizes and test choice. No AI. The idea, in plain language, is this. Exam-format items on Weeks 7–9. Each answer: method and why; formula; substitution; answer with units; one-sentence interpretation; one condition checked. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:26–1:54)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Two items require refusing a claim — a p-value misreading, or a causal verb on observational data. About 6 minutes per item. The most-missed items are usually interval wording and p-value interpretation. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:54–2:31)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:31–2:59)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:59–3:43)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Method → formula → numbers → interpretation → condition. Refuse when needed.
