========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-9.6/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-9.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-9.6  
**Title:** 9.6: Block D pre-check  
**Word count:** 617  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:07 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:55)

This short video is Topic 9.6: Block D pre-check, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It sits in the unit W9: Inference in Practice and the Capstone Question. The official map budgets 0.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:55–1:22)

Here is where we open. Before Block D: how do you currently read a fitted line? The idea, in plain language, is this. The Block D pre-check covers correlation, slopes and intercepts, R², residuals, adjustment and prediction. Baseline only. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:22–1:50)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Two items ask you to refuse a claim — e.g. “a slope of 0.61 means hours explain 61% of the score”. Answer without notes or AI. Week 10 builds the reading skills step by step. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:50–2:28)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:28–2:56)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:56–3:33)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Baseline only. Watch slope vs R².

## Beat 7 (3:33–4:07)

That is the one idea for Topic 9.6. Open #t/9.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M5/T-9.6_Block_D_pre_check.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M5/V-T-9.6.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-9.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-9.7  
**Title:** 9.7: Correlation and its limits  
**Word count:** 652  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:21 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:52)

This short video is Topic 9.7: Correlation and its limits, in official Module 5, Correlation, Regression and Prediction. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit W9: Inference in Practice and the Capstone Question. The official map budgets 1.4167 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:52–1:29)

Here is where we open. r = 0.30 between exercise and sleep quality in 50 students. Distinguishable from no linear association? The idea, in plain language, is this. Pearson's r describes the sample; inference targets the population correlation ρ . Test H₀: ρ = 0 with t = r√(n − 2)/√(1 − r²), df n − 2. CI via Fisher's z . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:29–1:58)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. The test is identical to the regression slope test (10.4.2). Fisher's z = atanh(r), SE = 1/√(n − 3); transform back with tanh → an asymmetric interval. Conditions: random independent pairs, roughly linear, no extreme outliers. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:58–2:44)

Correlation has limits, and the official 18-district scatter is a good place to say them out loud. Pearson’s r of minus 0.38, already calculated on Topics 4.1 and 4.2, is a moderate linear association between official 2025 district median incomes and official 2025 densities. It is a FlippedStat calculation, not an official C and SD correlation. n equals 18 is small. The association is ecological: these are district aggregates, not households. A moderate linear association is not a law for every district. And r does not describe a curve; look at the scatter before you trust the single number. OpenIntro scatterplots, the Spearman walk-through, and the Guided Practice check on this topic were not changed.

## Beat 5 (2:44–3:12)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:12–3:47)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. r describes; ρ is the target. t test with n − 2 df.

## Beat 7 (3:47–4:21)

That is the one idea for Topic 9.7. Open #t/9.7 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M5/T-9.7_Correlation_and_its_limits.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M5/V-T-9.7.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

## Beat 4 (1:31–2:23)

The stent trial remains the named historical case on this page; its counts, including 45 out of 224, and the checks, are not changed. A FlippedStat teaching two-by-two table, labelled as synthetic and not a CUHK, Hospital Authority, or official health study, uses the same “two groups, one event” shape. In a hostel exam-support programme, 12 of 80 programme students missed a midterm deadline, or 15 percent, against 24 of 80 comparison students, or 30 percent. The risk difference is 15 percentage points. A two-proportion z test of equal rates gives z about minus 2.27, p about 0.023, and Fisher’s exact p about 0.036. These are FlippedStat calculations on the teaching table, not evidence about a real programme’s effect, and not a substitute for the stent study’s design or findings.

## Beat 5 (2:23–2:51)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:51–3:18)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it.

## Beat 7 (3:18–3:52)

That is the one idea for Topic C4.1. # V-T-C4.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-C4.3  
**Title:** C4.3: Waiting for the first success: geometric and negative binomial  
**Word count:** 582  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 3:53 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:52)

This short video is Topic C4.3: Waiting for the first success: geometric and negative binomial, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit C4: Case Studies and Special Topics from OpenIntro Statistics. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:52–1:18)

The idea, in plain language, is this. Topic C4.3 asks you to master one idea and then check it on the site. The worked path lives on the page, not in a new claim I might add here. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:18–1:38)

Once you have the idea, read any result slowly. Ask what the unit is, what was included, and what was left out. The official page walks the worked path in more detail than this short video. I will not invent a worked number just to fill the time.

## Beat 4 (1:38–2:15)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:15–2:43)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:43–3:19)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number.

## Beat 7 (3:19–3:53)

That is the one idea for Topic C4.3. Open #t/C4.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

**Title:** C4.4: Sampling without replacement from a small population  
**Word count:** 569  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 3:48 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:51)

This short video is Topic C4.4: Sampling without replacement from a small population, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit C4: Case Studies and Special Topics from OpenIntro Statistics. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:51–1:18)

The idea, in plain language, is this. Topic C4.4 asks you to master one idea and then check it on the site. The worked path lives on the page, not in a new claim I might add here. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:18–1:37)

Once you have the idea, read any result slowly. Ask what the unit is, what was included, and what was left out. The official page walks the worked path in more detail than this short video. I will not invent a worked number just to fill the time.

## Beat 4 (1:37–2:14)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:14–2:42)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:42–3:14)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify.

## Beat 4 (1:30–2:12)

A “null other than zero” also appears for a single proportion. Suppose a teaching test asked whether a simple random sample of n = 1,000 mid-year land residents was consistent with H nought: p = 0.50, that the New Territories are not a majority, when the official 2025 share is 54.6 percent. The null value is 0.50, not 0 and not the official share; the official share would be the true p in that illustration, as in the power calculation on Topic 8.3. The official table itself is not a sample and is not tested. The machine-blade example and the checks on this page were not changed.

## Beat 5 (2:12–2:40)

If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:40–3:08)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it.

## Beat 7 (3:08–3:41)

# V-T-C4.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-C4.6  
**Title:** C4.6: Pooled standard deviation and ANOVA diagnostics  
**Word count:** 544  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 3:38 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:50)

This short video is Topic C4.6: Pooled standard deviation and ANOVA diagnostics, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit C4: Case Studies and Special Topics from OpenIntro Statistics. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:50–1:17)

The idea, in plain language, is this. Topic C4.6 asks you to master one idea and then check it on the site. The worked path lives on the page, not in a new claim I might add here. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:17–1:36)

Once you have the idea, read any result slowly. Ask what the unit is, what was included, and what was left out. The official page walks the worked path in more detail than this short video. I will not invent a worked number just to fill the time.

## Beat 4 (1:36–2:14)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:14–2:42)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:42–3:04)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify.

## Beat 7 (3:04–3:38)

That is the one idea for Topic C4.6. Open #t/C4.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. # V-T-C4.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-C4.7  
**Title:** C4.7: Regression case study: Mario Kart auctions  
**Word count:** 615  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:06 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:45)

This short video is Topic C4.7: Regression case study: Mario Kart auctions, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit C4: Case Studies and Special Topics from OpenIntro Statistics. This topic already uses a labelled labelled synthetic teaching table on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:45–1:12)

The idea, in plain language, is this. Topic C4.7 asks you to master one idea and then check it on the site. The worked path lives on the page, not in a new claim I might add here. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:12–1:31)

Once you have the idea, read any result slowly. Ask what the unit is, what was included, and what was left out. The official page walks the worked path in more detail than this short video. I will not invent a worked number just to fill the time.

## Beat 4 (1:31–2:28)

The Mario Kart auction analysis remains the named case study on this page; its coefficients and checks are not changed. A FlippedStat teaching scatter, labelled as synthetic and not an official price index, has eight second-hand textbook listings, with years since publication 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8, and prices in Hong Kong dollars 185, 155, 168, 142, 130, 108, 96 and 78. The least-squares line is price approximately 192.38 minus 15.39 times years since publication, with r = minus 0.983 and R-squared about 0.97. These are FlippedStat calculations on the teaching points, not a market study. The slope says that, on this tiny fitted line, each additional year is associated with about 15 Hong Kong dollars lower listed price; it is not a causal claim, and n = 8 is only an illustration beside the named Mario Kart analysis.

## Beat 5 (2:28–2:56)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:56–3:32)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number.

## Beat 7 (3:32–4:06)

That is the one idea for Topic C4.7. ## Continuous script (for the recording booth)

This short video is Topic C4.8: Logistic regression case study: résumé callbacks and discrimination, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit C4: Case Studies and Special Topics from OpenIntro Statistics. This topic already uses a labelled named case kept; parallel on Topic 12.6.3 on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

The idea, in plain language, is this. Topic C4.8 asks you to master one idea and then check it on the site. The worked path lives on the page, not in a new claim I might add here. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, read any result slowly. Ask what the unit is, what was included, and what was left out. The official page walks the worked path in more detail than this short video. I will not invent a worked number just to fill the time.

The Boston and Chicago résumé-callback experiment remains the named study on this companion card; its figures are not replaced. This short card itself was not rewritten in the wave-5 pass. The labelled Hong Kong proxy-logic parallel sits on Topic 12.6.3, the method page that already presents the same experiment: a name, a residential district, or another field correlated with a protected characteristic can act as a proxy in a model trained on past decisions, even if the protected characteristic itself is never entered. This video does not invent a local audit’s callback rates. Formal rights clearance remains deferred and is not claimed as done.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify.

That is the one idea for Topic C4.8. # V-T-C4.9 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-C4.9  
**Title:** C4.9: Regression case studies: possums, college aid and elections  
**Word count:** 539  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 3:36 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:47)

This short video is Topic C4.9: Regression case studies: possums, college aid and elections, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit C4: Case Studies and Special Topics from OpenIntro Statistics. This topic already uses a labelled named case kept; parallel on Topics 10.1--10.2 on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:47–1:14)

The idea, in plain language, is this. Topic C4.9 asks you to master one idea and then check it on the site. The worked path lives on the page, not in a new claim I might add here. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:14–1:33)

Once you have the idea, read any result slowly. Ask what the unit is, what was included, and what was left out. The official page walks the worked path in more detail than this short video. I will not invent a worked number just to fill the time.

## Beat 4 (1:33–2:07)

The possum, college-aid and election regression case studies remain on this companion card; their figures are not replaced. This short card itself was not rewritten in the wave-5 pass. The official descriptive income-on-density line — about 34,283 minus 0.121 times density — sits on Topics 10.1 and 10.2 as a census summary of 18 official pairs, not as slope inference, and not as a sampling estimate. Open those topics for the official-data line; do not treat the companion-card studies as official Hong Kong statistics.

## Beat 5 (2:07–2:35)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:35–3:02)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it.

## Beat 7 (3:02–3:36)

That is the one idea for Topic C4.9. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-E1.1/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-E1.1 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.1  
**Title:** E1.1: Pre-check  
**Word count:** 630  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:12 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:58)

This short video is Topic E1.1: Pre-check, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 0.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:58–1:26)

Here is where we open. The core taught you to judge evidence. E1 teaches you to design studies that produce good evidence. The idea, in plain language, is this. The E1 pre-check: ten items on experiments, surveys, measurement and robust comparisons. Baseline only. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:26–1:55)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Two items ask you to refuse a claim, e.g. “n = 40 students, so the evidence is strong” when treatment was assigned to whole classes. Answer without notes or AI. Compare with the post-check in E1.16.1. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:55–2:33)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:33–3:01)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:01–3:38)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Baseline only. Watch the unit of assignment.

## Beat 7 (3:38–4:12)

That is the one idea for Topic E1.1. Open #t/E1.1 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M6/T-E1.1_Pre_check.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M6/V-T-E1.1.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-E1.10 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.10  
**Title:** E1.10: Sampling designs  
**Word count:** 628  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:11 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:55)

This short video is Topic E1.10: Sampling designs, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:55–1:28)

Here is where we open. Imagine you need views from all faculties, but Medicine is small. A simple random sample might include three medics. The idea, in plain language, is this. Stratified sampling: random samples within strata — guarantees representation and can cut SE. Cluster sampling: sample whole groups — cheaper but usually inflates SE. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–1:54)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Allocation: proportional, or oversample small strata and weight back. Stratify on variables related to the outcome for the biggest gain. Clusters save travel and lists but cost precision. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:54–2:32)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:32–3:00)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:00–3:38)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Stratify for representation and precision. Cluster for cost.

## Beat 7 (3:38–4:11)

That is the one idea for Topic E1.10. # V-T-E1.11 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.11  
**Title:** E1.11: Non-response and weighting  
**Word count:** 608  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:03 (target 3–6 minutes)

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:55)

This short video is Topic E1.11: Non-response and weighting, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:55–1:26)

Here is where we open. 1,000 invited, 300 replied — mostly women, mostly satisfied. Is 70% satisfaction about everyone? The idea, in plain language, is this. Non-response bias arises when responders differ from non-responders on the outcome . A low rate raises the risk; it doesn't prove bias. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:26–1:50)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Compare respondents with the frame on known variables. Compare early and late responders (late ≈ reluctant). Follow up a sample of non-responders if you can. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:50–2:28)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:28–2:56)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:56–3:30)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Bias needs outcome differences. Compare with the frame.

## Beat 7 (3:30–4:03)

That is the one idea for Topic E1.11. # V-T-E1.12 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.12  
**Title:** E1.12: Rank-based tests  
**Word count:** 620  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:08 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic E1.12: Rank-based tests, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled labelled synthetic teaching table on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:24)

Here is where we open. Eight reaction times; one of 800 ms among values near 350. The mean is hijacked. The idea, in plain language, is this. Robust summaries — median, IQR, trimmed mean — are little affected by a few extremes. Report them alongside means when they disagree. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–1:48)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Use them for skewed data, outliers or small n. Disagreement between mean and median is informative. Investigate the extreme value; don't delete silently. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:48–2:38)

The quiet- and social-floor quiz scores from Topics 7.7 and 8.4 have no overlap — the quiet minimum is 69, the social maximum is 66 — so a two-sided Mann-Whitney test gives U = 36, the largest possible with n = 6 and 6, and p about 0.002. A Kruskal-Wallis test on all three floors gives H about 13.56, 2 degrees of freedom, p about 0.0011, in the same direction as the ANOVA F of about 25.12 on Topic 8.6. These are FlippedStat calculations on the labelled synthetic teaching sample, not official CUHK data. The reaction-time hook, the mood-gain worked examples, and the checks on this page were not changed. Do not mix these teaching-sample figures with the labelled book illustrations, such as U = 3.

## Beat 5 (2:38–3:06)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:06–3:34)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Median, IQR, trimmed mean. Report when they disagree.

## Beat 7 (3:34–4:08)

That is the one idea for Topic E1.12. Open #t/E1.12 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M6/T-E1.12_Rank_based_tests.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M6/V-T-E1.12.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-E1.13 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.13  
**Title:** E1.13: Protocols and pre-registration  
**Word count:** 630  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:12 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:58)

This short video is Topic E1.13: Protocols and pre-registration, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 0.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:58–1:31)

Here is where we open. Before the first student is recruited, write down what you'll measure and how you'll analyse it. The idea, in plain language, is this. A protocol and statistical analysis plan pre-specify question, design and randomisation, primary outcome, sample size, analysis and handling of missing data. Pre-registration time-stamps it publicly. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:31–1:52)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Separates confirmatory from exploratory. Prevents outcome switching and p-hacking. Makes null results publishable and credible. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:52–2:29)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:29–2:57)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:57–3:38)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Plan before data. Register it.

## Beat 7 (3:38–4:12)

That is the one idea for Topic E1.13. Open #t/E1.13 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M6/T-E1.13_Protocols_and_pre_registration.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M6/V-T-E1.13.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:29)

Here is where we open. Copilot lab: ask Copilot to design a small study — questionnaire, sampling plan and randomisation. The idea, in plain language, is this. Paste the contract and ask for: a 6–8 item questionnaire with scales, a sampling plan with sample-size arithmetic, and a randomisation plan with a seeded allocation script. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:29–1:53)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Choose a simple question, e.g. “Does a weekly reminder email increase quiz completion?”. Ask it to state every assumption. Save everything before auditing (E1.14.2). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:53–2:31)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:31–2:59)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:59–3:37)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Three drafts: items, sampling, randomisation. Ask for assumptions.

# V-T-E1.15 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.15  
**Title:** E1.15: Audit lab: four classrooms, not forty students  
**Word count:** 620  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:08 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:57)

This short video is Topic E1.15: Audit lab: four classrooms, not forty students, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:57–1:30)

Here is where we open. Audit lab. AI: “The new method works (p < 0.001, n = 40).” The method was assigned to two of four classrooms. The idea, in plain language, is this. Count the experimental units: 4 classrooms. The AI's Welch test treats 40 students as independent — pseudo-replication (H2) . Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:30–1:56)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Student-level t = 5.60, p = 0.0000023. Within-class similarity is high: ICC ≈ 0.62, DEFF ≈ 6.6, effective n ≈ 6.1. Memo line 1: the unit and its count. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:56–2:33)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:33–3:01)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:01–3:34)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. 4 units, not 40. Pseudo-replication = H2.

## Beat 7 (3:34–4:08)

That is the one idea for Topic E1.15. # V-T-E1.16 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.16  
**Title:** E1.16: Post-check and memo  
**Word count:** 572  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 3:49 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:58)

This short video is Topic E1.16: Post-check and memo, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 0.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:58–1:22)

Here is where we open. Parallel post-check for E1. The idea, in plain language, is this. The post-check repeats the E1 pre-check's skills with new items. Compare item types. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:22–1:43)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Tag missed items with their lessons. Most-missed areas are usually units and weighting. Saved in this browser. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:43–2:20)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:20–2:48)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:48–3:15)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Parallel post-check. Tag misses.

## Beat 7 (3:15–3:49)

That is the one idea for Topic E1.16. Open #t/E1.16 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-E1.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.2  
**Title:** E1.2: Elements of an experiment  
**Word count:** 622  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:09 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic E1.2: Elements of an experiment, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:28)

Here is where we open. A study tests a revision app. Is the unit a student, a tutorial or a course? The idea, in plain language, is this. The experimental unit is the smallest entity to which a treatment is independently assigned . It may differ from the observational unit (what is measured). Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–1:54)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Assign a method to a tutorial, measure students: unit = tutorial. n for inference = number of experimental units. Getting the unit wrong is the root of pseudo-replication (E1.3.2). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:54–2:32)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:32–3:00)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:00–3:35)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Unit = what treatment is assigned to. n = number of units.

## Beat 7 (3:35–4:09)

That is the one idea for Topic E1.2. Open #t/E1.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. # V-T-E1.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.3  
**Title:** E1.3: Randomisation, replication and blocking  
**Word count:** 614  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:06 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:59)

This short video is Topic E1.3: Randomisation, replication and blocking, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:59–1:34)

Here is where we open. Students choose whether to use the app. Keen students choose it — and score higher anyway. The idea, in plain language, is this. Random assignment gives every unit the same chance of each treatment. Groups become alike on average in every respect , measured or not, so differences can be attributed to treatment. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:34–1:58)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. It removes selection bias by researchers and participants. It justifies the randomisation test's p-value. Use a seeded computer RNG; record the allocation before outcomes. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:58–2:35)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:35–3:03)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:03–3:32)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. ## Continuous script (for the recording booth)

This short video is Topic E1.3: Randomisation, replication and blocking, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

Here is where we open. Students choose whether to use the app. Keen students choose it — and score higher anyway. The idea, in plain language, is this. Random assignment gives every unit the same chance of each treatment. Groups become alike on average in every respect , measured or not, so differences can be attributed to treatment. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. It removes selection bias by researchers and participants. It justifies the randomisation test's p-value. Use a seeded computer RNG; record the allocation before outcomes. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. # V-T-E1.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.4  
**Title:** E1.4: ANOVA for designed experiments  
**Word count:** 636  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:14 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic E1.4: ANOVA for designed experiments, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:28)

Here is where we open. Three fertilisers on 12 pots over four benches with different light. Bench differences could swamp everything. The idea, in plain language, is this. Completely randomised design: no restriction. Randomised block design: group similar units into blocks, randomise within each — removing block-to-block variation from the error. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–1:53)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Block on what you can't control but expect to matter (bench, class, day). Analyse with blocks in the model. Blocking costs df but can gain much precision. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:53–2:30)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:30–2:58)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:58–3:41)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Block on known nuisance variation. Randomise within blocks.

## Beat 7 (3:41–4:14)

That is the one idea for Topic E1.4. Open #t/E1.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-E1.5/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-E1.5 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.5  
**Title:** E1.5: Factorial designs  
**Word count:** 610  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:04 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:55)

This short video is Topic E1.5: Factorial designs, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:55–1:24)

Here is where we open. Does the app help? Does night study help? The idea, in plain language, is this. A factorial design crosses factors so every combination is tested. Two-factor ANOVA splits variation into A, B, A × B interaction and error. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–1:47)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Efficient: every participant informs both factors. Reveals interaction: whether one factor's effect depends on the other. 2 × 2 needs four cells, randomised. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:47–2:25)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:25–2:53)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:53–3:30)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Cross the factors. Main effects + interaction.

## Beat 7 (3:30–4:04)

That is the one idea for Topic E1.5. Open #t/E1.5 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M6/T-E1.5_Factorial_designs.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M6/V-T-E1.5.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.
