# V-T-E1.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.6  
**Title:** E1.6: Repeated measures, crossover and A/B/n tests  
**Word count:** 604  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:02 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic E1.6: Repeated measures, crossover and A/B/n tests, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:25)

Here is where we open. Students differ hugely in ability. If each tries BOTH apps, each becomes their own control. The idea, in plain language, is this. A within-subject (repeated-measures) design gives every unit every condition; comparisons within units cancel between-person variation. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:25–1:49)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Much more precise: often far fewer participants needed. Analysis: paired t (two conditions); repeated-measures ANOVA or mixed models (more). Risks: order and carry-over (E1.6.2). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:49–2:26)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:26–2:54)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:54–3:28)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Each unit gets every condition. Cancels between-person variation.

## Beat 7 (3:28–4:02)

That is the one idea for Topic E1.6. Open #t/E1.6 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. Simulation route: generate fake data under the assumed effect and design, analyse as planned, count rejections. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–1:53)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Formula is quick for simple designs; simulation handles clusters, attrition and complex analyses. Inflate for attrition and design effect. Power assumptions should be stated and defended. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

Here is where we open. How many students per arm to detect d = 0.4 with 80% power? Formula and simulation. The idea, in plain language, is this. Formula route: n per group ≈ 2(z₁₋α/₂ + z₁₋β)²/d². Simulation route: generate fake data under the assumed effect and design, analyse as planned, count rejections. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Formula is quick for simple designs; simulation handles clusters, attrition and complex analyses. Inflate for attrition and design effect. Power assumptions should be stated and defended. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Formula for simple designs. Simulate for complex ones.

That is the one idea for Topic E1.7. Open #t/E1.7 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. # V-T-E1.8 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.8  
**Title:** E1.8: Questionnaire design and Likert data  
**Word count:** 634  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:14 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:59)

This short video is Topic E1.8: Questionnaire design and Likert data, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:59–1:28)

Here is where we open. “How often do you use AI for assignments?” ChatGPT? Grammar checkers? The idea, in plain language, is this. Good survey items are clear , specific (time frame, behaviour), answerable and neutral . Define terms and give a reference period. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:28–1:52)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. “AI tools such as chatbots (e.g. Copilot), not spell-checkers”. “In the past four weeks”. Ask about behaviour you can recall, not opinions you can't. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:52–2:30)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:30–2:58)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:58–3:40)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Clear, specific, answerable. Define terms, give periods.

## Beat 7 (3:40–4:14)

That is the one idea for Topic E1.8. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-E1.9/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-E1.9 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E1.9  
**Title:** E1.9: Reliability and validity  
**Word count:** 621  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:08 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:55)

This short video is Topic E1.9: Reliability and validity, in official Module 6, Research Design and Non-parametric Methods. It sits in the unit E1: Research Design: Experiments, Surveys and Robust Comparisons. The official map budgets 0.5 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:55–1:27)

Here is where we open. A stress questionnaire gives 32 on Monday and 14 the next Monday, though nothing changed. The idea, in plain language, is this. Reliability is consistency. Test–retest reliability: the same people measured twice under similar conditions; summarised by correlation (or ICC); above about 0.7 often acceptable. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:27–1:52)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Interval too short → memory inflates it; too long → real change deflates it. Unreliable measures attenuate correlations and weaken power. Report reliability with the instrument. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:52–2:29)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:29–2:57)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:57–3:35)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Reliability = consistency. Test–retest r or ICC.

## Beat 7 (3:35–4:08)

That is the one idea for Topic E1.9. Open #t/E1.9 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M6/T-E1.9_Reliability_and_validity.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M6/V-T-E1.9.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-E5.1 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E5.1  
**Title:** E5.1: Pre-check  
**Word count:** 613  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:05 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:56)

This short video is Topic E5.1: Pre-check, in official Module 7, Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit E5: Time Series Analysis and Forecasting. The official map budgets 0.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:56–1:27)

Here is where we open. E5 treats data that arrive in order — and asks when a forecast deserves to be believed. The idea, in plain language, is this. The E5 pre-check: ten items drawn from Weeks 9–11 (correlation, regression, residuals), the ideas E5 builds on. Baseline only. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:27–1:49)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. No notes or AI. Keep your answers; E5.13.1 uses parallel items. Regression residuals reappear as the “residual” component. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:49–2:26)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:26–2:54)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:54–3:32)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Baseline only. Fit is not forecast.

## Beat 7 (3:32–4:05)

That is the one idea for Topic E5.1. Open #t/E5.1 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Many origins. Refit each time.

That is the one idea for Topic E5.10. # V-T-E5.11 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E5.11  
**Title:** E5.11: Copilot lab: a seasonal forecast  
**Word count:** 558  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 3:43 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:50)

This short video is Topic E5.11: Copilot lab: a seasonal forecast, in official Module 7, Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting. It sits in the unit E5: Time Series Analysis and Forecasting. The official map budgets 1.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract (optional practice, keys unchanged) on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:50–1:24)

Here is where we open. Copilot lab: ask Copilot to forecast the synthetic Harbourside file. The idea, in plain language, is this. Upload the file, paste the contract and ask for a time-ordered holdout , two baselines , a SARIMA chosen by AIC and test-only errors . Expect a confident headline; E5.11.2 tests it. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:24–1:46)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Expect an in-sample R² first — ask again for test error. Ask for every setting (order, seasonal_order, period). Log everything. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:46–2:10)

The official monthly Composite CPI extract, hk_cpi_composite_monthly_510-60001.csv, from C and SD table 510-60001, remains available for optional practice, as on Topic E5.2. It is a different series from the keyed Harbourside lab. Do not mix official CPI figures into the Harbourside test MAPE keys: the seasonal naive is 2.76 percent, and SARIMA is 2.34 percent. Those lab keys are unchanged.

## Beat 5 (2:10–2:38)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:38–3:10)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Time-ordered holdout. Baselines.

## Beat 7 (3:10–3:43)

That is the one idea for Topic E5.11. Open #t/E5.11 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.8-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 7e4349bfa0552fd6c896645502e439b627856d8f61616c95362feead4601a9f2 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M7/T-E5.11_Copilot_lab_a_seasonal_forecast.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M7/V-T-E5.11.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.8-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-E5.12 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E5.12  
**Title:** E5.12: Audit lab: the forecast that peeked  
**Word count:** 638  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:15 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:58)

This short video is Topic E5.12: Audit lab: the forecast that peeked, in official Module 7, Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit E5: Time Series Analysis and Forecasting. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:58–1:36)

Here is where we open. Audit lab. AI: “Our model forecasts monthly demand with only 1.19% error.” The idea, in plain language, is this. The AI decomposed the whole series — a centred trend that already used the test months — and scored the same months: H4 overclaim. Re-fitted on the training months only, the forecast error is 3.33% ; repeating last year gives 2.76%. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:36–2:07)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Line 4 (supported): “On the 36 held-back months, the decomposition forecast was off by 3.33% on average, slightly worse than repeating last year (2.76%).” Line 5 (refused): “The model forecasts demand with 1.19% error.” Suggest: holdout plus rolling origin, with a baseline. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:07–2:45)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:45–3:13)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:13–3:42)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Which months were fitted? Re-fit on the past only.

## Beat 7 (3:42–4:15)

That is the one idea for Topic E5.12. Open #t/E5.12 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M7/T-E5.12_Audit_lab_the_forecast_that_peeked.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M7/V-T-E5.12.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:57)

This short video is Topic E5.13: Post-check and memo, in official Module 7, Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit E5: Time Series Analysis and Forecasting. The official map budgets 0.25 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:57–1:23)

Here is where we open. Parallel post-check for E5. The idea, in plain language, is this. The post-check: components, smoothing, decomposition, baselines and error measures, autocorrelation and differencing, ARIMA settings and intervals — new items. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:23–1:44)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Tag misses by lesson. Most-missed: centred vs trailing; MAPE near zero; spurious correlation. Saved in this browser. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:44–2:22)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:22–2:50)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:50–3:30)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. Parallel post-check. Tag misses.

# V-T-E5.2 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E5.2  
**Title:** E5.2: What makes a time series different  
**Word count:** 646  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:18 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic E5.2: What makes a time series different, in official Module 7, Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit E5: Time Series Analysis and Forecasting. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic already uses a labelled official extract (optional practice) on the site. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:34)

Here is where we open. Every earlier week assumed the rows could be listed in any order. Here the order is the data. The idea, in plain language, is this. A time series is a sequence of measurements of one system at successive times, usually at a fixed frequency (daily, monthly). The time index — not a row number — identifies each value. Harbourside demand has 228 monthly values from 2006-01 to 2024-12. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:34–1:59)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Plot it against time first; a line chart, not a histogram. Check frequency, gaps and duplicated dates before modelling. Units matter: GWh per month, not per day. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:59–2:44)

A time series is identified by its date index, not by a row number. The keyed teaching series on this topic remains Harbourside demand: a synthetic Hong Kong series with 228 monthly values, from January 2006 to December 2024. Those keys are unchanged. Beside them, the site offers an official Composite CPI monthly extract, from C and SD table 510-60001, running from January 2015 to September 2026, for date-indexing practice. Do not mix official CPI figures into the keyed Harbourside decompositions. Think Stats US electricity generation stays a labelled textbook illustration. Copyright clearance for book material is a later stage; this video adapts the teaching point and does not copy book prose.

## Beat 5 (2:44–3:12)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:12–3:45)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Values tied to times. Fixed frequency.

## Beat 7 (3:45–4:18)

That is the one idea for Topic E5.2. Open #t/E5.2 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M7/T-E5.2_What_makes_a_time_series_different.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M7/V-T-E5.2.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. # V-T-E5.3 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E5.3  
**Title:** E5.3: Moving averages and smoothing  
**Word count:** 604  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:02 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic E5.3: Moving averages and smoothing, in official Module 7, Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting. It sits in the unit E5: Time Series Analysis and Forecasting. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:27)

Here is where we open. To see the trend, average away the season. The idea, in plain language, is this. A moving average replaces each value with the mean of a window of k consecutive values. A 12-month window covers one full season, so seasonal ups and downs cancel and the trend remains. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:27–1:54)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Longer windows: smoother, slower to react. The first k − 1 values have no full window (11 months lost for k = 12). Excel: =AVERAGE(B2:B13) in row 13, filled down. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:54–2:31)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:31–2:59)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:59–3:28)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Average a sliding window. 12 months removes the season.

## Beat 7 (3:28–4:02)

That is the one idea for Topic E5.3. Open #t/E5.3 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M7/T-E5.3_Moving_averages_and_smoothing.tex. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-E5.4 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E5.4  
**Title:** E5.4: Seasonal decomposition  
**Word count:** 653  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:21 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:57)

This short video is Topic E5.4: Seasonal decomposition, in official Module 7, Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit E5: Time Series Analysis and Forecasting. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:57–1:33)

Here is where we open. Put the three parts together as a sum. The idea, in plain language, is this. The additive model writes y t = T t + S t + R t . The seasonal effects are the same every year and sum to zero, so the size of the seasonal swing does not change with the level. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:33–1:58)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Check the assumption: is the swing roughly constant over the years? Harbourside: yes. Rooftop solar: no (E5.5). T + S is the “expected” value for each month. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:58–2:36)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:36–3:04)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:04–3:48)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. y = T + S + R. Same seasonal effects each year.

## Beat 7 (3:48–4:21)

That is the one idea for Topic E5.4. Open #t/E5.4 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M7/T-E5.4_Seasonal_decomposition.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M7/V-T-E5.4.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

If the seasonal swing grows with the level , model y = T × S × R: seasonal and residual parts are factors around 1. Rooftop solar: swing 14.2 GWh in 2014 versus 151.7 GWh in 2024; multiplicative seasonal factors run from -28.3% to +29.2%. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:31–1:54)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Read factors as percentages above/below trend. Residual factors: 95% within about ±6.1%. Additive on solar leaves a widening residual pattern. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:54–2:31)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:31–2:59)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:59–3:37)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. Swing grows → multiply. Factors around 1.

## Beat 7 (3:37–4:10)

# V-T-E5.6 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E5.6  
**Title:** E5.6: Forecasting and honest evaluation  
**Word count:** 637  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:15 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:58)

This short video is Topic E5.6: Forecasting and honest evaluation, in official Module 7, Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting. It is marked essential on the official map. It sits in the unit E5: Time Series Analysis and Forecasting. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:58–1:35)

Here is where we open. E3.4 introduced time-aware splits; here they are mandatory. The idea, in plain language, is this. Fit on a training series (the past), forecast the test series (the last h months) and compare. Harbourside: train to Dec 2021, test the last 36 months from Jan 2022. Nothing from the test months may touch the model — not even a centred trend. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:35–2:01)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. h should match the use (here, a three-year plan). One split is one exam; E5.10.1 repeats it from many origins. Think Stats uses the last 60 months (five years). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:01–2:39)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:39–3:07)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:07–3:41)

Verification is the skill, not the extra. Under C.R.O.S.S. you count, you recompute, you compare other tools, you test the result against statistical principles, and you record sources and scope. A language model can propose the code or even a number. It cannot be the referee. If a figure matters, you should be able to point to the file, the rule, and the second calculation that supports it. The short close on the page is this. Train on the past. Test on the last h months.

## Beat 7 (3:41–4:15)

That is the one idea for Topic E5.6. ========== FILE: ws/stage8/scripts/topics/V-T-E5.7/NARRATION.md ==========

# V-T-E5.7 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E5.7  
**Title:** E5.7: Autocorrelation  
**Word count:** 607  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:03 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:53)

This short video is Topic E5.7: Autocorrelation, in official Module 7, Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting. It sits in the unit E5: Time Series Analysis and Forecasting. The official map budgets 0.75 hours of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:53–1:31)

Here is where we open. Week 9’s correlation, applied to one series and its past. The idea, in plain language, is this. Shift a series by k steps to get its lag-k copy. The correlation between them is the autocorrelation at lag k; at lag 1 it is called serial correlation . Year-over-year Harbourside changes: lag 1 r = 0.572, lag 2 0.378, lag 3 0.225. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:31–1:54)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Positive lag-1 r: highs follow highs. Compute on a series without trend/season, or the r is dominated by them. Excel: =CORREL(B3:B229, B2:B228). If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:54–2:32)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:32–3:00)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:00–3:29)

Before you trust a number from a tool, walk C.R.O.S.S. Count. Recompute. Other tools. Statistical principles. Sources and scope. That last item matters on this topic: official figures, FlippedStat calculations on official figures, synthetic Hong Kong examples, and labelled book illustrations must stay distinct. The model can help you draft; you still have to verify. The short close on the page is this. Lag = shifted copy. Autocorrelation = corr with own past.

## Beat 7 (3:29–4:03)

That is the one idea for Topic E5.7. Open #t/E5.7 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M7/T-E5.7_Autocorrelation.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M7/V-T-E5.7.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-E5.8 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E5.8  
**Title:** E5.8: Autoregression and differencing  
**Word count:** 635  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:14 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic E5.8: Autoregression and differencing, in official Module 7, Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting. It sits in the unit E5: Time Series Analysis and Forecasting. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:33)

Here is where we open. The first idea of autoregression: the future will be like the past — last June predicts next June. The idea, in plain language, is this. The seasonal difference d t = y t − y t−12 removes a stable season and most of a slow trend. Harbourside differences have SD 104.9 GWh versus 343.0 GWh for the raw series — easier to predict. Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:33–1:52)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Lose the first 12 months. Differences can be negative. Excel: =B14-B2 filled down. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (1:52–2:30)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:30–2:58)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (2:58–3:40)

This course uses a simple contract, written C.R.O.S.S. Count the rows and the missing cells. Recompute the figure in a second tool, or by hand when the example is small. Try other tools if two answers disagree — agreement between two language models is not a check. Ask whether the method matches statistical principles, not only whether the sentence sounds plausible. And record your sources and the scope: an official extract, a synthetic Hong Kong example, or a labelled book illustration. AI can draft the code; you verify the number. The short close on the page is this. d = y − y(t−12). Removes stable season.

## Beat 7 (3:40–4:14)

That is the one idea for Topic E5.8. Open #t/E5.8 on the FlippedStat site and work the checks there, using build/FlippedStat_v10.7-dev_standalone.html — SHA-256 eee89a12f31e167a95e9bb5521627ab14ad649131ad930b5544434b9e4b06632 — or a later standalone if one has been issued. The matching short Beamer deck is stage8/slides/topics/M7/T-E5.8_Autoregression_and_differencing.tex. The editable OpenShot project is stage8/openshot/projects/M7/V-T-E5.8.osp, still a still sequence, not a finished film. The end-card version line is FlippedStat v9.9 / v10.7-dev. Do not claim accessibility conformance, psychometric validity, or institutional approval. When you are ready, go to the page, and verify.

# V-T-E5.9 — narration

**video_id:** V-T-E5.9  
**Title:** E5.9: ARIMA and SARIMA  
**Word count:** 649  
**Estimated duration at 150 words/minute:** 4:20 (target 3–6 minutes)  

Read in a warm, unhurried, conversational tone, as if talking a student through a blackboard. Do not rush the numbers. Pause briefly on every green verified figure and every red error.

## Beat 1 (0:00–0:54)

This short video is Topic E5.9: ARIMA and SARIMA, in official Module 7, Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting. It sits in the unit E5: Time Series Analysis and Forecasting. The official map budgets 1 hour of study time for the page, not for this video. This topic is mostly methods, assessment, or course framing. Where a dataset appears, keep its official, synthetic, or book label as it is on the page. I will stay with one idea, in English, in a few minutes. I will not invent official statistics, I will not copy textbook prose, and I will not change cut scores, certificate wording, or other items that wait for a human decision. When a figure is used, it is a figure already on the FlippedStat page, or a labelled FlippedStat calculation on an official extract.

## Beat 2 (0:54–1:33)

Here is where we open. The hand-built model in E5.8 is a SARIMA. One function fits it. The idea, in plain language, is this. ARIMA(y, order=(p, d, q), seasonal_order=(P, D, Q, s)): p AR lags, d ordinary differences, q MA lags; P, D, Q the seasonal counterparts with period s . Think Stats’ model: order = ([1, 2, 3], 0, [1, 6]), seasonal_order = (0, 1, 0, 12). Hold that idea before you ask a tool for a number. In this course, understanding comes first, a draft from a language model comes second, and verification comes third.

## Beat 3 (1:33–2:01)

Once you have the idea, here is how to read a result on this topic. Lists select specific lags; integers mean “lags 1 to p”. R: arima(y, order = c(3,0,0), seasonal = list(order = c(0,1,0), period = 12)). Estimation is by maximum likelihood, so numbers differ slightly from E5.8’s OLS. If a sentence on a slide or in a tool output skips that reading, pause and put the reading back in.

## Beat 4 (2:01–2:39)

The worked path lives on the topic page, with whatever official extract, synthetic Hong Kong example, or labelled book illustration that page already uses. This short video will not invent a new numerical example, and it will not copy a textbook paragraph to fill the time. When you open the page, look first at the label on the dataset, then at the question, then at the figure. If a number matters, recompute it. If a figure you expected is not spoken here, that is deliberate: treat the page as the source, not this narration.

## Beat 5 (2:39–3:07)

A common mistake is to treat a draft from a tool as the answer, or to quote a number without its unit, its n, and its source. Another is to mix an official extract with a synthetic file, or with a labelled book illustration, and then talk as if they were one dataset. If you feel rushed, that is usually the moment to slow down, not to skip the check.

## Beat 6 (3:07–3:46)

Keep the C.R.O.S.S. habit close at hand. Count what went into the figure. Recompute it, preferably in a tool you did not use to draft the first answer. Use other tools when two results disagree. Check the statistical principle, not the polish of the sentence. And write down the source and the scope, so an official extract is never mixed with a synthetic file or a book illustration. The rule of the course is short: AI writes, you verify. The short close on the page is this. order = (p, d, q). seasonal_order = (P, D, Q, s).

========== FILE: ws/stage8/slides/README.md ==========

# FlippedStat Beamer slides (Stage 8)

These are **editable LaTeX Beamer sources** for official Modules 1–8. Platform is Beamer, not PowerPoint or Google Slides. English only in this pass.

There are two products in this folder:

| Product | Where | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| **Module-length decks** | `M1_Statistical_Thinking.tex` … `M8_Responsible_Ethical_AI.tex` | One long source per official module, with a section per official topic (about 5–8 frames each inside the module file). |
| **Short per-topic decks** | `topics/M1/` … `topics/M8/` | One standalone short deck per official topic, plus one short overview deck per module to pair with the overview video scaffolds. |

Both reuse `theme/beamerthemeFlippedStat.sty`. Official reportable units are Modules 1–8 (153 official topics + 8 module overviews). Optional Module 9 is not generated in this official folder (human item H1 remains open).


**18 November 2026 (Asia/Hong_Kong):** short decks and the eight module-length files were regenerated from the v10.7-dev catalogue (`tools/extract_stage8_catalog.py`, then `build_topic_tex.py` and `build_tex.py`). Official Hong Kong data illustrations for the wave 1–4 topics (1.3, 2.1, 2.2, 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 6.3, 6.5, 9.7, 10.3, 10.6, 11.4, E5.2) are stored in `stage8/hk_official_frames.json` and re-injected on rebuild. No PDFs: there is no TeX engine in this environment (see `topics/COMPILE_STATUS.md`). Optional Module 9 decks were not generated. Footer rules are unchanged: self-paced draft, no crest, no implied approval. Cut scores and certificate wording are not redefined.

The footer and title page state that this is a **self-paced resource** from the CUHK department that maintains FlippedStat, and that **this draft is not itself an institutional approval**. Do not add a crest or lockup that would imply approval.

Official hours, KPIs, licences, placement cut scores and certificate wording are not redefined here.

## Theme

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `theme/beamerthemeFlippedStat.sty` | Layout, header/footer, title page. Short decks may set `\FSmodulenumber` so the footer shows the official module number; module-length decks leave the default (the section counter). |
| `theme/beamercolorthemeFlippedStat.sty` | Navy text, teal highlights, amber warnings, red errors, green verified numbers |
| `theme/beamerfontthemeFlippedStat.sty` | Title and body sizes |

## Module-length decks

Each module file opens with the official learning outcomes and the official topic list, then a short run of teaching frames per topic (condensed from the FlippedStat topic pages, not copied from a textbook). Overflow uses Beamer's `allowframebreaks`. An appendix lists essential topics and editing notes.

Regenerate the eight module `.tex` files from `../catalog/topic_frames.json`:

```bash
# from the FlippedStat_v99 folder
python3 tools/extract_stage8_catalog.py   # prefers v10.7-dev (or v10.8-dev if present)
python3 stage8/slides/build_tex.py
```

Re-running `build_tex.py` overwrites the eight module `.tex` files. Keep local edits in a copy or a git branch if you have changed wording by hand. The short-deck generator does **not** touch these eight files.

Compile with `sh compile_slides.sh`, or:

```bash
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode M1_Statistical_Thinking.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode M1_Statistical_Thinking.tex
```

## Short per-topic decks

Layout (161 official sources):

```
topics/M1/M1_overview.tex
topics/M1/T-1.1_Course_map_and_placement.tex
topics/M1/T-1.2_What_statistics_is.tex
…
topics/M8/T-14.6_Revision_reflection_and_exit_survey.tex
topics/manifest.csv
topics/manifest.json
```

Each short topic deck is meant for self-study of one official topic: a title frame, about four to eight teaching frames, and a closing “check / next step” frame that points at the site hash and the next official topic in the module. Teaching frames are condensed from `stage8/catalog/topic_frames.json` (and so from the topic pages), not copied from a textbook.

Nine companion case topics in Module 6 (C4.1–C4.9) have thin extracted lesson fields. Their short decks are honest and shorter (title, map metadata, the official outline, and a check / next step). They do not invent worked numbers. Open the site page for the worked path.

The eight short overview decks list official outcomes, the official topic map, essential topics, and the module checks. They are the slide companion for the existing `V-M1-OV` … `V-M8-OV` OpenShot scaffolds.

The inventory is `topics/manifest.csv` (topic id, title, module, kind, tex path, frame count, compile status).

Regenerate the short decks (this does not overwrite the eight module-length files):

```bash
# from the FlippedStat_v99 folder
python3 tools/extract_stage8_catalog.py   # if the official map or topic pages changed
python3 stage8/slides/build_topic_tex.py
```

The catalog extract taken from v10.1-dev still contains the stale phrase “177 topics” in topic 1.1. `build_topic_tex.py` replaces that with the current site fact (231 topics on this site: 24 units after the C4.10/C4.11 and D1 patches). Official reportable modules remain 1–8. Re-extracting the catalog after a site fix will make the substitution a no-op.

Compile a sample (one overview, one typical topic, one thin companion topic):

```bash
sh stage8/slides/compile_topic_slides.sh sample
```

Or compile one file / all official short decks:

```bash
sh stage8/slides/compile_topic_slides.sh M1/T-1.1_Course_map_and_placement.tex
sh stage8/slides/compile_topic_slides.sh
```

Each short source sets `\input@path` to `../../theme/`, so compile it from its `topics/M?/` folder (the script does this).

If a TeX engine could not be installed in the environment that generated these files, PDFs may be absent. The `.tex` sources are still complete and are the deliverable to edit.

## How to compile (engine)

You need a TeX engine with the **Beamer** class (TeX Live is enough). XeLaTeX also works:

```bash
xelatex -interaction=nonstopmode M1_Statistical_Thinking.tex
```

On Debian/Ubuntu, one typical install is:

```bash
sudo apt-get install texlive-latex-recommended texlive-latex-extra texlive-fonts-recommended
```

A previous TeX Live apt install in this environment failed on Debian InRelease 500 / unsigned mirrors. If install fails, the `.tex` sources remain the deliverable.

========== FILE: ws/stage8/slides/build_tex.py ==========

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Generate editable Beamer sources for FlippedStat Modules 1-8.

Usage (from the repository root or from this folder):
    python3 stage8/slides/build_tex.py
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import re
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
ROOT = HERE.parents[1]
CATALOG = ROOT / "stage8" / "catalog" / "topic_frames.json"
OFFICIAL_FRAMES_JSON = ROOT / "stage8" / "hk_official_frames.json"

UNSAFE = {
    "–": "--",
    "—": "---",
    "−": "-",
    "‐": "-",
    "‑": "-",
    "‘": "'",
    "’": "'",
    "“": "``",
    "”": "''",
    "…": "...",
    "×": " x ",
    "÷": " / ",
    "≤": r"$\leq$",
    "≥": r"$\geq$",
    "≠": r"$\neq$",
    "±": r"$\pm$",
    "μ": r"$\mu$",
    "ρ": r"$\rho$",
    "σ": r"$\sigma$",
    "χ": r"$\chi$",
    "α": r"$\alpha$",
    "β": r"$\beta$",
    "λ": r"$\lambda$",
    "θ": r"$\theta$",
    "π": r"$\pi$",
    "²": r"$^{2}$",
    "³": r"$^{3}$",
    "°": r"$^{\circ}$",
    "·": r"$\cdot$",
    "•": "-",
    "→": r"$\rightarrow$",
    "←": r"$\leftarrow$",
    "↔": r"$\leftrightarrow$",
    "≈": r"$\approx$",
    "∞": r"$\infty$",
    "\u00a0": " ",
    "\u202f": " ",
    "✓": "OK",
    "✗": "X",
    "−99": "-99",
}

LATEX_SPECIAL = re.compile(r"([#$%&_{}])")


def esc(s: str) -> str:
    if s is None:
        return ""
    s = str(s)
    from unicode_fold import fold as _fold  # v10.9-dev: pdflatex-safe glyphs
    for a, b in UNSAFE.items():
        s = s.replace(a, b)
    # After unicode fold, escape TeX specials but keep already-inserted math.
    out = []
    math = False
    for ch in s:
        if ch == "$":
            math = not math
            out.append(ch)
            continue
        if math:
            out.append(ch)
            continue
        if ch in "#%&_{}":
            out.append("\\" + ch)
        elif ch == "\\":
            out.append(r"\textbackslash{}")
        elif ch == "~":
            out.append(r"\textasciitilde{}")
        elif ch == "^":
            out.append(r"\textasciicircum{}")
        else:
            out.append(ch)
    s = "".join(out)
    s = re.sub(r"[\x00-\x08\x0b\x0c\x0e-\x1f]", " ", s)
    return _fold(s)


def hours_s(h):
    if h is None:
        return ""
    try:
        x = float(h)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return ""
    if abs(x - round(x)) < 1e-6:
        return f"{int(round(x))} h"
    return f"{x:.2f} h".rstrip("0").rstrip(".") + " h" if False else f"{x:.2f} h"


SLUG = {
    1: "Statistical_Thinking",
    2: "Descriptive_Statistics",
    3: "Probability_Distributions",
    4: "Estimation_Hypothesis_Testing",
    5: "Correlation_Regression",
    6: "Research_Design_Nonparametric",
    7: "Time_Series_Forecasting",
    8: "Responsible_Ethical_AI",
}


PREAMBLE = r"""\documentclass[aspectratio=169,11pt]{beamer}
%% FlippedStat Module %(mod)s -- editable teaching slides (English).
%% Compile (from this folder, after a TeX Live + Beamer install):
%%   pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode %(file)s
%%   pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode %(file)s
%% XeLaTeX also works if you have it:
%%   xelatex -interaction=nonstopmode %(file)s
\usepackage[T1]{fontenc}
\usepackage[utf8]{inputenc}
\usepackage{lmodern}
\usepackage[english]{babel}
\makeatletter
\def\input@path{{theme/}}
\makeatother
\usetheme{FlippedStat}

\title{%(title)s}
\subtitle{Module %(mod)s teaching slides -- FlippedStat draft}
\author{FlippedStat course team}
\institute{The Chinese University of Hong Kong\\[0.3em]
\textit{Self-paced resource. This draft is not itself an institutional approval.}}
\date{2026-11-18}

\begin{document}
\frame{\titlepage}
"""


def bullets(lines, limit=6):
    lines = [ln for ln in lines if ln and str(ln).strip()]
    if not lines:
        return ""
    out = ["\\begin{itemize}"]
    for ln in lines[:limit]:
        out.append("  \\item " + esc(ln))
    out.append("\\end{itemize}")
    return "\n".join(out)


def load_official_frames() -> dict:
    if not OFFICIAL_FRAMES_JSON.exists():
        return {}
    return json.loads(OFFICIAL_FRAMES_JSON.read_text(encoding="utf8"))


OFFICIAL_FRAMES = load_official_frames()


def write_module(mod: dict, out_path: Path):
    n = mod["n"]
    fname = out_path.name
    parts = [
        PREAMBLE
        % {
            "mod": n,
            "file": fname,
            "title": esc(f"Module {n}: {mod['title']}"),
        }
    ]
    # Outcomes
    parts.append("\\section{Module overview}\n")
    parts.append("\\begin{frame}{Learning outcomes}\n")
    parts.append("{\\small Official outcomes for Module~%d.}\n" % n)
    parts.append(bullets(mod.get("outcomes") or []))
    parts.append("\\end{frame}\n\n")

    # Topic map
    topics = mod["topics"]
    parts.append("\\begin{frame}[allowframebreaks]{Official topics}\n")
    parts.append(
        "{\\small %d official topics. A module is complete when at least 80\\%% of its topics are marked done on the site.}\n"
        % len(topics)
    )
    parts.append("\\begin{itemize}\n")
    for t in topics:
        flag = " {\\color{FSteal}\\textbf{(essential)}}" if t.get("essential") else ""
        hrs = hours_s(t.get("hours"))
        hrs = f" [{esc(hrs)}]" if hrs else ""
        parts.append(f"  \\item \\textbf{{{esc(t['id'])}}} {esc(t['title'])}{hrs}{flag}\n")
    parts.append("\\end{itemize}\n\\end{frame}\n\n")

    if mod.get("checks"):
        parts.append("\\begin{frame}{Checks in this module}\n")
        parts.append(esc(mod["checks"]) + "\n")
        parts.append("\\end{frame}\n\n")

    if mod.get("note"):
        parts.append("\\begin{frame}[allowframebreaks]{Module note}\n")
        parts.append("{\\small " + esc(mod["note"]) + "}\n")
        parts.append("\\end{frame}\n\n")

    for t in topics:
        tid = t["id"]
        title = t.get("title") or tid
        parts.append("\\section{" + esc(tid) + " " + esc(title) + "}\n")
        parts.append("\\begin{frame}{" + esc(tid) + ": " + esc(title) + "}\n")
        meta = []
        if t.get("essential"):
            meta.append("Essential topic on the official map.")
        if t.get("hours"):
            meta.append("Scheduled study time on the map: " + hours_s(t["hours"]) + ".")
        if t.get("activity"):
            meta.append("Activity type: " + t["activity"] + ".")
        if meta:
            parts.append("{\\small " + esc(" ".join(meta)) + "}\n\n")
        if t.get("ilos"):
            parts.append("\\textbf{Linked learning outcomes}\n")
            parts.append(bullets(t["ilos"], 5))
        else:
            parts.append("Open this topic on the site at {\\color{FSteal}\\texttt{" + esc(t.get("hash") or f"#t/{tid}") + "}}.\n")
        parts.append("\\end{frame}\n\n")

        fr = t.get("frames") or {}
        # Teaching frames -- condensed from the site, not a textbook extract.
        body_frames = []
        if fr.get("bridge"):
            body_frames.append(("Why we open here", [fr["bridge"]], "block"))
        if fr.get("concept"):
            body_frames.append(("The idea, in brief", [fr["concept"]], "block"))
        if fr.get("interp"):
            body_frames.append(("How to read it", fr["interp"], "block"))
        if body_frames:
            # One or two frames depending on length
            parts.append("\\begin{frame}[allowframebreaks]{" + esc(tid) + " --- teaching frames}\n")
            parts.append("{\\footnotesize Condensed from the FlippedStat topic page; paraphrase for teaching, not a verbatim extract.}\n")
            for heading, lines, _kind in body_frames:
                parts.append("\\begin{block}{" + esc(heading) + "}\n")
                if len(lines) == 1:
                    parts.append(esc(lines[0]) + "\n")
                else:
                    parts.append(bullets(lines, 4))
                parts.append("\\end{block}\n")
            parts.append("\\end{frame}\n\n")

        if tid in OFFICIAL_FRAMES:
            parts.append(OFFICIAL_FRAMES[tid].rstrip() + "\n\n")

        if fr.get("pitfalls"):
            parts.append("\\begin{frame}{" + esc(tid) + " --- common mistakes}\n")
            parts.append("\\begin{alertblock}{Watch for}\n")
            parts.append(bullets(fr["pitfalls"], 4))
            parts.append("\\end{alertblock}\n\\end{frame}\n\n")

        if fr.get("summary"):
            parts.append("\\begin{frame}{" + esc(tid) + " --- take-away}\n")
            parts.append("\\begin{exampleblock}{A short close}\n")
            parts.append(esc(fr["summary"]) + "\n")
            parts.append("\\end{exampleblock}\n\\end{frame}\n\n")

        subs = t.get("subs") or []
        if subs:
            parts.append("\\begin{frame}[allowframebreaks]{" + esc(tid) + " --- subtopics}\n")
            parts.append("{\\small Official subtopic list. Worked examples and checks stay on the site.}\n")
            parts.append("\\begin{itemize}\n")
            for s in subs:
                parts.append("  \\item \\textbf{" + esc(s['no']) + "} " + esc(s.get('title') or '') + "\n")
            parts.append("\\end{itemize}\n")
            parts.append(
                "\\vspace{0.4em}Open {\\color{FSteal}\\texttt{"
                + esc(t.get("hash") or f"#t/{tid}")
                + "}} in FlippedStat for the worked path and verification steps.\n"
            )
            parts.append("\\end{frame}\n\n")
        elif not (fr.get("concept") or fr.get("interp")):
            parts.append("\\begin{frame}{" + esc(tid) + " --- on the site}\n")
            parts.append(
                "This topic is listed on the official module map. Teaching frames were thin in the extracted lesson fields, so the site page is the source of depth.\n\n"
            )
            parts.append(
                "Open {\\color{FSteal}\\texttt{"
                + esc(t.get("hash") or f"#t/{tid}")
                + "}}.\n"
            )
            parts.append("\\end{frame}\n\n")

    # Appendix
    parts.append("\\section{Appendix}\n")
    parts.append("\\begin{frame}{Essential topics}\n")
    parts.append("{\\small These topics are marked essential on the official module map.}\n")
    parts.append(bullets(mod.get("essential") or ["(none listed)"], 12))
    parts.append("\\end{frame}\n\n")
    parts.append("\\begin{frame}{How to use these slides}\n")
    parts.append(
        """\\begin{itemize}
  \\item Edit the \\texttt{.tex} in this folder; the theme lives in \\texttt{theme/}.
  \\item Rebuild with \\texttt{pdflatex} twice, or \\texttt{xelatex} once.
  \\item Do not add a crest or lockup that would imply CUHK has approved this draft.
  \\item Official hours, KPIs, licences, placement cut scores and certificate wording stay on the site and are not redefined here.
  \\item English only in this pass.
\\end{itemize}
\\end{frame}\n
\\end{document}\n"""
    )
    out_path.write_text("".join(parts), encoding="utf8")


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--catalog", type=Path, default=CATALOG)
    ap.add_argument("--out", type=Path, default=HERE)
    args = ap.parse_args()
    data = json.loads(args.catalog.read_text(encoding="utf8"))
    args.out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    written = []
    for mod in data["modules"]:
        if mod["n"] > 8:
            continue
        slug = SLUG[mod["n"]]
        path = args.out / f"M{mod['n']}_{slug}.tex"
        write_module(mod, path)
        written.append(path)
        print("wrote", path.relative_to(ROOT), "topics", len(mod["topics"]))
    print("done", len(written), "module sources")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
